All four points are present: (1) the answer ties validity to the ground and its evidence, distinguishing a sale or offer for sale with vacant possession from a contract of sale (conditional vs unconditional, with the 14-day windows) and saying the notice needs the required documentary evidence; (2) it states 'The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given'; (3) it states the withdrawal 'must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person it was given to'; (4) it gives next steps, including asking the landlord to sign a withdrawal and challenging the notice at VCAT within 30 days.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, you probably don't have to pay the higher rent yet. A rent increase needs a valid written notice, and an email saying the rent is going up may not be one. The documents don't say what happens if no valid notice was ever given.

Both laws below were in force on 1 October 2025. The Act is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version 110, in force from 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Regulations are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version 004, in force from 1 July 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Written notice is required.** A rental provider must give at least 60 days' notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **The notice must include specific details.** It must state the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and your right to apply to the Director within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Only one increase per notice.** A notice may only provide for one rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No more than one increase every 12 months.** The rent can't be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Invalid increases.** A rent increase made in contravention of these rules is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Prescribed form.** The notice must use Form 5, which states that a valid notice is required for all rent increases [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Who must give it.** On Form 5, the rental provider's name "cannot be the agent's name," although the agent's address may be used for service [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

### Do you have to pay, and from when?

- **Not unless a valid notice was given.** An informal email or a verbal "no" to your negotiation is not a notice in the prescribed form. Based on the documents, an increase without a valid notice would be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Timing if a valid notice is served.** The notice must give at least 60 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 5 requires you to pay the increased amount from the start date on the notice, unless VCAT decides otherwise, if you apply to VCAT [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). So the earliest date would be the start date stated on a valid notice, and that date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given.
- **Documents don't cover the rest.** The documents don't say when an increase would take effect if no valid notice was ever given, whether the agent's email could count as notice, or how the 12-month rule applies to your tenancy, since I don't know your last increase date. They also don't cover back-rent claims.

### What you can do

1. **Ask for the formal notice in writing.** Check that it is on Form 5, is from the rental provider (not the agent), states the amount, the calculation method, and the start date, and was given at least 60 days before that date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Apply for an investigation if you get a valid notice.** You can apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given, if you think the proposed rent is excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Form 5 gives the address GPO Box 123 Melbourne 3001, the email renting@justice.vic.gov.au, and the phone number 1300 558 181 for Consumer Affairs Victoria [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **Apply to VCAT if needed.** After the Director's report, you can apply to VCAT within 30 days after receiving the report. You can also apply directly to VCAT with leave if there are reasonable grounds [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **Get advice.** Because the documents don't cover every scenario, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre to check your specific situation.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't allow you to quietly arrange a repair without telling the owner. They also don't say anything about the owner's insurance.

I've applied the versions in force on 15 October 2026: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* Authorised Version No. 115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* Authorised Version No. 009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Damage is a breach.** A renter and their visitors "must not intentionally or negligently cause damage" to rented premises. Fair wear and tear is excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether chewing by your dog counts as negligent damage depends on the facts, but it is not fair wear and tear.
- **You must give written notice.** A renter must give written notice to the rental provider "as soon as practicable after becoming aware of" damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The notice must state the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Notice can be given electronically under the *Electronic Transactions (Victoria) Act 2000* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs.** The Regulations' summary states that "only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Self-arranged repairs are limited to urgent repairs.** A renter may arrange urgent repairs only if they have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to repair immediately and the provider cannot be reached or does not act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The statutory list of urgent repairs covers things like burst water services, gas leaks, and dangerous electrical faults [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Chewed skirting boards do not appear on that list.
- **The owner can repair and charge you.** If damage is caused by the renter's failure to take care, the provider can give a repair notice. This must be in writing and state the nature of the damage, that it was caused by the renter's failure to take care, and the 14-day repair period [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the renter does not repair it "in a proper and tradesman-like manner" within 14 days, the provider may repair it at the renter's expense, and the renter is liable for the reasonable costs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Notify the owner or agent in writing now**, describing the damage (skirting boards chewed) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Include photos.
2. **Offer to repair it yourself** or ask the owner to arrange it. If you are repairing, the Act's repair-notice process gives you 14 days after a repair notice to repair the damage in a tradesman-like manner [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Any work should be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check the end-of-tenancy duties.** At the end of the agreement, you must leave the premises "as far as practicable" reasonably clean and in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner must complete the final condition report within 10 days after the end date, and must allow you to attend if possible [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- **Insurance:** Nothing in the retrieved documents addresses the owner's property insurance or whether this damage would affect a claim. You should ask the owner or check your lease and their policy terms.
- **Your specific lease:** I haven't seen your agreement, so any additional terms in it are not covered here.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't set a limit on the number of circuits a rental needs. The electrical rule that applies from 29 March 2023 is about how outlets and lighting are protected, and the documents don't say how many circuits that requires. On 1 March 2023 that rule was not yet in force. You can still ask your landlord to check the wiring under the electrical safety and repair duties.

**What the law says**

- **Upcoming rule (not yet in force on 1 March 2023):** The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 002, S.R. No. 3/2021) say: "On and from 29 March 2023, in relation to electrical safety, all power outlets and lighting circuits in the rented premises are to be connected to (a) a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000... and (b) a switchboard-type Residual Current Device that complies with" one of several listed standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). This is a rental minimum standard in Schedule 4, clause 9 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The documents do not say how many circuits are required.
- **Landlord's duty to comply:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 101, current to 7 September 2022) requires the landlord to ensure the premises comply with the rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The landlord must also ensure the premises are "provided and maintained in good repair" and in a "reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks:** The landlord must ensure an electrical safety check of the electrical installations and fittings it provides "is conducted every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician" and must give you the date of the most recent check in writing on request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If no check has been done within the last 2 years when you move in, the landlord "must arrange an electrical safety check as soon as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). You must notify the landlord in writing as soon as practicable of damage or a breakdown of facilities or equipment the landlord supplies [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**What you can ask or do**

1. **Give written notice now.** Tell the landlord in writing about the breaker tripping. The Act requires written notice "as soon as practicable" after you become aware of damage or a breakdown of facilities or equipment [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for an electrical safety check.** Request the date of the most recent electrical safety check in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If there has been no check in the last 2 years, the landlord must arrange one as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask for the wiring to be assessed as an urgent repair.** Urgent repairs include failure or breakdown of "any essential service or appliance provided for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Whether a tripping circuit counts as urgent is not clearly stated, so get a qualified electrician's assessment in writing to support the request.
4. **If the landlord doesn't act:** For urgent repairs, you may arrange them yourself if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and they haven't. You may then be reimbursed for the reasonable cost up to $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). You may also apply to VCAT for an order if you cannot meet the cost, the cost is over $2500, or the landlord refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
5. **For non-urgent repairs:** If the landlord doesn't carry out repairs within 14 days of receiving notice, you may apply to the Director to investigate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). You may also apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:** They don't state how many circuits a rental must have, or whether a shared circuit for a kettle and heater breaches the standard. An electrician would need to assess that.

The output says "The documents don't set a limit on the number of circuits a rental needs," which addresses the circuit-number point, since a statement that the documents do not set a rule counts. question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say whether a rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. They do set rules for charging residents for services, which may apply to you.

**Which law applies:** On 15 October 2026, the version of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* in force is Authorised Version (version) 115, which took effect on 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023* (version 002, in force from 1 December 2024) also apply [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says:**

- **Utility charges:** An operator may charge for electricity, gas and water only if the operator pays those bills, the room is separately metered, and the charge is no more than the supplier's charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This covers utilities, not washing machines.
- **Service charges:** If an operator charges for services, they must give you a separate schedule of those charges before you move in. If you use a service, they must give you an itemised account of your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Service charges by public housing bodies:** Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may charge for laundry services in a declared rooming house only where use can't practicably be measured. Any such charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This likely doesn't apply to a private operator, but I can't confirm your operator's status from the documents.
- **Laundry standard:** From 26 February 2024, a rooming house must provide a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, based on the maximum number of residents it can accommodate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether that machine must be free.
- **House rules:** An operator may make house rules about the use and enjoyment of facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Changes need at least 7 days' written notice, and the rules must be reasonable and enforced consistently and fairly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Excessive usage:** If a fault causes excessive usage charges, the operator is liable for the extra amount, but only if you notified them as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask:**

1. Ask the operator whether the machines are free or charged, and whether the charge appears in your written schedule of services. If you weren't given that schedule before moving in, you can ask for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. If a charge is made, ask for itemised accounts showing your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. If a house rule about the machines seems unreasonable, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for an order declaring it unreasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents I retrieved refer to "the Tribunal" but don't name it, so please check that with an official source.
4. If the machines are broken, report it to the operator [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your right to recover costs for excessive charges caused by faults is described above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Gap:** The retrieved documents don't address coin-operated washing machines or whether they can be charged for. For a definite answer, check the full Act and regulations or contact Consumer Affairs Victoria.

---

**Sources:**
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026)
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, version 002 (in force from 1 December 2024)

It notes that 'the documents don't say whether that machine must be free'. It states that operators 'must give you a separate schedule of those charges before you move in'. For the hardest point, the next step, it advises: 'ask... whether the charge appears in your written schedule of services. If you weren't given that schedule before moving in, you can ask for it.'

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether it's lawful to advertise a property with visible mould. They also don't say whether a photo alone proves a breach of the minimum standards. Both versions I relied on were in force on 1 October 2025: the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (version 004, in force from 1 July 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) and the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (version 110, in force from 6 August 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Mould standard:** Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). This is in Schedule 4 (Rental minimum standards) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty before occupation:** A provider "must ensure that rented premises comply with prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day on which the renter enters into occupation" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading advertising:** A provider must not induce someone to enter a lease through "misleading or deceptive conduct" or a false or misleading representation about "the characteristics of the premises" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Photos that accurately show mould are not obviously misleading, but the documents don't address whether they are permitted.

**What the renter can do or ask**

- If the premises don't meet the standards on or just after move-in, the renter "may issue a request to the residential rental provider for urgent repairs" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Before moving in, the provider must give a condition report specifying "the state of repair and general condition of the premises" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If it is signed by both parties, it is "conclusive evidence" of that state of repair on the day specified [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Ask for one to record the mould in writing.
- Within 30 days after a lease starts, either party may apply to the Tribunal to amend a condition report that is inaccurate or incomplete [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Is the photo enough?**

The documents don't answer this. They don't say how mould must be proven, whether advertising photos count as evidence, or whether a photo shows the mould is "caused by or related to the building structure," which the standard requires [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo is useful evidence, but the documents don't say it is sufficient on its own. The renter would need to show the condition existed and relates to the building structure, and the documents don't set out how to do that.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The output quotes the standard that each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure". It gives next steps, including that the renter "may issue a request to the residential rental provider for urgent repairs" and should ask for a condition report recording the mould.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act, your landlord (the "residential rental provider") can give you a notice to vacate for an unauthorised occupant, but the documents don't say what a renter must do to remove a friend who isn't a party to the lease. They also don't say whether an unpaid friend staying with you counts as a sub-letting. This answer uses the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115 (incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 15 October 2026.

**What the law says**

- A renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the landlord's written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- An assignment or sub-letting without that consent is invalid unless the Tribunal (VCAT) has determined consent is not required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The landlord may give you a notice to vacate if you have assigned or sub-let, or purported to, without consent. The notice must specify a termination date at least 14 days after it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A valid notice to vacate must be in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to you, signed by the landlord or their agent, state the reason(s), and specify the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The Regulations say the same thing in plain terms: you must not assign or sub-let without written consent, and the landlord may give you a notice to vacate if you do [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- You can challenge a notice to vacate by applying to the Tribunal within 30 days after it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask your friend to leave.** The documents don't set out a process for a renter to remove a non-party occupant, so check your agreement and get advice on your options.
2. **Be aware of the risk to your tenancy.** If the agent or landlord learns of the arrangement, they may give you a notice to vacate under the 14-day rule above. Also, a breach of your duties can lead to other consequences under the Act, which the documents don't cover in detail.
3. **Seek consent instead, if you want them to stay.** You can ask the landlord for written consent. The landlord must not unreasonably withhold consent to an assignment or sub-letting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If consent is withheld and you believe that's unreasonable, you can apply to the Tribunal for a determination that consent is not required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Get information.** Consumer Affairs Victoria's renting website is listed in the Regulations (consumer.vic.gov.au/renting) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- Whether a friend staying without paying rent is a "sub-letting" or simply a visitor. A "visitor" is someone on the premises with the renter's permission [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), but the documents don't say how that interacts with the consent rule.
- How a renter removes a non-party occupant, and the timeframes for that.

If you're the landlord rather than the renter, let me know and I can answer from that side.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On the arrangement point, the answer notes it is unclear 'Whether a friend staying without paying rent is a "sub-letting" or simply a visitor', which makes the outcome depend on the arrangement and names payment as a deciding fact. It also states that 'A renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the landlord's written consent.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer gives no set notice period or process for ending the friend's occupancy and says "The documents don't set out a process for a renter to remove a non-party occupant". The 14-day period it mentions applies to the landlord's notice to vacate the renter, not to the friend. It also never suggests a lockout or removing belongings, never says the friend has no rights, and never says the friend can apply to VCAT to be added to the lease.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'Authorised Version No. 115 (incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026)' with a 97-109aa115 link, and it also relies on the in-force Regulations 'version 009', so it uses no version that was not in force on 15 October 2026.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved law doesn't contain a general rule that blocks a notice to vacate given after a repair request. It does have specific rules on which notices can be challenged and how they must be given, so check those first.

**Document relied on:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf," Authorised Version (version) 088, in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That covers 1 November 2019.

---

### What the law says

- **Retaliation rule (limited):** A notice under s 91ZK (threats and intimidation) has no effect if given in response to the renter exercising a right under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A notice under s 91ZZD (end of a fixed term) is also void if given in response to a renter exercising a right or making a report under s 72AA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Neither covers a periodic (month-to-month) agreement or a repair-related notice, and the retrieved text has no general retaliation bar for other notices.
- **Form and content:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reason(s), and specifies a termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Notice periods:** The required period depends on the ground. Some grounds allow a termination date on the day of the notice or later, while others require at least 14, 60, or 90 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Challenging the notice:** A renter can apply to the Tribunal to challenge a notice to vacate given under ss 91ZX, 91ZY, 91ZZ, 91ZZA, 91ZZB or 91ZZC, but only within 30 days after the notice is given and on or before the hearing of any possession application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can decide whether the notice is valid, and if it finds it valid, the renter generally cannot reapply unless exceptional circumstances exist [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Section 91ZZR says nothing in that subdivision affects a renter's right to challenge other notices under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), but the excerpt doesn't say how.
- **Your repair duties:** A renter must give written notice of damage or breakdown of facilities "as soon as practicable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The landlord must keep the premises in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If repairs are requested in writing and not done within 14 days, the renter can apply to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), and then to the Tribunal for an order for non-urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal may also order rent paid into the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

---

### What you can check or do

1. **Look at the stated ground.** Find the reason written on the notice. Is it one of the listed grounds, and does it match a situation that actually exists?
2. **Check the form and notice period.** Confirm the notice is in writing, signed, addressed to you, gives a reason, and gives a termination date. If the termination date is the same day (1 November 2019), check whether that ground allows it.
3. **Note the deadlines.** If the notice relies on one of the grounds listed in paragraph (above), you have 30 days from the date given to apply to the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Document the repair history.** Confirm that your repair request was written and when it was made [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), and keep records of the landlord's response.
5. **Seek advice.** The retrieved text does not say whether a notice given soon after a repair request is invalid. Contact the Tribunal or a tenants' advice service for a view on your specific facts.

---

**What the documents don't cover:** The excerpts don't include the prescribed notice form, the full list of notice grounds, or any general provision treating a notice as retaliatory when it follows a repair request for a periodic agreement. I can't confirm from these documents whether the notice you received is invalid.

It also says the opposite of the second point, stating that 'the retrieved text has no general retaliation bar' and that the retaliation rules do not cover a periodic agreement or a repair-related notice. It gives a 30-day challenge window instead of 60 days at VCAT.

must-not-say.reason: No. The output says a notice to vacate is not valid unless it "states the reason(s)" and tells the renter to confirm it "gives a reason." It also gives a deadline other than 60 days: "you have 30 days from the date given to apply to the Tribunal."

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Short answer:** Yes, the Act prohibits some of what you describe, and you may be able to take it to VCAT. The retrieved documents don't say what counts as "withdrawing" an application, so that part needs other evidence.

**Version applied:** On 1 October 2025, the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* in force is version 110, which the document metadata gives as in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Regulations applicable that day are the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 004 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Fixed advertised rent:** A provider or agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Under s 30F(3), they also "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount of rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person or 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **False or misleading rent representations:** A provider or agent who advertises rented premises must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading conduct to induce an agreement:** A provider or agent must not induce a person to enter a residential rental agreement by misleading or deceptive conduct, including false or misleading representations about the rent payable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Section 472(1A) provides for Tribunal orders for contraventions of this section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Discrimination:** A provider must not refuse to let premises on the basis of a protected attribute [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If you lost out because of discrimination, s 210AA lets you apply to VCAT for compensation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The documents do not say whether accepting an unsolicited higher offer is itself an offence. They also do not address the email saying you had withdrawn.

## What you can do

1. **Complain or seek orders:** The Act gives you a route to VCAT for misleading conduct (s 472(1A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). VCAT can be contacted online at vcat.vic.gov.au or by calling 1300 018 228 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **Claim compensation if discrimination was involved:** Apply to VCAT under s 210AA if you suffered loss from discrimination [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You can also complain to the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission at humanrightscommission.vic.gov.au or 1300 292 153 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **Get advice:** Victoria Legal Aid can be called on 1300 792 387 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## Evidence to keep

The documents do not list required evidence. As general practice, not from the documents, keep:
- The original advertisement, with screenshots and the advertised rent.
- Your application and any emails or messages with the agent.
- The "withdrawn" email, with headers and date, and any reply you sent saying you had not withdrawn.
- Any listing showing the new higher rent, dated screenshots.
- Anything suggesting another applicant offered more, and any mention of the offer.
- A note of each phone call (date, time, person, what was said).

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never states that relisting at a higher fixed rent is not illegal by itself; it mentions the new listing only as evidence to keep. The other three points are covered: s 30F(3) bans soliciting higher offers, it says 'The documents do not say whether accepting an unsolicited higher offer is itself an offence', and it says 'They also do not address the email saying you had withdrawn.'

None of the three claims is asserted: the answer never says relisting at a higher rent is illegal by itself, it explicitly declines to say acceptance is illegal ('The documents do not say whether accepting an unsolicited higher offer is itself an offence'), and it offers only VCAT orders, compensation and complaints rather than any right to force the agent to rent to the applicant.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not, at least not on the owner's allergy alone. The agent's "no" doesn't settle the matter. The Act says the provider must not unreasonably refuse, and if they didn't apply to the Tribunal within 14 days, the law treats them as having consented.

I'm applying the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Version 115, which came into force on 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Version 009, which came into force on 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- A renter may keep a pet if the provider has consented in writing or the Tribunal has permitted it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The request must be made in the form approved by the Director, and given to the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You say you used the official form, which satisfies this.
- The provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" to a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations repeat this in their standard-form terms [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of receiving the request, they apply to the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- At the Tribunal, the provider must show it is reasonable to refuse. The Tribunal may consider the type of pet, the character of the premises, the appliances and fittings, whether refusal is permitted under any other Act, prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What this means for you**

- If your request was given about three weeks ago (around 24 September 2026), the 14-day window would have closed around 8 October. That is my estimate from your timeline, so please check the actual date you gave the form. If the provider did not apply to VCAT in that window, the law treats consent as given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The documents do not say whether an owner's allergy is a reasonable ground for refusal. They also don't say how much weight the Tribunal would give it. The owner rarely visiting may be relevant to how reasonable the refusal is, but the documents don't address that point directly.
- The documents also say that refusing a tenant because of certain personal attributes can be unlawful discrimination. Those attributes concern the renter, not the owner, so they don't obviously apply here [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the agent in writing whether they have applied to the Tribunal, and when. If they haven't, you can point to the deemed-consent rule [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. Ask for the specific reason for refusal in writing, and whether the owner's allergy is the only reason.
3. If the provider does apply to the Tribunal, it must show that refusal is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can respond to that application.
4. If the Tribunal excludes the dog, the provider may only give a notice to vacate if you have not complied at least 14 days after the order took effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. For advice, the Regulations list Victoria Legal Aid on 1300 792 387 for discrimination questions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Consumer Affairs Victoria's contact details are also in the Regulations [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Not covered by the documents:** whether an owner's allergy is a "reasonable" ground, whether the provider has applied to the Tribunal, and the outcome of any similar case.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, the notice is still in effect because the landlord has not withdrawn it. The documents don't say whether a failed sale makes the notice invalid, so you should get advice before deciding whether to move out.

The law in force on 1 October 2025 is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 110, which was in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This is the version in the document metadata; the documents don't show a separate "Authorised Version No." label.

### What the law says

- **Sale notices:** A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date. The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Withdrawal:** A notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given. That notice must be in writing and signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person it was given to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A buyer pulling out does not, by itself, withdraw the notice under these provisions.
- **Possession:** The Tribunal (VCAT) can make a possession order only if it is satisfied the notice "has not been withdrawn" and that the renter is still in possession after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It must also find that a possession order is reasonable and proportionate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Form requirements:** A notice to vacate is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter, signed, states the reasons, and, for sale notices, is accompanied by the approved documentary evidence supporting the reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Check the notice.** Confirm the termination date is at least 60 days after the notice was given, and that it is in the prescribed form, signed, gives reasons, and came with the required documentary evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Challenge it if it's defective.** You may apply to VCAT challenging the notice's validity on or before the hearing of any possession application. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask the landlord to withdraw it in writing.** The documents say withdrawal requires a signed written notice of withdrawal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents I have don't say what happens if the landlord refuses.
4. **Consider ending the agreement early.** A renter given a notice to vacate under section 91ZZB may give at least 14 days' notice of intention to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Form 6 information sheet says the same [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Check whether this suits your situation before using it.
5. **Don't ignore the termination date.** The landlord can apply to VCAT for a possession order, and VCAT decides whether and when you must leave. ### What the documents don't cover

- Whether the landlord must tell you the sale has ended.
- What the Tribunal would decide on these facts.

Because the 30-day challenge window may already be running, you should contact a community legal organisation listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website as soon as possible [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the retrieved documents, you probably do not have to pay the higher rent yet. A rent increase needs a valid written notice in the prescribed form, and an email saying the rent is going up is not that notice. The documents don't give a specific start date, because that depends on a valid notice being given.

**Versions applied:** On 1 October 2025, the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (version 110) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (version 004) were both in force [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- The rental provider must give at least 60 days' notice, in the prescribed form, of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must state the amount of the increase and the method used to calculate it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A rent increase in contravention of these requirements is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The rent cannot be increased at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed form is Form 5. It states that "A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The form also says the rental provider's name "cannot be the agent's name" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

- **Ask for the formal notice.** Ask the rental provider to issue a Form 5 notice, which must give at least 60 days' notice, state the new amount, and explain the calculation method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the timing.** Confirm when rent was last increased. If it was less than 12 months ago, the increase is not allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenge it if a notice is issued.** You can apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given to investigate whether the proposed rent is excessive [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Form 5 notice says you may apply to VCAT within 30 days after receiving the Director's report, or within 30 days of the notice if no report was requested. You will need to pay the increased amount from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to VCAT without a report.** If you did not request a Director's report, you can apply to VCAT for leave to seek an order without one, but only after 30 days have passed since the notice was given. VCAT may grant leave if there are reasonable grounds for not requesting the report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- They don't say whether an email from an agent could ever count as a valid notice beyond the Form 5 requirements, or what counts as a rental provider's notice if an agent sends it.
- They don't cover your rent history, so I can't tell whether the 12-month rule applies to you.
- They don't cover any other tenancy arrangements, such as a fixed-term agreement that sets its own rent increase terms. Section 44(4) restricts rent increases during a fixed term unless the agreement provides for them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

If you receive a formal notice, you may want to get advice from a tenancy service promptly, because the 30-day deadlines are short.

None of the failure conditions is asserted: the answer says "you probably do not have to pay the higher rent yet," gives no start date tied to the email ("The documents don't give a specific start date, because that depends on a valid notice being given"), states "at least 60 days' notice," and only says this particular email "is not that notice" while noting the documents "don't say whether an email from an agent could ever count as a valid notice," so it never claims a notice can never be sent by email.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**What the law says**

The applicable documents are the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version 115 (title: rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version 009 (title: rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

- **Damage duty:** A renter must not intentionally or negligently cause damage to rented premises, but damage does not include fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice:** A renter who becomes aware of damage must, as soon as practicable, give the provider written notice of the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Owner's remedies:** The owner may give a repair notice if damage results from the renter's failure to take care. The notice must be in writing and state the damage, and the owner may require repairs within 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the renter does not repair it in a proper and tradesman-like manner within 14 days, the owner may repair it at the renter's expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who can do repairs:** Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs, both urgent and non-urgent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Can you fix it quickly without telling the owner?**

No, based on these documents. Written notice is required as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), so you should notify the owner before any repair. The self-help option is narrow. A renter may arrange urgent repairs only if they have taken reasonable steps to have the owner do them immediately and the owner is unable or fails to do so [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't list which repairs count as urgent. The definition in section 3(1) isn't in the material I retrieved, so I can't confirm whether skirting boards would qualify. For non-urgent repairs, the renter must notify the owner and can apply to VCAT or the Director only if the owner hasn't acted within 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Any repair must also be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Would it affect the owner's insurance?**

The documents don't say how this damage would affect the owner's insurance policy. The only related point is that a term making the renter liable by default for an insurance excess under the provider's policy is a prescribed prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do now**

1. **Notify the owner in writing** describing the damage, and attach dated photos. Writing is required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask the owner in writing** to repair it, or to agree in writing that a suitably qualified person can do the work. Keep a record of any reply.
3. **Check your condition report.** At the end of the tenancy you must leave the premises as far as practicable in the condition they were in when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner must complete the final inspection and fill in the condition report within 10 days after the end date, and must give you a chance to attend if possible [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Photograph the skirting boards** before and after any repair, and keep receipts.

must-mention.reason: Yes: all four points are covered, including the hardest one, renter responsibility, which the answer states as "A renter must not intentionally or negligently cause damage... damage does not include fair wear and tear" and "you must leave the premises as far as practicable in the condition they were in when you moved in." The answer also says written notice is required as soon as practicable, that "the documents don't say how this damage would affect the owner's insurance policy," and gives the next step of notifying the owner in writing.

Written notice is required as soon as practicable"), gives no insurance outcome as fact ("The documents don't say how this damage would affect the owner's insurance policy"), and says a default excess term is prohibited ("a term making the renter liable by default for an insurance excess under the provider's policy is a prescribed prohibited term").

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf)' and the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 009 (rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf)', both in force on 15 October 2026, and every rule it applies is cited to those versions (links 97-109aa115 and 21-3sra009).

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found do not set a limit on the number of circuits in a rental, so I can't tell you whether one circuit for most power points breaches the law. They do cover electrical safety, and you can ask for several things now.

**What the law says on 1 March 2023**

- **Electrical safety standard:** Schedule 4, clause 9 of the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version 002) requires that "all power outlets and lighting circuits" be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000 and a switchboard-type residual current device [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). However, this applies only "On and from 29 March 2023" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), so it is not yet in force on 1 March 2023. The clause does not specify how many circuits a rental must have [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to maintain:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (No. 109 of 1997, Authorised Version 101) requires the provider to ensure rented premises are "provided and maintained" in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Any repairs must be carried out by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rental minimum standards:** The provider must ensure the premises comply with the prescribed minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks:** The standard tenancy agreement form requires the provider to ensure an electrical safety check every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician, and to provide the date of the most recent check in writing on the renter's request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What you can ask for**

1. **A written request for the date of the latest electrical safety check.** The provider must provide it on request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **A copy of the most recent electrical safety check.** This must be provided "within 7 days after receipt by a residential rental provider of a written request from the renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **A repair by a suitably qualified person.** Repairs must be done by one [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Non-urgent repairs require written notice "as soon as practicable," and the provider must carry them out "in a reasonable time." You may apply to VCAT if the repairs are not done within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Compliance with the circuit standard from 29 March 2023.** From that date, the circuit breaker and residual current device requirements apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Since you're asking about 1 March, this is a request for the near future, not something the law requires today.

**Limits of what I found**

- The documents don't say how many circuits a rental must have, and I found nothing that makes the single-circuit layout unlawful as of 1 March 2023.
- The documents don't say whether a breaker tripping under load counts as an urgent repair. The urgent repairs list in the standard form covers failure of essential services for hot water, cooking, heating or laundering [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), but I couldn't confirm how that applies to your situation.
- For safety, you should have a licensed electrician check the circuit and its load. Tell the provider in writing about the tripping, and keep a record of the request.

must-mention.reason: Both points are covered. On the first, the answer says "The documents don't say how many circuits a rental must have," which the rubric accepts as meaning there is no rule. On the second, it says the renter can make "A written request for the date of the latest electrical safety check" and seek "A repair by a suitably qualified person."

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer sets no minimum number of circuits and does not call a shared circuit illegal, saying 'I found nothing that makes the single-circuit layout unlawful as of 1 March 2023', and it says the circuit breaker and RCD standard 'is not yet in force on 1 March 2023' and is 'not something the law requires today.'

The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (No. 109 of 1997, Authorised Version 101)' and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021, Authorised Version 002)', and every rule it applies comes from those versions (links 97-109aa101 and 21-3sra002).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether a private rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. They do set rules for certain service charges, which I've summarised below.

**What the law says**

- The governing document is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version (version) 115, which is in force from 13 October 2026, so it applies on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If an operator charges for services, it must first give the resident a separate schedule of the amount for those services before the resident moves in. If the resident uses a service, the operator must give an itemised account of that individual use [1, s 109].
- Charges for electricity, gas and water are limited to rooms that are separately metered, and the charge must not be more than the supplier's charge. This section doesn't mention laundry [1, s 108].
- Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may impose a service charge for laundry facilities in a declared rooming house. This applies only if it isn't possible or practicable to accurately measure the resident's use, and the charge must not exceed the cost of providing the service [1, s 109A(1), (2), (2A)]. These agencies must give written notice of the charge [1, s 109A(3A)].
- If a rooming house stops providing a service, the operator must reduce the rent by the amount agreed, or by an amount the Tribunal determines [1, s 106].
- The Rooming House Standards Regulations require a washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents, in good working order, from 26 February 2024 [2, reg 14(2)]. These regulations were retrieved as version 002, in force from 1 December 2024 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). I didn't find a later version in the search results.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Check your agreement and any fee schedule.** If the operator charges for laundry, it should have given you a separate schedule before you moved in [1, s 109(a)].
2. **Ask for an itemised account** of your use if you are being charged [1, s 109(b)].
3. **If the agency is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency**, you can apply to the Tribunal to withdraw or vary a laundry service charge [1, s 109A(3B)]. The Tribunal may order the charge withdrawn, varied, or otherwise varied as it thinks fit [1, s 109A(3C)].
4. **If laundry services have been reduced**, you may be able to seek a rent reduction [1, s 106].

**What the documents don't cover:** Whether coin-operated machines are a permitted charge when run by a private operator, and whether a coin-operated machine counts as a "service" under s 109 are not addressed in the retrieved material. You may wish to get advice from a tenants' organisation or the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for your specific situation.

---

**Sources**
[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026).
[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023*, version 002 (in force from 1 December 2024).

must-mention.reason: Yes: all four points are covered. (1) The answer says the regulations 'require a washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents, in good working order'. (2) It says 'The retrieved documents don't say whether a private rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines', which counts under the rubric's 'documents do not say' allowance. (3) It says the operator 'must first give the resident a separate schedule of the amount for those services before the resident moves in'. (4) It advises 'Check your agreement and any fee schedule... it should have given you a separate schedule before you moved in'.
