question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says — 1 March 2023

The documents **do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits** that a Victorian rental must have. The electrical rental minimum standard then in force required compliance **from 29 March 2023**—not yet on 1 March 2023—that all power outlets and lighting circuits be connected to a compliant switchboard-type circuit breaker and residual-current device (RCD). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must nevertheless maintain the premises **in good repair** and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation, with repairs carried out by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask for or do

- Give the rental provider or agent **written notice** that the breaker trips when the kettle and heater are used together, and ask for a **licensed or registered electrician** to investigate and rectify the electrical installation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- Ask in writing for the date of the most recent electrical safety check. The rental provider must provide that date on request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- You can also request a copy of the most recent electrical safety-check record; the rental provider must provide it within **7 days** after receiving the written request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- The electrical safety check must cover the electrical installations, appliances and fittings provided by the rental provider, and must be conducted every **2 years** by a licensed or registered electrician. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- If the issue is not repaired within a reasonable time, you may apply to the Director for an investigation after giving written notice and waiting **14 days**. You may also apply to VCAT for an order requiring specified non-urgent repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

Do **not** repeatedly reset the breaker or use the circuit in a way that creates a safety risk; ask the provider for an electrician’s assessment rather than asking simply for “more circuits.” The retrieved documents do not say that you can require a particular number of circuits.

**Documents and versions applicable on 1 March 2023:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version v002** (in force from 1 June 2022), and *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version v101** (in force from 7 September 2022). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered: the answer says 'The documents do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits', and it gives next steps of a written repair request ('ask for a licensed or registered electrician to investigate and rectify') and asking 'in writing for the date of the most recent electrical safety check.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer states that the documents "do not specify a minimum number of electrical circuits" and that the circuit breaker and RCD requirement applies "from 29 March 2023—not yet on 1 March 2023", so it asserts neither a minimum circuit count nor that the RCD standard already applies.

Every rule it applies comes from those versions, and it mentions the 29 March 2023 electrical standard only to say it was not yet required.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115** (in force from 13 October 2026). [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act requires a rooming house to provide a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents. It does **not** expressly say in the retrieved documents that using that machine must be free. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

If the rooming house operator charges you for a service, they must give you a separate schedule of the service charge before you move in and, if you use the service, an itemised account showing your individual use. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) For Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, a laundry service charge is permitted only where use cannot practicably be measured accurately, and it must not exceed the cost of providing the service. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** specifically state whether a coin-operated washing machine is lawful in every type of rooming house.

## What you can ask or do

Ask the operator for:

- the separate schedule explaining the laundry charge; and
- an itemised account showing your individual use. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You can also ask whether the operator is **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency**, because the specific laundry service-charge rules in section 109A apply to those providers. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) If the operator will not provide the required information, the retrieved documents do not state a specific enforcement step for this situation.

All four points are covered: the one machine per 12 or fewer residents requirement, that the documents do 'not expressly say... that using that machine must be free', the separate schedule required 'before you move in', and the next step to 'Ask the operator for: the separate schedule explaining the laundry charge'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the three failure conditions is asserted. question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable documents were:

- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version 110** (in force from 6 August 2025); and
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version 004** (in force from 1 July 2025). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A rental provider is not expressly prohibited by these documents from putting a photograph showing apparent mould in a rental advertisement. However, each room must be free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Before entering into the rental agreement, the provider must disclose whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. They must also disclose whether, in the previous three years, they received a repair notice concerning mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

If the premises do not comply with the minimum standards when the renter moves in, the provider must ensure compliance and the renter may request urgent repairs. The Act also treats failure to comply with a rental minimum standard as an urgent-repair matter. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A photograph suggesting mould is **not stated in the retrieved documents to be conclusive proof** that the premises fail the minimum standard. The documents do say that photographs may be useful in a dispute about the condition of rented premises, but they do not specify that one rental-advertisement photograph is sufficient evidence by itself. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can do or ask

Before applying, ask the provider or agent **in writing**:

1. whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards; and  
2. whether they have received a mould- or damp-related repair notice in the last three years. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents **do not explain the procedure for making your friend leave**, including whether you must give them a notice, how much notice is required, or whether your friend has independent renter or sub-renter rights. They therefore do not provide enough information to say exactly what you must do to remove them.

You should not change the locks, use force, or otherwise remove your friend based only on these documents. Ask the rental provider or agent in writing about the unauthorised occupant and obtain advice about the correct removal process.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law said on 1 November 2019

The applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088, dated 2 July 2019**—the version in force from 2 July to 3 December 2019. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

- A landlord had to maintain the rented premises in good repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- For **non-urgent repairs**, after giving written notice, you could apply to the Director for an investigation if the repairs were not completed within 14 days; after the Director’s report, you could apply to the Tribunal for a repair order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- A **month-to-month agreement is a periodic agreement**. For a notice to vacate **without specifying a reason**, the notice generally had to give at least **120 days’ notice**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- A notice under the no-reason provision had **no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- Any notice to vacate had to be in the relevant prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason if one was relied on, and state the termination date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- If the notice claimed the landlord needed to carry out repairs, the landlord had to show that the work required you to vacate, that necessary permits and consents had been obtained, and give at least **60 days’ notice**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you should check and do

1. **Check the notice’s stated ground.** If it says “no reason,” check whether the termination date is at least **120 days after the notice date** and whether the notice was issued because you exercised a repair-related right. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Check the timing and evidence.** Keep your repair requests, photographs, messages, emails and dates showing that the notice followed your request for repairs on the same day. Those facts may support an argument that the notice was retaliatory. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **If it relies on repairs as the reason,** check for the required documentary evidence, permits or consents, proof that the work cannot be done while you remain, and the **60-day minimum**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

4. **Do not simply leave or stop paying rent.** The retrieved document does not state that a retaliatory notice automatically permits you to stop paying rent.

5. **Consider applying to the Tribunal to challenge the notice.** The document states that a renter may challenge the validity of certain repair-related notices within **30 days after the notice is given**, and that the Tribunal may determine whether the notice is valid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

6. **Continue pursuing the repairs through the statutory process:** for non-urgent repairs, written notice followed by a Director investigation and, where appropriate, a Tribunal repair application; for urgent repairs, the Act provides separate urgent-repair procedures. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No: the output covers the 120-day no-reason notice and says such a notice 'had no effect if it was given in response to your exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act,' but it misses the VCAT challenge point. It says a renter may challenge 'certain repair-related notices within 30 days after the notice is given,' which changes the required 60-day period.

must-not-say.reason: No: the answer states a challenge deadline other than 60 days, saying "a renter may challenge the validity of certain repair-related notices within **30 days after the notice is given**" and presenting this under "Consider applying to the Tribunal to challenge the notice."

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 — Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

- The property had to be advertised or offered at a **fixed amount of rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider or agent must not **solicit or invite an offer higher than the advertised rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Advertising the property at one rent and then changing it may be unlawful if the original advertising was a **false or misleading representation about the rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- The Act also prohibits misleading or deceptive conduct, including a false or misleading representation about rent, but that provision applies to conduct **inducing a person to enter into a residential rental agreement**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, if the agent withdrew your application because another applicant offered more—or invited higher offers—those facts could indicate a contravention of the rental-auction prohibition. The documents do not establish whether that is what happened, nor do they provide a specific procedure for challenging an allegedly false “withdrawn” record. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent, in writing, to:

1. confirm whether you withdrew your application and provide the date and method of that alleged withdrawal; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
2. explain why the property was relisted at a higher rent; and [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
3. confirm whether any applicant was invited or permitted to offer more than the advertised rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

You may also raise the matter with the relevant Victorian tenancy authority or tribunal, but the retrieved document does not state the applicable complaint process, jurisdiction, time limit, or remedy for this particular prospective-renter dispute. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The Act does not specify what evidence a prospective renter must save. To support your account, preserve the original advertisement, its rent and timestamps, your complete application and submission confirmation, the email saying you withdrew, all correspondence, screenshots of the later listing, and any message or witness evidence about a higher offer. The recommendation to preserve those materials is practical guidance; the retrieved document itself does not prescribe it.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never says that accepting an unsolicited higher offer was lawful on 1 October 2025, when only inviting such offers was banned. It also suggests the opposite by saying that withdrawing the application 'because another applicant offered more' could 'indicate a contravention of the rental-auction prohibition'.

must-not-say.reason: No. The answer suggests that accepting a higher offer could breach the law, saying "if the agent withdrew your application because another applicant offered more—or invited higher offers—those facts could indicate a contravention of the rental-auction prohibition." This treats another applicant simply offering more as a possible breach, without noting that accepting an unsolicited higher offer was not prohibited on this date. Read strictly, that counts as asserting the prohibited point, although the hedged wording makes this a close call. The other two points are not asserted: relisting is called unlawful only if the original advert was misleading, and the answer never says the applicant can force the agent to rent to them.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

A renter may keep a pet if the rental provider has given written consent or the Tribunal has made an order permitting it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The rental provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Because you sent the approved request form about **three weeks ago**, more than the statutory **14-day** period has passed. The rental provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of receiving the request, it **applied to the Tribunal** for an order that refusing consent was reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not say that an owner’s allergy automatically justifies refusal, nor do they say that the owner’s infrequent visits make refusal unreasonable. If the matter goes to the Tribunal, it may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the apartment, its appliances, fixtures and fittings, whether another Act permits refusal, prescribed matters, and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent in writing whether the rental provider made a Tribunal application under **section 71D within 14 days** of receiving your request. If no such application was made, you can state that consent is taken to have been given under **section 71C(2)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Do not keep the dog solely on the basis of the agent’s refusal unless you are satisfied that the 14-day deemed-consent rule applies; under section 71A, keeping the pet requires written consent or a Tribunal order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not set out a renter-initiated procedure for obtaining a Tribunal order, so they do not provide further steps for you to take.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
### What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable document was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 (in force from 6 August 2025)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A landlord may give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, **“to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession.”** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The fact that a buyer has pulled out does **not automatically withdraw** the notice. Under section 91ZZQ, a notice is withdrawn only by a **written notice of withdrawal signed by both the person who gave the notice and the renter**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, unless the notice is invalid, withdrawn in that way, or set aside by VCAT, you should not assume that you can stay merely because the buyer withdrew. If the landlord applies for a possession order, VCAT must consider whether the landlord was entitled to give the notice and whether it has been withdrawn. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

### What you can do or ask

- Ask the landlord to give you a **written notice of withdrawal**, signed by both sides. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- If you believe the sale reason is no longer genuine or the notice was otherwise invalid, you may apply to VCAT to challenge it **within 30 days after it was given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Check that the notice was in the prescribed form, stated the sale reason and termination date, and included supporting documentary evidence. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) The relevant prescribed form is **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- The documents do not state that a buyer’s withdrawal, by itself, cancels a sale-based notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No: the answer never states the 60-day minimum notice period. It also does not clearly explain that the outcome depends on the ground stated in the notice (a planned sale with vacant possession versus a signed contract). It does cover withdrawal only by a written notice signed by both parties and gives next steps (asking for a signed withdrawal, or challenging at VCAT within 30 days).

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

On 1 October 2025, the applicable law was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 (in force from 6 August 2025)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) It requires the rental provider to give **at least 60 days’ notice in the prescribed form** of a proposed rent increase. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed form is **Form 5** under the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) The form states that a valid notice is required for **all** rent increases and must specify the current rent, new rent, start date, and calculation method. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Email delivery is permitted only if the renter has consented to receiving notices by email. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, **if the agent only sent an ordinary email and did not give you a completed prescribed notice, the rent increase is not valid**. You do not have to pay the higher rent on the basis of that email. A rent increase that contravenes these requirements is invalid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not specify a payable date for your particular increase because no valid notice date is provided. If a valid notice is later given, the increase could take effect **no earlier than 60 days after that notice is given**, subject to the other statutory requirements. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Continue paying the existing rent while there is no valid rent-increase notice.  
- Ask the agent to provide the completed **Form 5**, including the calculation method and proposed start date. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)  
- If you receive a valid notice and consider the proposed rent excessive, you may apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria **within 30 days after the notice is given** for an investigation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

It states that 'if the agent only sent an ordinary email and did not give you a completed prescribed notice, the rent increase is not valid. You do not have to pay the higher rent', adding that 'a rent increase that contravenes these requirements is invalid'. For next steps, it says to 'Continue paying the existing rent' and to apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after a valid notice.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026**. The Act says a renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises; dog-chewed skirting boards would likely be damage rather than fair wear and tear. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

You must give the rental provider **written notice as soon as practicable** stating that the damage occurred and describing its nature. Electronic communication is permitted. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The prescribed rental agreement also says renters must notify the rental provider in writing of damage. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, you should **not simply arrange a repair secretly**. The retrieved documents do not establish that you may engage someone to repair this non-urgent damage without notifying the rental provider or obtaining their agreement. They do state that only a **suitably qualified person** may do repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The Act provides a specific process: the rental provider may give you a written repair notice requiring you to repair the damage at your expense within **14 days**, and if you do not repair it properly and in a tradesman-like manner, the rental provider may repair it at your expense. Alternatively, the rental provider may state that they will undertake the repairs and recover the reasonable cost from you. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider may claim from the bond the **reasonable cost** of repairing or restoring damage caused by the renter or a renter’s visitor, taking fair wear and tear into account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Notify the owner or agent **in writing now**, describing the skirting-board damage.
- Ask whether they want to arrange the repair themselves or consent to your using a named, suitably qualified tradesperson.
- If they agree that you arrange it, keep photographs, the invoice and proof of payment.
- Do not assume that repairing it quickly removes the obligation to disclose it; the Act separately requires written notice of damage.
- The retrieved documents contain **no information about whether concealing or repairing the damage would affect the owner’s property insurance**, so I cannot answer that part from the documents. question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
### What the law says — 1 March 2023

The documents do **not** state a required number of power circuits for a rental, so they do not establish that your rental must have more than one circuit. **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002**, in force on 1 March 2023, requires the electrical minimum standard only **from 29 March 2023**: all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to compliant circuit breakers and residual-current devices. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must ensure that an electrical safety check of all electrical installations, appliances and fittings they provide is conducted every **2 years** by a licensed or registered electrician. On request, they must give you the date of the most recent check in writing. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must also maintain the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation, with repairs carried out by a suitably qualified person. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

### What you can ask for

Write to the rental provider or agent and report that the breaker trips whenever the kettle and heater run together. Ask them to:

1. arrange a **licensed electrician** to investigate the circuit and make any necessary safety repairs; [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)  
2. provide the date of the most recent electrical safety check; [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) and  
3. provide a copy of the most recent electrical safety-check record, which must include the electrician’s details, date, results, required repairs and the report prepared under AS/NZS 3019. That copy must be provided within **7 days** after a written request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

You may ask for additional or separate circuits as a proposed remedy, but the retrieved documents do **not** say that you are legally entitled to a particular number of circuits or specifically to a circuit upgrade. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

If the issue is not fixed within a reasonable time, give written notice that repairs are required. If the rental provider has not carried out non-urgent repairs within **14 days** after receiving that notice, you may apply to the Director to investigate or to VCAT for an order requiring specified repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not establish that a breaker tripping in these circumstances is automatically an “urgent repair”; urgent repairs expressly include failure or breakdown of an essential service or an appliance provided for heating, cooking or other listed purposes. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

**Applicable documents:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version 002** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf); *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version 101** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Both points are covered. On the number of circuits, the output says 'The documents do not state a required number of power circuits for a rental', which the rubric accepts as stating that no such rule exists. On next steps, it advises asking the rental provider to arrange a licensed electrician to investigate and repair the circuit, and to 'provide the date of the most recent electrical safety check'. The hardest point to match is the 'and/or' next step, and these words satisfy it.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never sets a minimum number of circuits or says sharing a circuit is illegal ('The documents do **not** state a required number of power circuits'), and it says the circuit breaker and RCD standard applies 'only **from 29 March 2023**', not on 1 March 2023.

version-cited.reason: Yes — the answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002' (link 21-3sra002) and 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101' (link 97-109aa101), and every rule it applies is sourced only from those versions.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The Act does **not expressly mention coin-operated washing machines**. However:

- A rooming-house operator that charges for services must give the resident a **separate schedule of the service amount before residency begins**, and an **itemised account** showing the resident’s individual use of the service. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency** may impose a service charge for laundry services or facilities only where it is **not possible or practicable to accurately measure use**. The charge must **not exceed the cost of providing** the service or facility, and written notice must be given when the charge is imposed or changed. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rooming-house standards require, from **26 February 2024**, at least **one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents**, based on the maximum capacity of the rooming house. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) The standards do not state that the machine must be free to use. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

**Therefore, the retrieved documents do not establish a general rule that coin-operated washing machines are either always allowed or always prohibited.** A charge may be subject to the disclosure, accounting and—if the operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency—the specific service-charge limits above. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the operator for:

1. The written **schedule of the laundry-service charge** given before you moved in. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. An **itemised account** showing your individual use of the laundry service. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
3. If the operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, written notice explaining the charge and evidence that it does not exceed the cost of providing the laundry facility. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the charge appears inconsistent with those requirements, the documents indicate that a resident may apply to the **Tribunal** to require Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency to withdraw or vary such a service charge. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: the standard requiring 'at least one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents'; 'The standards do not state that the machine must be free to use'; the requirement for 'a separate schedule of the service amount before residency begins'; and the next step of asking the operator for 'The written schedule of the laundry-service charge given before you moved in.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the machines must be free (it notes 'The standards do not state that the machine must be free to use'), it describes rules on charges (a 'separate schedule of the service amount' and an 'itemised account'), and it limits the cost cap to operators that are 'Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency' rather than all rooming houses.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Authorised Version 115" (link 97-109aa115) and the rooming-house standards by the link 23-10sra002 (version 002). Both are the versions in force on 15 October 2026, and the answer relies on no other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the applicable documents were:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, **Authorised Version No. 110**, in force from 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, **Authorised Version No. 004**, in force from 1 July 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Each room must be **free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure** under Schedule 4 clause 8 of the Regulations. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must ensure the premises comply with the minimum standards **on or before the day the renter enters occupation**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** expressly prohibit putting a photograph showing apparent mould in a rental advertisement. They do, however, require the rental provider to disclose to a rental applicant whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) They must also disclose whether, in the previous three years, they received a repair notice about mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

A photograph may be relevant evidence: the prescribed condition-report form says photographs may be useful in a dispute about the condition of the premises. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) But the documents do **not** say that a photograph alone proves that the premises fail the minimum standard. The photo may not establish, by itself, whether the substance is mould, whether it is damp-related, or whether it was caused by the building structure.

## What the renter can do or ask

- Ask the rental provider or agent directly whether the premises comply with the minimum standards, and specifically whether the bedroom is free from structurally caused mould or damp. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- Ask whether the provider has received a mould-or-damp repair notice in the previous three years. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- Keep a copy or screenshot of the advertisement and photograph. The retrieved documents support photographs as potentially useful evidence in a condition dispute, but do not specify that an advertising photo is conclusive proof. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- If the renter takes the property, record the bedroom’s condition in the condition report and attach dated, labelled photographs identifying the room or location. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- If the premises do not comply when the renter moves in, the renter may request urgent repairs to bring them into compliance with the minimum standards. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The output states the standard that each room must be 'free from mould and damp caused by, or related to, the building structure'. It also says the documents 'do not say that a photograph alone proves that the premises fail the minimum standard', which covers the hardest point. Finally, it gives next steps: asking the agent about compliance and requesting urgent repairs after moving in.

must-not-say.reason: Yes — the answer asserts neither failure condition: it says the documents "do not expressly prohibit putting a photograph showing apparent mould in a rental advertisement" and "do not say that a photograph alone proves that the premises fail the minimum standard."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with the versions in force on 1 October 2025: 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, in force from 6 August 2025' (link 97-109aa110) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004, in force from 1 July 2025' (link 21-3sra004). Every rule it applies comes from these versions.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the applicable document is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115**, in force from **13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If your friend is **subletting all or part of the property**, you must not do that without the **rental provider’s written consent**—telling or not telling the agent is not the statutory test. An unauthorised subletting is invalid unless VCAT has determined that consent is unnecessary. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The regulations state that a rental provider **may give the renter a notice to vacate** if the renter assigns or sublets without consent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) However, the retrieved documents do **not** state the specific notice period or the complete procedure for this particular situation.

## What you can do or ask

The documents do not explain how a renter can directly remove a friend who is merely an occupant rather than a subtenant. They also do not say whether your friend’s arrangement is legally a subletting; that depends on the facts, such as whether your friend has been given part of the premises as a separate arrangement.

If it is a subletting, you should:

1. **Check whether you have written consent** from the rental provider. Without it, the subletting is invalid unless VCAT has ruled that consent is unnecessary. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. **Ask the rental provider or agent in writing** what action they require and whether they will give or support the appropriate notice. The documents do not provide a separate “friend removal” notice.
3. If a notice to vacate is used, it must be the prescribed notice and include the required termination date, reason, relevant Act section, and delivery details. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not contain enough information to state exactly what notice you must give your friend, or how you can lawfully make them leave.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer says subletting requires 'the rental provider's written consent'. It also says whether this is a subletting 'depends on the facts, such as whether your friend has been given part of the premises as a separate arrangement', which names a deciding fact about a space that is only theirs.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the four failure conditions appear: the answer says "the retrieved documents do not state the specific notice period or the complete procedure" and "do not contain enough information to state exactly what notice you must give your friend," so it states no fixed notice period as certain, and it never suggests a lockout, says the friend has no rights, or says the friend can apply to VCAT to be added to the lease.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 115, in force from 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115), and the only other document it relies on is the in-force Regulations version 009 (link 21-3sra009); it applies no rule from a version not in force on 15 October 2026.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
On 1 November 2019 the law that applied was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088** (document *rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf*, dated 2 July 2019, in force 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law said

**1. A "no reason" notice given in retaliation has no effect.** A landlord could give a notice to vacate without giving a reason under **s 263** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). But a notice under s 261 or s 263 "is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act" (**s 266(2)**) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**2. Asking for repairs is a right under the Act.** The landlord had to keep the premises "in good repair" (**s 68(1)**) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Act gave you these repair rights:
- arranging urgent repairs yourself after taking reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them (**s 72**) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- applying to the Tribunal for urgent repairs (**s 73**) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- applying to the Director for an investigation after giving written notice and waiting 14 days (**s 74**) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- applying to the Tribunal for non-urgent repairs (**s 75**) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- asking to pay rent into the Rent Special Account (**s 77**) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

**3. Notice period for a month-to-month tenancy.** A s 263 notice had to give a termination date "not less than 120 days after the date on which the notice is given" (**s 263(2)(c)**). If your periodic tenancy fell under s 230(3A), the period was the prescribed period, or 120 days if none was prescribed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**4. Strict time limit to challenge.** You could not apply to the Tribunal to challenge a s 263 notice "after the end of 60 days after the date on which the notice is given" (**s 266(3)(c)**) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**5. The protection only covers some notices.** s 266(2) applies only to notices under **s 261 or s 263** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If your notice gives a reason, different rules apply (see point 4 below).

---

## What you should check or do

1. **Which section is the notice under?** Is it a "no specified reason" notice under s 263? If so, s 266(2) can apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Is it valid in form?** Under **s 319**, a notice is not valid unless it is in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed by the landlord or agent, and states a termination date. It must also give reasons, except for s 263 notices [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Is the date far enough away?** For a periodic tenancy, check it is at least 120 days after the notice was given (s 263(2)(c)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **If the notice gives a reason**, check that the reason is real:
   - A **s 255 (repairs)** notice needs the landlord to intend to repair, renovate or reconstruct, to have "obtained all necessary permits and consents," and the work must be impossible to do properly unless you leave. The date must be at least 60 days away [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - For notices under ss 255–260, you can challenge validity within **30 days** of the notice (**s 321B**) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Keep evidence that the notice followed your request.** The landlord can only get a possession order if the Tribunal is satisfied they were "entitled to give the notice" (**s 330(1)(a)(i)**) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Keep your written repair requests, the dates you sent them, any replies, and the notice served the same day.
6. **Apply to the Tribunal in time.** For a s 263 notice, apply within **60 days** of receiving it (s 266(3)(c)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
7. **Keep pursuing the repairs separately**, using the s 72–77 options above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
8. **If you decide to leave anyway**, a tenant given a s 263 notice can leave on **14 days'** notice of intention to vacate (**s 237(1)(a), (3)**) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

---

## Limits of the documents

- The retrieved text does not include the Act's definition of "urgent repairs," so I can't confirm whether leaking fixtures count as urgent.
- The documents don't say what evidence the Tribunal needs to decide a notice was given "in response to" a repair request.
- The same document also contains later amendment text in its endnotes, such as s 91ZZI using the terms "renter" and "residential rental provider." That text was **not in force on 1 November 2019**, so I haven't relied on it.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are stated: s 263 allows a no-reason notice with a termination date 'not less than 120 days after' it is given; s 266(2) says such a notice 'is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise... by the tenant of a right under this Act'; and the hardest point, the VCAT challenge, is covered by 'For a s 263 notice, apply within 60 days of receiving it (s 266(3)(c))', where 'the Tribunal' is VCAT.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the landlord needed to give a reason; it states "A landlord could give a notice to vacate without giving a reason under s 263." For challenging this notice it gives only the 60-day deadline: "For a s 263 notice, apply within 60 days of receiving it (s 266(3)(c))." It mentions 30 days only for a different, reason-based type of notice ("For notices under ss 255–260 ... within 30 days"), not as the deadline for this notice.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the required document with its version, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088" (file rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf, link 97-109aa088). Every rule it applies (ss 263, 266(2)–(3), 319, 330 and the repair provisions) is sourced from that in-force version, and it mentions later 'renter' amendment text only to say it was not in force and was not relied on.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
# Rent bidding and a "withdrawn" application: Victoria, as at 1 October 2025

**Law that applies:** the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file **rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf**, **Authorised Version No. 110**, which includes amendments up to 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it was in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025, so it covers 1 October 2025. I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file **rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf** (version 004, dated 1 July 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

**1. Advertised rent must be a fixed amount, and agents can't invite higher offers (s 30F)**
- A rental provider or their agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A rental provider or agent **must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of rent higher than the advertised amount** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Penalty: **60 penalty units** for an individual, **300 penalty units** for a company [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- ⚠️ This section bans the agent or provider *asking for or inviting* a higher offer. The documents don't say it's illegal for another applicant to offer more without being asked. So the key question is whether the agent invited it.

**2. No false or misleading advertising of rent (s 30G)**
- A rental provider or agent who advertises a property must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent. Penalty: 60 or 300 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- This section only covers providers and agents who are not acting in trade or commerce. It "does not limit the operation of the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria)" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Relisting at a higher *fixed* price isn't banned by itself in the sections I found. It may matter if the new listing is misleading about the rent.

**3. False and fraudulent misrepresentation (s 501)**
- A person must not make a false and fraudulent misrepresentation about a proposed rental agreement, including about "a matter affecting a person's rights or duties" under the Act or a proposed agreement. Penalty: **150 penalty units** for an individual, **750 penalty units** for a company [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- A made-up "you withdrew" email *may* fall under this section. Whether it does depends on the facts, especially whether it was deliberate rather than a mistake.

**4. Discrimination (s 30A), if relevant**
- A rental provider must not refuse to let premises because of a protected attribute under the *Equal Opportunity Act 2010* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If you suffered loss because of discrimination, you can apply to VCAT for compensation under s 210AA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

---

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the agent in writing** to confirm when and how you supposedly withdrew, and to show you the record they relied on. Ask whether they asked for or accepted offers above the advertised rent.
- **Get advice or information:**
  - Consumer Affairs Victoria: consumer.vic.gov.au/renting or **1300 558 181** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
  - If discrimination may be involved: Victoria Legal Aid (**1300 792 387**), VEOHRC (**1300 292 153**), or VCAT (**1300 018 228**) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- **Limits on what the Act gives you:** most of the provisions above are offences with penalties. The general compensation provisions in the Act (s 210 at VCAT, s 215 in court) are for *parties to a residential rental agreement* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). As a rejected applicant you aren't a party. The documents I found don't set out a way for an unsuccessful applicant to win the property or claim compensation for rent bidding, except the discrimination route [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Get advice before relying on any particular remedy.

---

## What to save as evidence

The documents don't list what evidence is needed. These suggestions are mine, based on what each section above prohibits:

| Save this | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| The original ad (screenshot with date, URL and price) | Shows the fixed advertised rent (s 30F) |
| The new listing at the higher rent (screenshot with date) | Compare with the original; possible misleading rent advertising (s 30G) |
| Your application and confirmation that you submitted it | Shows you applied at the advertised price |
| The "you have withdrawn" email, with full header details | Possible false misrepresentation (s 501) |
| Proof you didn't withdraw (sent messages, call logs, portal history) | Contradicts the email |
| Any message from the agent inviting higher offers, or asking if you'd "pay more" | Key evidence of soliciting (s 30F(3)) |
| Details of who told you someone offered more, plus anything written from them | Supports the bidding claim, though hearsay alone is weak |
| Dated notes of every phone call or conversation (who, when, what was said) | Builds a timeline |

**Bottom line:** if the agent asked for or invited an offer above the advertised rent, that breaches s 30F(3) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), and a deliberately false withdrawal notice may breach s 501 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Save the evidence now, before the listings change, and get advice before you take it further.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Probably not, if the owner didn't apply to VCAT within 14 days of getting your request.** The agent saying "no" doesn't count as a refusal under the Act. To refuse, the owner has to apply to the Tribunal (VCAT).

**Law used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 115**, which includes amendments up to **13 October 2026** (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf"). That's the version in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

- **You can keep a pet if** the owner (the Act calls them the "residential rental provider") has agreed in writing, **or** VCAT has made an order allowing it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your request:** It must be made on the form approved by the Director and given to the owner [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You've done this.
- **They can't refuse unreasonably:** The owner "must not unreasonably refuse to consent to the renter keeping a pet on the rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard rental agreement says the same thing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The 14-day rule:** The owner "is taken to have consented" to your request **unless, within 14 days after being given the request,** they apply to VCAT under section 71D [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your request went in three weeks (about 21 days) ago. So if no VCAT application was made in time, the law treats your request as approved, whatever the agent told you.
- **The allergy:** If the owner did apply in time, VCAT decides. It may consider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  - the type of pet
  - the character and nature of the premises
  - the appliances, fixtures and fittings
  - whether refusing is allowed under any Act
  - any prescribed matters
  - "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant"

  The documents don't mention allergies or how often the owner visits, so I can't say how VCAT would weigh those. They would fall under "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant."

## What you can do

1. **Ask the agent in writing** whether the owner applied to VCAT under section 71D within 14 days of receiving your request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they didn't, point out that under section 71C(2) consent is taken to have been given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Keep proof** of the date you gave them the form. The 14 days run from that date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If they did apply in time,** you can take part in the VCAT hearing. VCAT can either allow the pet, or find refusal reasonable and order the pet excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You could argue that the owner rarely visits, since VCAT can consider "any other matter" it finds relevant [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Be careful about bringing the dog in while it's disputed.** If VCAT orders the pet out and you haven't complied 14 days after the order takes effect, the owner can give you a notice to vacate with at least 28 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

⚠️ **One caveat:** You made the request around late September, and the 14-day period would have ended around early October. Both dates are before Version 115 started on 13 October 2026. I only have Version 115, not the earlier one. The history notes on the pet sections don't list any recent amendments, but the documents can't confirm the wording was the same during your 14-day period.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
# Do you still have to leave if the sale fell through?

**Short answer:** Not straight away, and not unless VCAT orders it. The notice stays in force until it's formally withdrawn. But the landlord can only make you leave by getting a possession order from the Tribunal, and you can challenge the notice.

**Source:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025). This version was in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025, so it applies on 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:** The Act doesn't say what happens to a notice to vacate when a buyer pulls out. The points below come from the general rules.

---

## What the law says

**1. The notice doesn't cancel itself.** A notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given. That withdrawal must be in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person who received it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). So the buyer pulling out doesn't withdraw it.

**2. The sale ground isn't only about a signed contract.** A landlord can give a notice to vacate if, immediately after the termination date, the premises are "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the landlord is still trying to sell with vacant possession, the reason for the notice may still apply. Other rules for this notice:
- If there's a contract of sale with conditions, the notice can be given within 14 days after the last condition is met. For an unconditional contract, it's within 14 days after the contract is signed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The termination date must be at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**3. Your tenancy doesn't end automatically on the termination date.** It ends if you move out on or after that date, or under the possession-order process in section 334 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A tenancy can't be ended except as the Act allows [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It's an offence for a landlord to force or try to force you out other than under the Act. The penalty is up to 150 penalty units for an individual or 750 for a company [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**4. The landlord needs a VCAT possession order.** The landlord must apply no later than 30 days after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). VCAT can't decide the application before the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). To make the order, VCAT must be satisfied that:
- the landlord was entitled to give the notice, and the notice hasn't been withdrawn [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- making the order is "reasonable and proportionate," taking into account the interests of both you and the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**5. The notice may be invalid from the start if:**
- it wasn't in the prescribed form, wasn't signed, didn't state the reason or termination date, or didn't come with supporting documents for the sale [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- you're on a fixed-term lease and the termination date is before the lease ends [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- giving it was direct discrimination under the *Equal Opportunity Act 2010* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**6. Limit on re-letting.** If the landlord gets possession under a sale notice, they can't rent the property out as a home to someone else for 6 months after the notice was given, unless VCAT allows it. The penalty is up to 150 or 750 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

---

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask the landlord to withdraw the notice in writing.** Both of you would sign it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If they won't, ask whether they're still selling with vacant possession, because that affects whether the reason for the notice still applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenge the notice at VCAT.** You must apply **within 30 days after the notice was given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If VCAT decides the notice is valid, you generally can't challenge it again unless there are exceptional circumstances [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Oppose the possession order if the landlord applies.** At the hearing, you can argue that the landlord wasn't entitled to give the notice, or that an order wouldn't be reasonable and proportionate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the notice for defects:** the form, signature, reason, termination date, supporting documents, the 60-day minimum, and the end date of any fixed term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Leave early if you'd prefer.** Because you got a sale notice, you can give a notice of intention to vacate with at least 14 days' notice, even during a fixed term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Report pressure to leave.** If the landlord tries to force you out without a VCAT order, that's an offence under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

On the hardest one, the answer says "The sale ground isn't only about a signed contract" and "If the landlord is still trying to sell with vacant possession, the reason for the notice may still apply," and it also mentions the supporting documents required for the sale. It states the 60-day minimum and that a withdrawal must be "in writing, signed by the person who gave the notice, and signed by the person who received it." For next steps, it advises asking for a written withdrawal signed by both and challenging the notice at VCAT "within 30 days after the notice was given."
