question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
# Short answer: no, not on the information you've given

I've used the versions in force on 1 October 2025:
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110** (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf, dated 6 August 2025, in force 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004** (rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf, dated 1 July 2025, in force 1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

---

## What the law says

**1. A rent increase needs a notice in the official form.** Your rental provider "must give a renter at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form of a proposed rent increase" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). That form is **Form 5, "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises"** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Form 5 itself says: *"A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases."* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

**2. The notice must contain certain things.** It must state:
- the amount of the increase
- how the increase was calculated
- a statement of your right to ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria, within 30 days, to investigate the proposed rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

A notice can only cover one increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**3. An increase that doesn't follow these rules is invalid.** The Act says: *"A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid."* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) If you only got an informal email, and not a Form 5 notice with the required details, the increase isn't valid. You don't have to pay it.

**4. "From when?"** There's no start date yet, because no valid notice has been given. The earliest the rent can go up is **60 days after** a proper Form 5 notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). These limits also apply:
- Rent can't be increased **more than once every 12 months** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If you're on a **fixed-term agreement**, the rent can't go up before the term ends. The exception is if the agreement sets out the amount of an increase, or how it will be calculated [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**5. Refusing to negotiate doesn't change this.** The agent saying no to your counter-offer doesn't make the increase valid. The notice rules still apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

---

## What you can do

- **Check the email.** Form 5 can be sent by email, but only if you've agreed to receive notices that way [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). See whether the email attached a completed Form 5 that includes the start date and how the increase was calculated [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). If it didn't, it isn't a valid notice.
- **Keep paying your current rent.** Tell the agent in writing that you haven't received a valid Form 5 notice under section 44, and ask them to give you one if they want to raise the rent.
- **If you later get a valid notice and think the new rent is too high:**
  - Apply in writing to the **Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days** of receiving it. This is free [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You can tick the investigation box on Form 5 and send it to GPO Box 123 Melbourne 3001 or renting@justice.vic.gov.au [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
  - After you get the Director's report, you can apply to **VCAT within 30 days** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If you didn't ask for a report, you can apply to VCAT directly once 30 days have passed since the notice, but you'll need VCAT's permission and reasonable grounds for not getting a report first [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
  - With a valid notice, you'll have to pay the increased rent from the start date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **For more help,** contact Consumer Affairs Victoria at consumer.vic.gov.au/renting or **1300 558 181** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:** They don't say what happens if you've already started paying the higher rent based on the email, or whether you can get that money back. You'd need advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy service on that.

It states that an email without a Form 5 is invalid: 'If you only got an informal email, and not a Form 5 notice with the required details, the increase isn't valid. You don't have to pay it.' It also gives next steps, including 'Keep paying your current rent' and telling the agent in writing.

All of its citations link to 97-109aa110 and 21-3sra004, and it relies on no other version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
# Dog damage to skirting boards when moving out (Victoria, as at 15 October 2026)

**Short answer:** No. You can get the damage fixed, but you have to tell the owner in writing first. The documents don't say how this affects the owner's insurance.

**Sources used:**
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, *rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf*, Authorised Version No. 115, including amendments up to 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This was the version in force on 15 October 2026.
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, *rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). No later version was retrieved.

---

## What the law says

**1. You must tell the owner in writing.**
- If you become aware of damage, you must give the rental provider (the owner) written notice "as soon as practicable." The notice must say that the damage happened and what kind of damage it is (s 62(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Email is fine (s 62(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Section 72AA repeats this duty to report damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The standard rental agreement form says the same: "Where damage occurs, the renter must notify the rental provider in writing" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

Fixing it quietly without telling the owner would break this duty.

**2. Pet damage is probably your responsibility.**
- You and your visitors must not damage the premises on purpose or through carelessness. Fair wear and tear doesn't count as damage (s 61) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- When you move out, you must leave the property "in the same condition as when the renter entered into possession," allowing for fair wear and tear (s 63(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Chewed skirting boards are unlikely to count as wear and tear.

**3. The owner can ask you to repair it or pay for the repair (ss 78–79).**
The owner can give you a written repair notice that says either:
- you must repair the damage at your own cost within **14 days**, and if you don't do it "in a tradesman-like manner," the owner can repair it and charge you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf); or
- the owner will do the repair and you are liable for the "reasonable cost" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

If the owner does the repair:
- You must pay them back within **14 days** after the repair is finished, once they give you the cost details in writing (s 79(3)–(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If you're in hardship, you can give written notice asking for an extra **14 days** (s 79(6)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- You can also apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for more time (s 79(5)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**4. The owner can claim from your bond.** They can claim "the reasonable cost of repairs to, or the restoration of, the rented premises" for damage caused by the renter, taking fair wear and tear into account (s 411AB(1)(a)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**5. The owner's final inspection.** At the end of the lease, the owner or agent must do a final inspection and fill in the condition report within 10 days. They must give you a chance to attend if possible [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A patch-up done without telling them is likely to be noticed then anyway.

## Would it affect the owner's insurance?

**The documents don't cover this.** Neither the Act nor the Regulations say how a repair, or not reporting damage, affects the owner's insurance.

The only related rule is that a rental agreement term can't make you liable **by default** for the excess on the owner's insurance policy (reg 11(h)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). That's about who pays an excess, not about how the insurance is affected.

---

## What you can do

1. **Email the owner or agent now.** Say the dog damaged the skirting boards and describe the damage (s 62) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Take dated photos.
2. **Offer to arrange the repair yourselves** and ask them to agree in writing. Repairs should be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) and to a "tradesman-like" standard [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep the invoice.
3. **Or ask the owner to do the repair** and send you the cost details in writing. You then have 14 days to pay, plus 14 more if you give hardship notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **If they claim from your bond, ask for evidence.** The claim is limited to a *reasonable* cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you disagree with it, you can dispute it at VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **Attend the final inspection** if you can [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
6. **Ask the owner directly about insurance.** The documents don't cover it, so it's a question for the owner or their insurer.

*Side note:* the Act says a renter may keep a pet with the owner's written consent or a Tribunal order (s 71A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you didn't have consent for the dog, that's a separate issue you might want to check.

It says the renter must not damage the premises and must leave them 'in the same condition as when the renter entered into possession,' allowing for fair wear and tear. It says 'The documents don't cover this' on insurance. It lists next steps such as 'Email the owner or agent now' and 'Offer to arrange the repair yourselves and ask them to agree in writing.' The hardest point is pet-damage responsibility. 'Pet damage is probably your responsibility' is hedged, but it still clearly points one way, and 'Chewed skirting boards are unlikely to count as wear and tear' backs it up.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
# Circuits and a tripping breaker in a Victorian rental (as at 1 March 2023)

**Short answer:** None of the documents sets a minimum number of circuits for a rental. On 1 March 2023 you can't demand extra circuits under a specific rule. You can ask for an electrical safety check and its report, and you can ask for repairs if an electrician finds a fault.

## Which versions apply on 1 March 2023

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 101**, incorporating amendments as at 7 September 2022. The file is rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf, in force from 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021.** The file is rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf, in force from 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The file name and metadata call it "version 002", but the text I retrieved doesn't show its Authorised Version number, so I can't confirm that number.

---

## What the law says

**1. There is no rule on the number of circuits.** The electrical safety minimum standard is about protection devices, not how many circuits you have. It says that **"On and from 29 March 2023"**, all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf):
- a switchboard-type circuit breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000; and
- a switchboard-type residual current device (RCD) that complies with AS/NZS 3190, 61008.1 or 61009.1.

⚠️ **On 1 March 2023 this standard is not yet in force.** It starts 28 days later. Even then, it only requires that the circuits are protected, not that power points are spread over several circuits [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**2. Rules already in force on 1 March 2023:**
- **Duty to maintain.** The rental provider must keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation." This applies no matter the age of the property or how much rent you pay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks.** A licensed or registered electrician must check the electrical installations every 2 years. If no check was done in the 2 years before you moved in, the rental provider must arrange one as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Safety check records.** The record of a check must include the electrician's name and licence number, the date, the results and the repairs needed. It must also include a report prepared under AS/NZS 3019. The rental provider must give you a copy within **7 days** of your written request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs** include "a dangerous electrical fault" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). A breaker tripping under heavy load may simply be the breaker working as designed, so whether you have a "fault" is a question for an electrician. The documents don't answer it.

## What you can do or ask for

1. **Tell the rental provider in writing** about the tripping. You must do this as soon as practicable for a breakdown of facilities they provided [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask in writing for the date of the latest electrical safety check and a copy of the report.** They must provide the report within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If no check has been done in the last 2 years, ask them to arrange one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **If an electrician finds a dangerous fault (urgent repair):**
   - If you've taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider to fix it and they haven't, you can arrange the repair yourself. They must repay reasonable costs up to **$2,500** within 7 days of your written notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
   - Or you can apply to VCAT, which must hear the case within **2 business days** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **If it's a non-urgent repair:** if the rental provider hasn't acted within **14 days** of your written notice, you can:
   - ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf); or
   - apply to VCAT, which must hear the case within **7 days** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

   VCAT can also let you pay your rent into the Rent Special Account [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Ask permission to add a circuit.** You need the rental provider's written consent to install fixtures [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). However, they must not unreasonably refuse changes that are "required for health and safety purposes," and they can require the work to be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If they refuse unreasonably, you can apply to VCAT, which must hear the case within 5 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
6. **After 29 March 2023,** if outlets or lights aren't protected by a compliant circuit breaker and RCD, that's a breach of a rental minimum standard. A failure to meet a minimum standard counts as an urgent repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**Don't** bypass or tamper with the RCD. It's a prescribed safety device, and renters must not interfere with one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer says 'None of the documents sets a minimum number of circuits for a rental', which covers the no-rule point. For next steps, it tells the renter to notify the rental provider in writing and to 'Ask in writing for the date of the latest electrical safety check and a copy of the report', and it explains the urgent-repair route if an electrician finds a dangerous fault.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither forbidden claim: it says 'None of the documents sets a minimum number of circuits for a rental' and 'On 1 March 2023 this standard is not yet in force. It starts 28 days later.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as 'Authorised Version No. 101' (link 97-109aa101) and the Regulations by file name 'rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf' and link 21-3sra002 ('version 002'), and every rule it applies comes from those in-force versions, including the 29 March 2023 electrical standard, which appears in version 002 itself.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
# Can a rooming house operator charge you to use coin-operated washing machines? (as at 15 October 2026)

**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say directly whether coin-operated laundry charges are allowed or banned. The Act doesn't specifically ban charging for services, but it does set conditions when an operator charges for them.

**What I used:** On 15 October 2026 the law in force is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115** (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf"), which includes amendments up to 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the **Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023** ("rt-rooming-house-standards-regs-2023-v002-2024-12-01.pdf", in force from 1 December 2024) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** ("rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", in force from 30 June 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Standards Regulations file doesn't show its Authorised Version number, only "v002". I also didn't find a newer version, so I can't confirm it was still current on 15 October 2026.

---

## What the law says

- **You have a right to use the facilities.** You have the right to use the facilities in the rooming house [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The operator must give you access to them "during all reasonable hours" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Washing machines are required.** Since 26 February 2024, the operator must provide a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, based on the maximum number the house can hold. They must also provide a laundry trough with hot and cold water and a clothes line or other drying facility [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). The standard says the machine must be provided. **It doesn't say whether the operator can charge to use it** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).
- **Conditions if the operator charges for services.** If an operator charges for services, they must:
  - (a) give you a separate schedule of the amounts for those services **before you move in**; and
  - (b) if you use any of those services, give you an **itemised account showing your individual use** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Only certain charges are expressly allowed.** The Act expressly allows charges outside rent only for electricity, gas and water used **in your room**, and only if the room is separately metered. Those charges can't be more than the supplier charges [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This rule doesn't apply to shared rooms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Laundry isn't mentioned.
- **Public and community housing operators have a cap.** If your operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, it may charge a service charge for laundry. This applies only where your individual use can't practically be measured. The charge must not be more than the cost of providing the service [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Fixed-term agreements.** A fixed-term rooming house agreement must not include a term that "unreasonably limits the resident's use of utilities" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the schedule of charges.** The operator should have given you the laundry charges in writing before you moved in. You can also ask for an itemised account of your use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the house rules and your agreement.** If a house rule about the laundry seems unreasonable, you can ask VCAT to declare it unreasonable. VCAT may declare it invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can also ask VCAT to cancel or change a term of your agreement that is harsh or unconscionable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If a machine breaks down:** the operator must keep facilities and equipment in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A breakdown of an appliance supplied for laundering counts as an urgent repair [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **If the operator stops providing a service,** your rent must be reduced by an agreed amount or an amount set by VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **If your operator is Homes Victoria or a registered agency,** you can apply to VCAT to have a service charge withdrawn or changed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Bottom line:** None of these documents says coin-operated machines are unlawful. If you're unsure, Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181) can give advice on your situation [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: the answer says the operator must provide 'a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents', notes the standard 'doesn't say whether the operator can charge to use it', states the schedule must be given 'before you move in', and advises 'Ask for the schedule of charges.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never says the machines must be free ("None of these documents says coin-operated machines are unlawful"), it states there are rules ("it does set conditions when an operator charges for them"), and it limits the cost cap to "Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency" rather than all rooming houses.

It also relies only on the in-force Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 version 009 ('21-3sra009').

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
# Mould in rental ad photos (law as at 1 October 2025)

**Versions in force on 1 October 2025:**
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110** (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", in force 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004** (file "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf", in force 1 July 2025 to 24 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

---

## 1. Can they advertise it like that?

**Short answer: the documents don't contain a rule that stops a place with mould from being advertised.** In Version 110, the advertising rules I found only deal with rent. The rent must be advertised as a fixed amount (s 30F), and an ad must not make a false or misleading statement about the rent (s 30G) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Neither section covers a property's condition. I can't say whether later versions add such a rule because I didn't retrieve them.

Other rules do still apply:

- **Mould is covered by the minimum standards.** "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" (Schedule 4, clause 8) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **The place must meet the standards by move-in day.** The rental provider must make sure the premises meet the minimum standards "on or before the day on which the renter enters into occupation" (s 65A(1)). The penalty is **60 penalty units for a person** or **300 penalty units for a company** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). One penalty unit is **$203.51** for the financial year starting 1 July 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **They must tell you certain things before you sign.** Before signing, the rental provider must tell you whether the premises meet the minimum standards. On and from 31 December 2021, they must also tell you if they've received a repair notice **in the last 3 years** about mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure (s 30D(e); reg 16(2)(b)–(c)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **They can't mislead you.** A rental provider or agent must not get you to sign by making false or misleading statements about "the characteristics of the premises" (s 30E(3)(d)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## 2. Is the photo enough to prove the place fails the standards?

**The documents don't say what evidence is enough.** Keep two points in mind:

- The standard only covers mould and damp **"caused by or related to the building structure"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo might show that mould is there, but it can't show what caused it. Mould from something else wouldn't break this standard.
- Breaking the rule depends on the condition **on or before move-in day** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A photo taken earlier doesn't show that the mould will still be there on the day you move in.

---

## What you can do or ask

1. **Before signing:** Ask the agent in writing whether the premises meet the minimum standards and whether they've had a mould or damp repair notice in the last 3 years. They're required to tell you both [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **If you've signed but haven't moved in:** You can end the agreement before you take possession if the premises "do not meet any rental minimum standards" (s 91L(f)) or "are not in good repair" (s 91L(a)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **On or right after move-in:** If the premises don't meet the standards, you can ask the rental provider for **urgent repairs** to fix them (s 65A(2)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). They must also keep the premises in good repair and reasonably fit to live in, even if you knew about the problem before moving in (s 68(1), (1A)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Record it in the condition report:** You have **5 business days** after moving in to return the condition report, and you can note where you disagree (s 35(2)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The form tells you to take photos [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). When the rental provider receives the report, it counts as notice of the defects listed in it (s 36(1A)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This is where your own photos become useful.
5. **If you think the ad is misleading:** When an agent makes claims in trade or commerce before an agreement is signed, the Director can require them to back those claims up within **21 days** (s 510L) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Proceedings for an offence under the Act can be brought by the Director, by someone the Director authorises, or by a police officer (s 508) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The answer quotes the mould standard ('free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'). It says the photo alone doesn't prove a breach ('A photo might show that mould is there, but it can't show what caused it'). It gives several next steps, including asking the agent, ending the agreement before moving in under s 91L, and requesting urgent repairs.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not claim the photo proves illegality or that advertising a non-compliant property is banned; it says "the documents don't contain a rule that stops a place with mould from being advertised" and "A photo might show that mould is there, but it can't show what caused it."

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
# Getting a friend out when you let them move in without the agent's consent

**Version applied:** On 15 October 2026 the law in force is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 115**, which includes amendments up to 13 October 2026 (file: rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 (file: rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**Short answer:** The documents don't set out any steps you have to follow to make your friend leave. What they do show is the risk to *your* tenancy.

---

## What the law says

- **Consent is required.** A renter "must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the residential rental provider's written consent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard rental agreement says the same thing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **A sub-let without consent is invalid.** It is invalid "unless the Tribunal has determined that consent is not required" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your landlord could end your tenancy over it.** The landlord can give you a notice to vacate if you have "assigned or sub-let or purported to assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the residential rental provider's consent." The termination date in that notice must be **at least 14 days** after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Any such notice must be done properly.** It is only valid if it uses the prescribed form, is addressed to you, is signed, gives the reasons and states the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **You're responsible for visitors.** A renter and any visitor must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises or common areas [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You also must not let visitors use the premises in a way that interferes with neighbours' "reasonable peace, comfort or privacy" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Sub-tenant or guest?** These rules apply if your friend is a **sub-tenant**, for example someone paying you rent to live there. The documents don't explain how to tell a sub-tenant from a guest, so I can't say which one your friend is.

---

## What you can do or ask

1. **Removing your friend.** The documents contain **no procedure** for a renter to give notice to, or evict, a person they let in, such as a sub-tenant or lodger. They don't say what notice period applies or whether a tribunal order is needed. I can't fill that gap.
2. **If you plan to move out yourself, be careful.** Someone who lives at the premises as their main home, but isn't on the lease, can ask the Tribunal to order the landlord to give them a lease. They can do this if, for example, you give notice of intention to vacate or hand back vacant possession [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can make that order if it's satisfied of three things [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
   - the person could reasonably be expected to meet a renter's duties
   - they would likely suffer severe hardship if forced to leave
   - their hardship would be greater than the landlord's
3. **If the landlord gives you a notice to vacate, you can challenge it.** You can apply to VCAT, for example if you disagree with the reason or the notice wasn't given properly [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If you don't leave, the landlord has to apply to VCAT for a possession order. Landlords "cannot personally use force to remove you"; only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **Get advice.** The regulations point renters to community legal organisations listed on the Consumer Affairs Victoria website, and to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting or 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Given the gaps above, it's worth asking them how to get your friend to leave lawfully.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On the arrangement, the answer says the rules apply only if the friend is a "sub-tenant, for example someone paying you rent to live there" rather than a guest, which names payment as a deciding fact. On consent, it quotes that a renter "must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the residential rental provider's written consent."

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the four fail conditions is asserted. The answer says 'The documents contain no procedure for a renter to give notice to, or evict, a person they let in'. The 14-day period applies only to the landlord's notice to the renter. Nothing suggests a lockout or that the friend has no rights. The friend's Tribunal application is limited to listed situations, such as 'if, for example, you give notice of intention to vacate or hand back vacant possession'.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115' (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115), and the only other document it relies on is the in-force 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 009' (link 21-3sra009), with no rules taken from any other version.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Which law applies:** On 1 November 2019 the version in force was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088** (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf", dated 2 July 2019). It was in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That version has endnotes with later amending text that uses words like "renter" and "residential rental provider" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That text wasn't in force on your date, so I haven't relied on it.

---

## What the law says

**1. Asking for repairs is a right under the Act.**
- Your landlord must keep the premises "maintained in good repair" (s 68(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You can ask the Director to investigate non-urgent repairs if you gave the landlord written notice and the repairs weren't done "within 14 days after being given the notice" (s 74) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You can also ask the Tribunal for urgent or non-urgent repair orders (ss 73, 75) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**2. A retaliatory notice can be "of no effect", but only for certain notices.**
- A notice to vacate under **s 263 (no specified reason)** or **s 261 (end of fixed term)** "is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act" (s 266(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You're month to month (periodic), so the relevant one is most likely a **s 263** notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. There's a deadline to challenge a s 263 notice.**
- You can't apply to the Tribunal to challenge the validity of a s 263 notice "after the end of **60 days** after the date on which the notice is given" (s 266(3)(c)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

---

## What to check

| Check | What the Act says |
|---|---|
| **Which section is the notice under?** | The retaliation rule in s 266(2) covers only s 261 and s 263 notices [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). |
| **Is the notice period long enough?** | A s 263 notice must give **at least 120 days** (s 263(2)(c)). For a periodic tenancy under s 230(3A), it's the prescribed period, or 120 days if none is prescribed (s 263(2)(b)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). |
| **Is the notice in the right form?** | A notice to vacate isn't valid unless it's in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed by the landlord or agent, and states a termination date. It must also give a reason, except for a s 263 notice (s 319) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). |
| **Is the landlord's order already in place?** | A landlord can't give a s 263 notice while an excessive-rent order under s 47 is in force (s 265) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). |
| **If the notice is under s 255 (repairs)** | It needs **at least 60 days** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The landlord must also intend to do the work right after the termination date, have all permits and consents, and the work must be impossible to do properly unless you leave [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can challenge it **within 30 days** after it's given (s 321B) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). |

---

## What you can do

1. **Apply to the Tribunal within 60 days** of the date the notice was given, arguing that it's of no effect under s 266(2) because it responded to your repair request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Keep copies of your repair requests and the notice. The same-day timing is the link you'll be relying on.
2. **Keep pursuing the repairs** through the Director (s 74) or the Tribunal (ss 73, 75) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. **If the landlord applies for a possession order:** for a s 263 notice, they can apply only after the termination date has passed and you haven't left, and no later than 30 days after that date (ss 322(2), 326(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal must be satisfied the landlord "was entitled to give the notice" before making the order (s 330(1)(a)(i)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:** They don't say what evidence the Tribunal needs to find a notice was "given in response to" a repair request, or how to lodge an application. You'd need to check those with the Tribunal or a tenancy advice service.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer names a s 263 notice as the 'no specified reason' notice and says it 'must give at least 120 days (s 263(2)(c))'. (2) It quotes s 266(2): such a notice 'is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act', and links this to the repair request. (3) It says to 'Apply to the Tribunal within 60 days of the date the notice was given' (s 266(3)(c)), and the Tribunal is VCAT.

must-not-say.reason: Yes, none of the listed errors are asserted. The answer says a notice must give a reason "except for a s 263 notice" and gives the challenge deadline for this s 263 notice as "60 days after the date on which the notice is given". Its other periods do not apply to challenging this notice: the "within 30 days" figure is for a different, hypothetical s 255 notice, and the other 30-day figure is the landlord's possession-order window.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Authorised Version No. 088" (file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf", dated 2 July 2019, link 97-109aa088), which is the version in force on 1 November 2019. Every rule it applies (ss 263, 266(2)–(3) and others) comes from that version, and it mentions later amending text in the endnotes only to say it was not relied on.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
# Rent bidding and the "withdrawn" email under Victorian law (as at 1 October 2025)

**Law applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 110**, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025 (document "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf"). It was in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025, so it covers 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

**1. Rent must be advertised at a fixed amount.** A rental provider or their agent must not advertise or offer a property unless the rent is stated as a fixed amount. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a person or 300 for a company [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**2. Rent bidding: the agent can't ask for more, but the Act doesn't stop another applicant offering more.** Under section 30F(3), a rental provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount." The same penalties apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This bans the provider or agent from asking for higher offers. If the other applicant offered more without being asked, the Act doesn't say that alone is an offence. So the key question is whether the agent invited or encouraged a higher offer.

**3. The rent can't be advertised misleadingly.** A provider or agent who advertises a property must not make a false or misleading statement about the rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This section applies to providers and agents who are **not** acting in trade or commerce. It doesn't limit the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria), which would cover agents acting in trade or commerce [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**4. Relisting at a higher rent.** The Act text I found doesn't ban relisting at a higher price, as long as the new rent is also advertised as a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**5. The email saying you withdrew.** The documents have no provision that deals directly with an agent falsely recording that you withdrew. I can't tell you from these documents which rule, if any, that breaks.

**6. Related protections that may apply:**
- Your application information can only be used to assess your suitability as a renter or for another requirement of the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If you were refused because of a protected attribute (such as race, age, disability or having children), that is unlawful [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You could then apply to VCAT for compensation under section 210AA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

---

## What you can do

- **Go to VCAT.** VCAT can hear "any matter arising in relation to a residential rental agreement **or a proposed residential rental agreement**" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You never became a party to a lease, so you would need VCAT's **leave** (permission) to apply. VCAT gives leave only if it's satisfied you have "an interest and personal involvement" in the matter that is enough to justify it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Note the possible consequences for the provider.** Sections 30F and 30G are offences [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If a provider is convicted of an offence under the Act, they can be entered on the Rental Non-compliance Register [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **If discrimination is involved,** you can apply to VCAT for compensation (but not if you've already brought the same dispute under the *Equal Opportunity Act 2010*) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You can also call Victoria Legal Aid on 1300 792 387 or complain to VEOHRC on 1300 292 153 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Questions to put to the agent in writing:**
  - When and how was your "withdrawal" recorded?
  - Did the agent ask anyone, including the other applicant, to offer more than the advertised rent?
  - Why was the advertised rent changed?

The documents don't explain how to report a suspected section 30F breach to Consumer Affairs Victoria, so you should seek advice on that, for example from Victoria Legal Aid [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

---

## What to save as evidence

The documents don't give an evidence checklist. These items match what you would need to show under the sections above:

- **The original advertisement** (screenshots with the date, the listing URL and the advertised rent). This supports a fixed-amount or misleading-advertising claim under sections 30F and 30G.
- **Your application and confirmation that it was received,** showing you applied at the advertised rent.
- **The "withdrawn" email,** kept in full, including the original headers, sender, date and time. Also save anything showing you never withdrew, such as your sent messages and call logs.
- **The new listing at the higher rent,** with dated screenshots.
- **Anything showing the agent invited higher offers,** such as messages, call notes, or wording like "offers above" or "best offer". This is the core of a section 30F(3) claim.
- **Details of what you heard about the higher offer:** who told you, when, and what exactly they said. Second-hand information is weaker evidence, so try to get it in writing.
- **Your costs or losses,** if you plan to claim compensation.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: (1) relisting: 'The Act text I found doesn't ban relisting at a higher price, as long as the new rent is also advertised as a fixed amount'; (2) soliciting: section 30F(3) bars a provider or agent from soliciting or inviting an offer above the advertised rent; (3) unsolicited offer, the hardest point: 'If the other applicant offered more without being asked, the Act doesn't say that alone is an offence. So the key question is whether the agent invited or encouraged a higher offer,' which signals that only inviting was banned; (4) the email: 'The documents have no provision that deals directly with an agent falsely recording that you withdrew.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the three claims is made. The answer says "The Act text I found doesn't ban relisting at a higher price," says that if the other applicant offered more unprompted "the Act doesn't say that alone is an offence," and never claims the applicant can force the agent to rent the property to them.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025' (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf, link 97-109aa110), and its only other source is the Regulations link 21-3sra004, which is version 004, the version in force on 1 October 2025.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer: no. A "no" from the agent doesn't count as a valid refusal. To refuse properly, the rental provider (the landlord) must apply to VCAT within 14 days of getting your request. Your request went in about 21 days ago, so if no application was made in time, the law treats your request as approved.**

**Law in force on 15 October 2026:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 115**, including amendments as at 13 October 2026 (document "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", dated 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

### What the law says

- **When you can keep a pet:** You can keep one if the rental provider agrees in writing, or if VCAT makes an order allowing it (s 71A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your request:** It must be made on the Director's approved form and given to the rental provider (s 71B) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You've done this.
- **No unreasonable refusals:** The rental provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent to the renter keeping a pet" (s 71C(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The 14-day rule:** The rental provider "is taken to have consented" unless, "within 14 days after being given the request," it applies to VCAT under s 71D (s 71C(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Act doesn't give the rental provider any other way to refuse. An email or phone call from the agent saying no is not enough.
- **If they applied to VCAT in time,** VCAT can either allow the pet or, if it's satisfied that refusing is reasonable, order that the pet be kept out (s 71E(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT may consider:
  - the type of pet
  - the type and nature of the premises
  - the appliances, fixtures and fittings
  - whether any law allows the refusal
  - any prescribed matters
  - "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" (s 71E(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

**About the allergy and the owner rarely visiting:** The documents don't say whether an owner's allergy makes refusing reasonable, or how much it matters that the owner rarely visits. If VCAT hears the matter, both points would only come in under "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't tell you how VCAT would weigh them.

The standard rental agreement form says the same thing in summary: the renter must ask before keeping a pet, and the rental provider "must not unreasonably refuse a request to keep a pet." This is item 30 of Form 1 in the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (document "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", dated 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

---

### What you can do

1. **Ask the agent in writing:** "Did the rental provider apply to VCAT under s 71D within 14 days of receiving my pet request?" If they didn't, point out that under s 71C(2) the rental provider is taken to have consented [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Work out exactly when they got your request.** The 14 days run from when the request was *given* to them [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Keep proof of the date you sent it, and the agent's reply.
3. **If an application was made in time,** take part in the VCAT hearing. You can argue that refusing is unreasonable, for example by explaining the dog and the apartment, and that the owner rarely visits [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Don't ignore a VCAT order to remove the dog.** If VCAT orders the pet out and you haven't complied 14 days after the order takes effect, the rental provider can give you a notice to vacate. That notice must give you at least 28 days (s 91ZZG) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**Also worth knowing:**
- If the dog is an assistance dog under the *Equal Opportunity Act 2010*, it isn't a "pet" under this Act at all [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If your lease started before the pet rules began, they still apply, because you now want to keep a pet (s 533) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** No, you don't automatically have to leave on the date in the notice. But the notice also hasn't been cancelled. In law it stays in place until it's properly withdrawn or VCAT rules on it.

This is based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110** (file rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf, in force 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025), which was the version in force on 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

---

### What the law says

- **The notice doesn't lapse on its own.** A notice to vacate is withdrawn *only* if a notice of withdrawal is given. That notice must be (a) in writing, (b) signed by the person who gave the notice, and (c) signed by the person who received it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). So the buyer pulling out doesn't cancel it.
- **Your landlord can't make you leave by themselves.** A rental agreement ends only in the ways the Act allows [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). After a notice to vacate, it ends if you move out on or after the termination date, or under section 334 (after a possession order) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A landlord who forces or tries to force you out other than as the Act allows faces up to 150 penalty units (an individual) or 750 penalty units (a company) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Only Victoria Police can forcibly evict you, and only under a VCAT warrant [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **VCAT has to check several things before ordering you out.** It must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice, that the notice hasn't been withdrawn, and that a possession order is "reasonable and proportionate" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Whether the sale ground still applies is less clear.** The sale ground (s 91ZZB) covers premises that are "to be sold *or offered for sale* with vacant possession" straight after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). So a failed sale doesn't automatically make the notice invalid. If your landlord still plans to sell with vacant possession, the ground may still apply. If they've dropped the sale, you have a stronger argument. The Act doesn't directly say what happens when a buyer pulls out, so the documents don't settle this.
- **Other ways the notice can be invalid:**
  - It must give at least **60 days'** notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
  - It must use the prescribed form, give reasons, and come with supporting documentary evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
  - On a fixed-term lease, it has no effect if the termination date is **before the end of the fixed term** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
  - It has no effect if giving it would be direct discrimination [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask

1. **Ask your landlord to withdraw the notice in writing.** It's only withdrawn if it's in writing and you both sign it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Challenge the notice at VCAT.** You can do this on or before a possession order hearing, but you must apply **within 30 days after the notice was given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Stay and defend a possession application.** If you're still there after the termination date, the landlord has to apply to VCAT, and you can argue the points above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **Know the re-letting rule.** If the landlord gets the property back under a sale notice, they can't rent it out as a home for **6 months** unless VCAT allows it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
5. **If you'd rather go,** you can leave early with at least **14 days'** notice of intention to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The rental forms suggest getting advice quickly, for example from a community legal centre or Consumer Affairs Victoria on **1300 558 181** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The hardest one, that the answer depends on the notice's ground and evidence, is met by: 'covers premises that are "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession"... If your landlord still plans to sell with vacant possession, the ground may still apply. If they've dropped the sale, you have a stronger argument', together with the documentary evidence requirement. The answer also states the 60-day minimum, that withdrawal must be in writing and signed by both parties, and next steps including written withdrawal or a VCAT challenge within 30 days.

None of the failure conditions are asserted: the answer says "the buyer pulling out doesn't cancel it," that withdrawal must be "signed by the person who gave the notice, and (c) signed by the person who received it," and that the notice "must give at least **60 days'** notice"; the 14-day figure is about the tenant's own notice of intention to vacate, not the landlord's notice to vacate.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
# Short answer: No, not yet. Without a valid rent increase notice, the higher rent isn't legally payable.

**Law in force on 1 October 2025:**
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110** (file *rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf*, dated 6 August 2025, in force 6 August to 24 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The version number comes from the file's title and metadata; the cover page with "Authorised Version No." wasn't in the text I retrieved.
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004** (file *rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf*, "incorporating amendments as at 1 July 2025") [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

**1. A rent increase needs proper notice.** The rental provider must give you **at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form** of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The prescribed form is **Form 5, "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises"** (regulation 21) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Form 5 says plainly: *"A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases."* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

**2. The notice must include specific details** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):
- the amount of the increase
- how the increase was calculated
- a statement of your right to ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria, within 30 days after the notice is given, to investigate and report on the proposed rent

Form 5 also has to show the current rent, the new rent, the start date and how it was delivered [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**3. An email only counts if both are true:**
- it actually is the prescribed form, and
- you agreed to receive notices by email. Form 5 lists email delivery only "if consent has been provided by the renter" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

Replying to an agent's emails doesn't count as agreeing to receive notices that way [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**4. Other limits:**
- Rent can't be increased more often than once every 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- During a fixed-term agreement, rent can only go up if the agreement itself sets the amount or method of the increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**5. An increase that breaks these rules is invalid** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### So, do you have to pay, and from when?
- **Right now:** No. Based on what you've described (an informal email and no Form 5), the increase doesn't meet section 44, so it is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Keep paying your current rent on time.
- **Their refusal to negotiate doesn't change this.** Whether the increase is valid depends on the notice, not on whether you agreed.
- **From when:** The higher rent can only start on the start date in a valid Form 5 notice, and that date must be **at least 60 days after the notice is given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). If you get a valid notice, you'll then need to pay the new rent from that date unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

---

## What you can do

1. **Reply in writing** and ask the agent for a notice in the prescribed form (Form 5) under section 44(1) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Keep a copy of their email and your reply.
2. **Check your lease** to see whether you agreed to receive notices by email [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Also check whether it's a fixed-term agreement and whether it allows increases during the term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check when the rent last went up.** If it was less than 12 months ago, an increase can't happen yet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **If you get a valid notice and think the new rent is too high:**
   - Apply in writing to the **Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days** after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This is free [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
   - After you get the Director's report, you can apply to **VCAT within 30 days** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
   - You can also go straight to VCAT without a report, with its permission ("leave"). You'd need to apply after the 30 days have passed and show good reasons for skipping the Director [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
5. **For more help,** contact Consumer Affairs Victoria at consumer.vic.gov.au/renting or 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

---

**Gaps in the documents:**
- These two documents don't say whether you can get back extra rent you pay on an invalid increase. Only the rooming house, caravan and Part 4A sections have refund rules, and those don't apply to an ordinary rental [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The documents don't cover what happens if the agent insists on the higher rent anyway.

This is general information from the legislation, not legal advice. Consumer Affairs Victoria can help with your specific situation.

It states that an informal email without Form 5 'doesn't meet section 44, so it is invalid', so the higher rent isn't payable yet. It also gives next steps, including 'Keep paying your current rent on time' and replying in writing to ask the agent for Form 5.

Keep paying your current rent on time"), never says the increase starts from the email date, gives only "at least 60 days notice", and allows email delivery "if consent has been provided by the renter".
