The answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110' (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf, link 97-109aa110) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004' (rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf, link 21-3sra004, as at 1 July 2025); both are the versions in force on 1 October 2025, and it relies on no other version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** You can arrange the repair, but you can't legally do it without telling the owner. The law requires you to notify them in writing. The documents don't say how this would affect the owner's insurance.

**Which law applies on 15 October 2026:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 115**, which includes amendments up to 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", in force from 13 Oct 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I've also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009 (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", in force from 30 June 2026). That file's Authorised Version number isn't shown in what I retrieved [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

---

### What the law says

- **You must not damage the property.** Renters and their visitors must not "intentionally or negligently cause damage" to the property. Fair wear and tear doesn't count as damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 61). The Act doesn't mention pets in this context. Whether dog-chewed skirting boards count as damage or wear and tear isn't something the documents settle, but chewing is generally hard to call wear and tear.
- **You must tell the owner in writing.** Once you know about damage, you must give the rental provider written notice "as soon as practicable." The notice must say that the damage happened and what it is [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 62(1)). You can send it by email [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 62(2)). Section 72AA repeats the same duty to report damage in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). So fixing it quietly would go against these rules.
- **Only a qualified person may do repairs.** The standard rental agreement says "only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The owner can ask you to fix it, or fix it and charge you.** If you caused the damage, the owner can give you a written repair notice. The notice can either:
  - require you to repair it at your own cost within **14 days**, done "in a tradesman-like manner", or
  - say the owner will do the repairs and you'll pay the reasonable cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 78).

  If the owner does the repairs, you must pay them back within **14 days** after the work is finished, once they give you written details of the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 79(3)–(4)). If you're in hardship, you can give written notice that you need an extra 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 79(6)).
- **The bond can cover it.** The owner can claim "the reasonable cost of repairs to, or the restoration of, the rented premises… as a result of damage caused by the renter," taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 411AB(1)(a)). At least **3 days** before claiming, they must give you evidence supporting the claim, and that evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 411(1A)–(1B)).
- **The final inspection will show it anyway.** Within **10 days** after the agreement ends, the owner or agent must complete the condition report. They must do it with you present, or give you a reasonable chance to attend [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 35(5)).

### Insurance

The documents **don't say** whether this damage, or a repair done without telling the owner, would affect the owner's insurance. The only related rule is that a lease term making you liable "by default for an insurance excess" under the owner's policy is banned [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (reg 11(h)). That means you can't be made to pay their excess automatically just because a clause says so.

---

### What you can do

1. **Email the owner or agent now** saying the skirting boards were damaged and describing the damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Offer to have it fixed by a suitably qualified tradesperson** at your cost, and ask them to agree in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This matches what a repair notice could require of you anyway [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Take dated photos** before and after the repair. Go to the final inspection so the condition report reflects the repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
4. **If the owner claims from your bond**, ask for the evidence they must give you at least 3 days before claiming, and check it against the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **If the dog was approved**, keep the written consent or Tribunal order. You can only keep a pet with one of these [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) (s 71A).

The other three points are covered: written notice 'as soon as practicable', the insurance question left unsettled, and the email-the-owner next step.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## Short answer
Neither document sets a rule on how many circuits a rental must have. There is an electrical safety standard, but on 1 March 2023 it had not started yet. You can still ask for the safety check records and for repairs.

**Versions that applied on 1 March 2023:**
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 002**, incorporating amendments as at 1 June 2022 (file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf", dated 1 June 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 101** (file "rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf", dated 7 September 2022) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

---

## What the law says

**Number of circuits:** The minimum standards don't require a set number of circuits, and they don't say how power points must be split across circuits.

**Electrical safety standard (not yet in force):** "On and from 29 March 2023", all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to both of these [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf):
- a switchboard-type circuit breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000
- a switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) that complies with AS/NZS 3190, 61008.1 or 61009.1

On 1 March 2023 this was still 28 days away. Even once it applies, it's about protection devices, not how many circuits you have.

**Safety checks:** The landlord must have a licensed or registered electrician do an electrical safety check every 2 years [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If no check was done in the 2 years before you moved in, they must arrange one as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**Repairs:** The landlord must keep the premises in good repair and reasonably fit for living in. This applies regardless of the property's age or the rent you pay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). "Urgent repairs" include a "dangerous electrical fault" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a breaker tripping under heavy load counts as one. A breaker that trips may just be doing its job.

**What you must not do:**
- You must not remove, switch off or interfere with an RCD [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- You can't make alterations, such as rewiring or adding a circuit, without the landlord's written consent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

---

## What you can do or ask for

1. **Tell the landlord in writing.** You must give written notice as soon as practicable when facilities break down [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Describe the tripping and ask an electrician to look at it.
2. **Ask for the safety check records.**
   - The landlord must tell you the date of the most recent check, in writing, if you ask [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
   - They must give you a copy of the latest check within 7 days of your written request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). It must include the electrician's name and licence number, the results and any repairs needed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
   - If no check has been done in the last 2 years, ask for one.
3. **If an electrician finds a dangerous fault (urgent repair):**
   - Ask the landlord or agent to fix it immediately. If they don't, you can arrange the repair yourself. They must pay you back the reasonable cost, up to $2,500, within 7 days of your written notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
   - You can apply to VCAT if you can't afford the repair, it costs more than $2,500, or the landlord refuses to pay. VCAT must hear the case within 2 business days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **If it isn't urgent:** If repairs aren't done within 14 days of your written notice, you can do either of these [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf):
   - ask the Director (Consumer Affairs Victoria) to investigate
   - apply to VCAT, which must hear the case within 7 days
5. **From 29 March 2023:** You can check that all power and lighting circuits have a compliant circuit breaker and RCD [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Not meeting a minimum standard counts as an urgent repair [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

You can **ask** the landlord to add a circuit. However, these documents don't require them to add one just because power points are shared.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On the number of circuits, the answer says "Neither document sets a rule on how many circuits a rental must have" and "The minimum standards don't require a set number of circuits." On next steps, it tells the user to notify the landlord in writing and request repairs, says a dangerous fault is an urgent repair, and advises asking for the safety check records: "The landlord must tell you the date of the most recent check, in writing, if you ask."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never sets a minimum number of circuits or calls shared circuits illegal ('The minimum standards don't require a set number of circuits'), and it says the circuit breaker and RCD standard is 'not yet in force' and 'On 1 March 2023 this was still 28 days away'.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 002' (21-3sra002, dated 1 June 2022) and 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 101' (97-109aa101, dated 7 September 2022), and cites every rule it applies, including the 29 March 2023 standard, to those versions only.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say directly whether a rooming house operator can use coin-operated washing machines. Nothing I found bans charging for laundry, but the law does set some conditions.

**What I relied on (the versions in force on 15 October 2026):**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115 (rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023*, Authorised Version No. 002 (rt-rooming-house-standards-regs-2023-v002-2024-12-01.pdf, dated 1 December 2024) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). This is the latest version I found.
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 009 (rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf, in force from 30 June 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)

---

### What the law says

1. **The operator must provide washing machines.** Since 26 February 2024, the rooming house must have the following "in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents": a laundry trough with hot and cold water, a space for a washing machine with water outlets, a clothes line or other drying facility, and **a washing machine** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). Two machines would cover a house of up to 24 residents. The rule says a machine must be provided, but it doesn't say whether it must be free [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

2. **Charging for services has conditions.** If the operator charges residents for services, they must:
   - give you a separate list of those charges **before you move in**, and
   - if you use the services, give you an **itemised account** of your own use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

3. **Rent already covers use of facilities.** Under the Act, rent is the amount you pay "to occupy a room and use facilities and services" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). "Facilities" includes laundry facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The only charges the Act lists as separate from rent are those under ss 108 and 109A, and neither covers coin laundries:
   - **s 108** covers electricity, gas and water used in a separately metered room [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - **s 109A** lets only Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency charge for laundry, and only when use "it is not possible or practicable to accurately measure". Even then, the charge can't be more than what the service costs to provide [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

   The documents don't say whether a coin machine counts as a lawful extra "service" or as a facility your rent already pays for.

4. **Other duties of the operator:**
   - Keep facilities and equipment in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - Let you use facilities "during all reasonable hours" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - Not unreasonably restrict your "proper use and enjoyment" of the facilities [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - A broken laundry appliance counts as an **urgent repair** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

---

### What you can do or ask

- **Ask for the list of charges.** Ask whether you were given a separate list of service charges before you moved in, and ask for an itemised account of your use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the machines.** Make sure there is at least one working machine for every 12 residents [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). Report any breakdown, which you're required to do anyway [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can treat it as an urgent repair [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenge house rules.** If the coin-machine charge is set out in the house rules, those rules must be reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can ask VCAT to declare a rule unreasonable, and it can declare the rule invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Report non-repairs.** If repairs aren't done within 14 days of your notice, you can ask Consumer Affairs Victoria (the Director) to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Get advice.** Because the documents don't settle this, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 558 181 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes: all four points are covered, and the hardest one is met by the words 'The rule says a machine must be provided, but it doesn't say whether it must be free.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the machines must be free; it says the rule 'doesn't say whether it must be free'. It never says there are no rules on charges; it says 'Charging for services has conditions'. It never applies the cost cap to all rooming houses; it limits s 109A to cases where it 'lets only Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency charge for laundry'.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115 (... in force from 13 October 2026)' and 'Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, Authorised Version No. 002 (... dated 1 December 2024)'; it also cites the in-force 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009', and it relies on no other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## Short answer

**Ad photos:** The documents don't ban advertising a place with visible mould. Showing it honestly isn't misleading. What the law controls is whether the place meets the minimum standards by move-in day, and what the landlord must tell you before you sign.

**Proof:** No. A photo can suggest a problem, but it can't show on its own that the minimum standard is breached. The standard only covers mould "caused by or related to the building structure."

The versions in force on **1 October 2025** are:
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110** (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf, dated 6 August 2025), in force 6 Aug 2025 to 24 Nov 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004** (rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf, dated 1 July 2025), in force 1 Jul 2025 to 24 Nov 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

---

## What the law says

**1. The mould standard.** Each room must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" (Schedule 4, clause 8) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Mould from something else, such as how the room is used, may not breach this standard. A photo usually can't show the cause.

**2. When the standard applies.** The landlord must make sure the place meets the minimum standards **on or before the day the renter moves in**. The maximum penalty is 60 penalty units for a person and 300 for a company (s 65A(1)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The infringement penalty is 12 penalty units for a person and 60 for a company [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). So a place can show mould while it's advertised, as long as it's fixed by move-in day.

**3. Rules on advertising.** The documents only cover:
- **False or misleading representations.** A landlord or agent must not get someone to sign by misleading them, including about "the characteristics of the premises" (s 30E) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This section applies to landlords not acting in trade or commerce. Accurate photos of mould aren't misleading.
- **Rent.** False or misleading advertising of the rent is banned (s 30G) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Images taken while a current renter lives there.** These rules protect the current renter's privacy, not the condition of the property (s 89A) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**4. What the landlord must tell you before you sign.** Under reg 16(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), the landlord must disclose:
- whether the property meets the rental minimum standards (reg 16(2)(b))
- whether they've received a repair notice about mould or damp "caused by or related to the building structure" in the **last 3 years** (reg 16(2)(c))

---

## What you can do or ask

- **Before signing:** Ask the landlord or agent to confirm in writing whether the property meets the minimum standards and whether there's been a mould or damp repair notice in the last 3 years. They must tell you this [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Inspect it yourself** and ask what caused the mould and whether it will be fixed before move-in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **If it isn't fixed before you move in:** You can end the agreement by giving notice on the ground that the place doesn't meet the minimum standards (s 91L(f)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **If it isn't fixed when you move in:** You can request **urgent repairs** to bring it up to standard (s 65A(2)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Record it in the condition report:** Note the mould and attach dated, labelled photos taken close-up and from further away. A condition report listing a needed repair counts as notice to the landlord. If the report turns out wrong, you can apply to VCAT to correct it within **30 days** of the agreement starting (s 35A; s 36(1A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **If repairs aren't done:** You can apply to VCAT for a repair order and compensation (s 76), or to pay rent into the Rent Special Account (s 77) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **If you were misled:** For example, if you were told there was no mould problem, s 30E may apply [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover:** They don't say what evidence VCAT needs to decide that mould breaches the standard, or whether a photo would be enough. The condition report form only says photos "may be useful in a dispute" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You may need evidence of the cause, such as a leak, rising damp or poor ventilation, but the documents don't spell this out. For advice on your situation, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 558 181 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes: all three points are covered. The output states the mould standard ("free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure"). It says the photo alone isn't proof ("No. A photo can suggest a problem, but it can't show on its own that the minimum standard is breached"). It also gives next steps, including asking the agent, inspecting, requesting urgent repairs, and ending the agreement before move-in.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden thing: it states 'A photo can suggest a problem, but it can't show on its own that the minimum standard is breached,' and 'The documents don't ban advertising a place with visible mould... a place can show mould while it's advertised, as long as it's fixed by move-in day.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with the versions in force on 1 October 2025, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110 (rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf, dated 6 August 2025)" and "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004 (rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf, dated 1 July 2025)", and relies on no other version for the rules it applies (s 65A, s 91L, Sch 4 cl 8).

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
# Getting a friend to leave when you didn't get consent (Victoria, as at 15 October 2026)

**Law applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", **Version 115**, in force from 13 October 2026, so it applies on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", **Version 009**, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The version numbers come from the files' metadata. The excerpts don't show the "Authorised Version No." line itself.

**Short answer:** The documents don't say how a renter can make someone they let in leave. They do explain your legal position and the risks.

---

## What the law says

**1. You needed written consent.** A renter "must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the rented premises without the residential rental provider's written consent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard rental agreement terms say the same thing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**2. An arrangement without consent is invalid.** Sub-letting without consent "is invalid unless the Tribunal has determined that consent is not required" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This only matters if your friend is a sub-tenant, for example if they pay you rent for part of the place. The documents don't define sub-letting or say what happens if your friend is just staying with you.

**3. The landlord can end your tenancy over this.** If you sub-let without consent, the landlord can give you a **notice to vacate with at least 14 days' notice** (s 91ZV) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The notice must be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, state the reason and give the termination date (s 91ZZO) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- If you don't leave, the landlord can ask VCAT for a possession order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- VCAT will only make the order if it is "reasonable and proportionate" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It considers things like whether the breach is trivial, whether it has been fixed as far as practicable, and whether something short of eviction would work (s 330A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Your friend leaving could help you on the "fixed" point, but the documents don't say it would stop a notice.

**4. You're responsible for your friend's behaviour.** You must not let visitors disturb the neighbours' peace, comfort or privacy (s 60) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You and any visitor must not intentionally or negligently damage the property (s 61) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask your friend to leave.** The documents give no procedure, notice period or VCAT application for a renter removing someone they let in without consent. I can't tell you how much notice you have to give them or what to do if they refuse.
- **Be careful if you plan to move out yourself.** If you give notice that you're leaving, someone who has lived there as their main home but isn't on the lease can apply to VCAT to be given their own lease (s 91S) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT can grant this if they could reasonably meet a renter's duties, would face severe hardship, and that hardship would outweigh the landlord's (s 91T) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The consent rules, if they're useful later:** the landlord must not unreasonably refuse consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) or charge a fee for giving it. Charging a fee carries a penalty of 60 penalty units (s 84) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Get advice.** Because the documents don't cover removing your friend, contact a community legal service or Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer states that a renter 'must not assign or sub-let... without the residential rental provider's written consent'. For the hardest point, it makes the outcome depend on the arrangement and names payment as a deciding fact: 'This only matters if your friend is a sub-tenant, for example if they pay you rent for part of the place... or say what happens if your friend is just staying with you.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the fail conditions are asserted: the answer declines to give a notice period for the friend ("I can't tell you how much notice you have to give them"), never suggests a lockout or removing belongings, does not say the friend has no rights, and ties any VCAT lease application to a listed trigger ("If you give notice that you're leaving, someone who has lived there as their main home but isn't on the lease can apply to VCAT").

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
# Notice to vacate after a repair request: which law applied on 1 November 2019

This answer uses **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088** ("rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf", dated 2 July 2019). It was in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers 1 November 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

⚠️ The endnotes of that same document include amendment text that uses words like "renter" and "residential rental provider" (for example, ss 91ZZD and 91ZZI) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Those provisions were **not yet in force** on 1 November 2019, so I haven't relied on them.

---

## What the law says

**1. The key retaliation rule (s 266(2))**
A notice to vacate under **s 263 (no specified reason)** or **s 261 (end of a fixed term)** "is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**2. Asking for repairs is a right under the Act**
- The landlord must keep the rented premises "in good repair" (s 68(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- For urgent repairs, you can arrange them yourself if you can't get the landlord to act. The landlord must then repay the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less (s 72) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You can apply to the Tribunal for urgent repairs, and it must hear the application within 2 business days (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- For non-urgent repairs, you can apply to the Director to investigate. You must first have given the landlord written notice and waited 14 days without the repairs being done (s 74) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You can also ask the Tribunal for a repair order (ss 75–76), or for an order letting you pay rent into the Rent Special Account (s 77) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Notice periods for a month-to-month tenancy**
- **No reason given (s 263):** the termination date must be at least **120 days** after the notice is given. For a periodic tenancy under s 230(3A), it is the prescribed period or, if none, 120 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs ground (s 255):** at least **60 days**. The landlord must also intend to repair, renovate or reconstruct, have "obtained all necessary permits and consents," and the work must be impossible to do properly unless you leave [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**4. The retaliation rule doesn't cover every notice**
In this version, s 266(2) only applies to notices under **s 261 and s 263** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If the notice gives a different ground (for example s 255 repairs), you'd challenge it by showing that ground's conditions aren't met.

**5. Deadline to challenge a no-reason notice (s 266(3)(c))**
You can't apply to the Tribunal to challenge a s 263 notice **more than 60 days after it was given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**6. The landlord needs a Tribunal order to remove you**
If you stay past the termination date, the landlord has to apply for a possession order. The Tribunal must be satisfied of certain matters, including that you are still in possession after the termination date (s 330) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

---

## What to check or do

1. **Find the section the notice relies on.**
   - No reason given (s 263): the retaliation rule in s 266(2) can apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - Repairs ground (s 255): check for the 60-day period, the permits and consents, and whether you really need to leave for the work [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the termination date.** It should be at least 120 days away for s 263, or at least 60 days for s 255 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Gather evidence linking the notice to your repair request.** Collect your written repair requests, the dates, and the fact that the notice arrived the same day. This goes to whether it was "given in response to" you using a right under the Act (s 266(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Act within 60 days of receiving the notice** if you want to challenge a s 263 notice at the Tribunal (s 266(3)(c)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Keep pursuing the repairs.** You can still use the urgent repair process (ss 72–73) or the Director and Tribunal processes (ss 74–77) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Don't move out just because of the notice.** The landlord needs a possession order from the Tribunal (s 330) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

---

## What the documents don't cover

- **s 319 (form requirements for a notice) and ss 321B–321C (challenging a notice):** the search only found their titles in the table of contents, not their wording [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I can't tell you their exact requirements.
- **Whether leaking fixtures count as "urgent repairs":** the retrieved text doesn't include the definition.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: s 263 notices need at least 120 days; under s 266(2) a notice 'is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act'; and the answer says to 'Act within 60 days of receiving the notice if you want to challenge a s 263 notice at the Tribunal (s 266(3)(c))', where the Tribunal is VCAT.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not say the landlord needed to give a reason, since it treats a no-reason notice as valid under 's 263 (no specified reason)'. The only challenge deadline it gives is that you can't apply 'more than 60 days after it was given' (s 266(3)(c)); its other figures (the 60-day s 255 notice period and the 14-day s 74 wait) are not deadlines for challenging the notice at VCAT.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088" ("rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf", dated 2 July 2019, link 97-109aa088), and every rule it applies (ss 263, 266(2)–(3), 255, 68, 72–77, 330) comes from that in-force version, while it expressly declines to rely on the not-yet-in-force amendment text in the endnotes.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
# Rent bidding and a false "withdrawn" email: what the Act says (as at 1 October 2025)

**Version applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 110**, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf"). This version was in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025, so it covers 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

**1. Rent must be advertised as a fixed amount (s 30F(1)).**
A rental provider or their agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). There's one exception: a sign at or near the property that doesn't state any rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**2. Rent bidding is banned (s 30F(3)).**
A rental provider or agent "must not solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The penalty is **60 penalty units** for a natural person and **300 penalty units** for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The ban covers *asking for or inviting* a higher offer. The Act text I found doesn't say it's illegal to receive or accept a higher offer that nobody asked for. So the key question is whether the agent or provider invited the other person's higher offer. What you've heard secondhand doesn't prove that on its own.

**3. False or misleading statements about rent (s 30G).**
A provider or agent who promotes or advertises premises must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The penalty is the same: 60 or 300 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This section applies to providers and agents who are *not* acting in trade or commerce. It doesn't limit the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**4. The higher relisting and the "withdrawn" email.**
- **Higher relisting:** I found nothing in the documents that stops a property being relisted at a higher fixed rent. The new listing still has to state a fixed amount [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **False "withdrawn" email:** No provision in the documents deals specifically with falsely telling an applicant they withdrew.
  - Section 30E bans misleading conduct, but only conduct that *induces a person to enter* a rental agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). That doesn't clearly fit your situation.
  - The email may still matter as evidence of what happened, for example if it was used to push your application aside in favour of a higher bid.

---

## What you can do

**Report it to the Director (Consumer Affairs Victoria).** You can't prosecute this yourself. Only the Director, a person the Director authorises, or a police officer can bring proceedings for an offence under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Director also has these powers:
- **Substantiation notice (s 510L):** If the provider or agent made a claim or representation about the premises in trade or commerce, the Director can require them to provide information or documents backing it up within **21 days** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Giving false or misleading information in response is an offence carrying 60 or 300 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Infringement notices:** Authorised officers can issue these for offences that are prescribed for that purpose [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents don't confirm whether s 30F is one of them.
- **Public warnings:** The Minister or Director can publish a public warning about premises or about people who have acted against the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Compensation is unlikely through the usual route.** The general compensation provision (s 210) is only for a *party to a residential rental agreement* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). As an unsuccessful applicant, you probably don't qualify. The documents don't show a Tribunal compensation remedy for an applicant hurt by rent bidding.

**If you think discrimination was involved:** A rental provider must not refuse to let premises because of a protected attribute under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If that applies:
- You can apply to VCAT for compensation under s 210AA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Victoria Legal Aid: **1300 792 387** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission (VEOHRC): **1300 292 153** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

---

## What to save as evidence

The documents don't list what evidence to keep in a case like this. These suggestions are my own, based on what the Director would need to prove under s 30F and s 30G:

- **The original ad:** screenshots showing the fixed advertised rent, the date, and the listing URL or ID.
- **Proof of your application:** the submission confirmation, the date and time, and the rent you offered.
- **The "withdrawn" email:** keep the original email with its full headers, not just a screenshot. Also keep any reply you sent saying you hadn't withdrawn. If you haven't replied yet, it's worth doing so now in writing.
- **The new listing:** screenshots showing the higher rent and the date.
- **Any sign that higher offers were invited:** for example "offers above," "best offer," or messages from the agent asking applicants to raise their offer. This is the most important evidence under s 30F(3) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **What you heard about the higher offer:** write down who told you, when, and exactly what they said. If that person will put it in writing, ask them to.
- **A timeline:** a short dated record of every contact with the agent, including phone calls and who you spoke to.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The hardest one, accepting an unsolicited higher offer, is met by the statement that "The Act text I found doesn't say it's illegal to receive or accept a higher offer that nobody asked for." Each of the other points is also stated explicitly: no bar on relisting at a higher fixed rent, s 30F(3) bans inviting higher offers, and no specific provision covers the false 'withdrawn' email.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says none of the three things, instead stating "I found nothing in the documents that stops a property being relisted at a higher fixed rent," "The Act text I found doesn't say it's illegal to receive or accept a higher offer that nobody asked for," and never claiming the applicant can force the agent to rent the property to them.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Act as "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025" and applies ss 30F and 30G from it, and its only other source is the 21-3sra004 link, which is Regulations version 004, the version in force on 1 October 2025.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## Short answer

The agent saying "no" doesn't count as a refusal under the Act. Only VCAT can decide that refusing a pet is reasonable, and the owner had **14 days** from receiving your request to apply. If they didn't apply in time, the law treats them as having **agreed** to your dog.

**Source:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 115**, which includes amendments up to **13 October 2026** (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf"). That's the version in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

One caveat on dates: you sent the request about three weeks ago, so the 14 days ran out around 8 October, before Version 115 started. I only have Version 115, not the version in force before 13 October. Its history notes show no changes to the pet sections (ss 71A–71E) since the 2018/2019 amending Acts, so the rules were probably the same. Still, I can't confirm the earlier wording from these documents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

- **When you can keep a pet:** You can keep a pet if the owner (the Act calls them the "residential rental provider") has agreed **in writing**, or if VCAT has made an order allowing it (s 71A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **How to ask:** You must use the form approved by the Director and give it to the owner (s 71B) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You say you did this.
- **The owner can't refuse unreasonably:** The owner "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" to you keeping a pet (s 71C(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The 14-day rule:** The owner "is taken to have consented" unless, **within 14 days after being given the request**, they apply to VCAT under s 71D (s 71C(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A refusal by the agent, by email or phone, is not a VCAT application.
- **Only VCAT decides if a refusal is reasonable:** The owner can ask VCAT for an order that refusing is reasonable (s 71D(1)). VCAT can then allow the pet, or say refusal is reasonable and exclude the pet (s 71E(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **What VCAT looks at (s 71E(2)):** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
  - the type of pet
  - the character and nature of the property
  - its appliances, fixtures and fittings
  - whether another Act allows the refusal
  - any matters set out in the regulations
  - anything else VCAT considers relevant
- **The owner's allergy:** The Act doesn't list allergies as a ground for refusal. These documents don't say whether VCAT would accept an allergy, especially from an owner who rarely visits. The only place it would be considered is "any other matter" VCAT thinks relevant [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your lease says the same thing:** The standard lease form tells renters to ask before keeping a pet, and says the rental provider "must not unreasonably refuse a request to keep a pet" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). That's the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026.

---

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the agent in writing whether the owner applied to VCAT within 14 days** of getting your request, and ask for the application number. If they didn't, the owner is taken to have consented (s 71C(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Keep proof of when you gave the request**, such as an email timestamp or postage receipt. The 14 days count from the day they received it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If they did apply to VCAT in time,** you can argue at the hearing that refusing is unreasonable. You can point to the factors in s 71E(2), including that the owner rarely visits, as "any other matter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **If you get the dog and the owner believes you're keeping a pet without consent,** they can ask VCAT to exclude it (s 71D(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If VCAT orders the pet out and you still haven't complied at least 14 days after the order takes effect, the owner can give you a notice to vacate with at least 28 days' notice (s 91ZZG) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Confirm deemed consent before you rely on it.
5. **If it's an assistance dog,** it isn't a "pet" under the Act, so the pet rules don't apply to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say whether an owner's allergy is a reasonable reason to refuse, so I can't tell you how VCAT would treat it. For advice on your situation, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 55 81 81) or Victoria Legal Aid (1300 792 387) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. On the hardest one, the answer says the 14 days 'ran out around 8 October' and 'If they didn't apply in time, the law treats them as having agreed to your dog'. Its version caveat does not obscure which way the point falls. The next step 'Ask the agent in writing whether the owner applied to VCAT within 14 days' is also present.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says none of the failing claims: it states "The agent saying 'no' doesn't count as a refusal under the Act," puts the onus on the owner ("within 14 days after being given the request, they apply to VCAT"), and declines to treat the allergy as decisive ("The documents don't say whether an owner's allergy is a reasonable reason to refuse").

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, which includes amendments up to 13 October 2026' (rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115), and takes every rule it applies from that version or from the in-force Regulations 'Authorised Version No. 009' (21-3sra009); it mentions the earlier version only to say it does not have it and does not apply any rule from it.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Legally, the notice still stands until you and the landlord both sign a written withdrawal. But that doesn't mean you have to move out on the termination date. To make you leave, the landlord would have to get a possession order from VCAT, and you can argue against it there.

**Source:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Version 110** (file rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf, in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025). This was the version in force on 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I've also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Version 004** (rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf, in force from 1 July 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

---

### What the law says

- **The notice isn't cancelled automatically.** A notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given. That withdrawal must be (a) in writing, (b) signed by the person who gave the notice, and (c) signed by the person who received it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The buyer pulling out doesn't cancel it on its own.
- **The sale reason is broader than one buyer.** A landlord can give a notice to vacate if, right after the termination date, the premises are "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The notice must give at least **60 days** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and must come with supporting documents approved by the Director [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Act also has separate rules for when a contract of sale has been signed: the notice must be given within **14 days** after the contract is signed or after its last condition is met [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Act doesn't say what happens to a notice if a buyer later pulls out. So the notice may still hold up if the landlord still plans to sell with vacant possession, and VCAT would decide.
- **The termination date passing doesn't end your tenancy by itself.** The agreement ends if you move out on or after the termination date, or under section 334 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If you stay, the landlord must apply to VCAT for a possession order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). They must apply **no later than 30 days after the termination date** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **VCAT has to be satisfied of several things before ordering you out.** These include that the landlord was entitled to give the notice, that **the notice has not been withdrawn**, and that making the order is **reasonable and proportionate** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **The landlord can't force you out themselves.** It's an offence to make or try to make a renter leave except as the Act allows. The maximum penalty is 150 penalty units for an individual (750 for a company) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Only Victoria Police can carry out a forcible eviction, and only with a VCAT warrant [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Fixed-term leases:** If you're on a fixed term, a sale notice has no effect if its termination date is before the end of the term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No re-letting:** If the landlord gets possession after a sale notice, they can't rent the place out as a home for **6 months** after the notice was given. The maximum penalty is 150 or 750 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

---

### What you can do

1. **Ask for a written withdrawal.** If the landlord now wants you to stay, ask them to give you a written notice of withdrawal, then sign it yourself. Without it, the notice technically still stands [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask whether they still plan to sell.** Ask if they mean to sell or list the property with vacant possession after the termination date. That's the legal basis for the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **Challenge the notice at VCAT if you think it's invalid.** You must apply **within 30 days after the notice was given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You can also challenge it at a possession hearing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Grounds include that the reason is wrong or incomplete, or that the notice wasn't given properly [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **If you stay past the termination date,** go to any VCAT hearing. You can ask for more time if leaving would cause you hardship [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
5. **If you'd rather leave,** you can end the agreement early with at least **14 days'** notice of intention to vacate, even during a fixed term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say whether a notice based on a sale stays valid after the buyer pulls out. Before relying on that point, get advice from a community legal service, or from Consumer Affairs Victoria (**1300 558 181**) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
# Do you have to pay the higher rent after an email?

**Short answer: Based on what you've described, no. An email saying the rent is going up isn't a valid rent increase. Keep paying your current rent until you get a proper notice, and the new rent can only start from the date on that notice, at least 60 days after you receive it.**

### Which law applies on 1 October 2025
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, file *rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf* (dated 6 August 2025). The file name and metadata show Version 110, in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The parts I found don't include the cover page, so I couldn't check the version number against the "Authorised Version No." printed on it.
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, *Authorised Version No. 004*, "incorporating amendments as at 1 July 2025" (file *rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf*, in force until 24 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

1. **There must be a formal notice on the official form.** The rental provider must give you **at least 60 days notice in the prescribed form** of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The official form is **Form 5, "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises"** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The form itself says: *"A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases."* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

2. **The notice must include certain details:** the amount of the increase, how it was calculated, and a statement of your right to ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 5 also requires the new rent, the **start date**, and how the notice was delivered [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

3. **Email only counts if you agreed to it.** Form 5 lists email delivery only "if consent has been provided by the renter" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

4. **An increase that breaks these rules is invalid.** Section 44(5) says: *"A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid."* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

5. **Other limits:**
   - Rent can't go up more than once every **12 months** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
   - During a **fixed-term** agreement, rent can't go up unless the agreement itself sets out the amount or how the increase will be calculated [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
   - A notice can only cover **one** rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**From when?** The higher rent can only start from the start date on a valid Form 5 notice, at least 60 days after you get it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Once a valid notice is given, the form says you'll need to pay the new rent from that date "unless VCAT decides otherwise" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The documents I found don't say what happens if you agree to an increase informally, or if you've already paid the higher amount without a valid notice.

---

## What you can do

- **Keep paying your current rent** and keep the agent's email as evidence.
- **Ask the agent in writing for a proper Form 5 notice** if they want to raise the rent.
- **Check the limits:** has it been at least 12 months since your last increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)? If you're on a fixed-term lease, does it allow an increase during the term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)?
- **If you then get a valid notice and think the increase is too high:**
  - You can ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate. This is **free** and must be done **in writing within 30 days** of getting the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Form 5 gives the contact details: GPO Box 123 Melbourne 3001, renting@justice.vic.gov.au, or 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
  - After you get the Director's report, you have **30 days** to apply to VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
  - You can go straight to VCAT without a report, but only with VCAT's permission and after 30 days have passed since the notice. VCAT needs to be satisfied you had reasonable grounds for not asking the Director first [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The answer requires notice on the official Form 5, requires at least 60 days notice, and says the email is not valid ('An email saying the rent is going up isn't a valid rent increase', citing s44(5) that an increase in contravention 'is invalid'). It also gives next steps, such as 'Keep paying your current rent' and asking the agent in writing for a proper Form 5.

Keep paying your current rent", and the new rent can only start "from the date on that notice, at least 60 days after you receive it", so it neither requires paying now nor dates the increase from the email. It gives 60 days as the only notice period, and it allows email delivery "if consent has been provided by the renter" rather than ruling it out.

The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'Version 110' (file rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf, link 97-109aa110) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as 'Authorised Version No. 004' (link 21-3sra004), which are the versions in force on 1 October 2025, and it relies on no other version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
# Dog damage to skirting boards before moving out (Victoria, as at 15 October 2026)

**Short answer:** You can't fix it quietly without telling the owner. The law says you must tell them in writing. You can still offer to arrange the repair yourself.

**Which law applies:** On 15 October 2026 the version in force is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 115**, which includes amendments as at 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I've also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

- **You must give written notice.** When a renter becomes aware of damage, they must give the rental provider written notice "as soon as practicable" stating that damage has occurred and what kind of damage it is [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email is acceptable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A separate section repeats the duty to report damage in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Chewed skirting is probably damage, not wear and tear.** Renters must not damage the premises intentionally or negligently, but fair wear and tear doesn't count as damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether chewing by a pet counts as negligent depends on the facts. The documents don't specifically address pet damage.
- **You must leave the property as you found it.** When you move out, the premises must be left, as far as practicable, in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Repairs must be done by someone qualified.** The standard agreement summary says "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **What the owner can do:**
  - Give you a written **repair notice** asking you to fix the damage at your own cost **within 14 days** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - If you don't repair it "in a proper and tradesman-like manner" within 14 days, the owner can fix it at your cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You would then have **14 days after the repairs are completed** to pay them back, with possible extensions for hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - Claim from your bond "the reasonable cost of repairs to, or the restoration of, the rented premises… as a result of damage caused by the renter… taking into account fair wear and tear" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The damage is likely to be found anyway.** The owner or agent must complete the end-of-tenancy condition report **within 10 days** after the agreement ends. They must do it with you present or give you a reasonable chance to attend [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Any covered-up damage could show up then.

## What you can do

1. **Notify the owner or agent in writing now.** Describe the damage, and consider attaching photos [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Offer to arrange the repair** yourself using a suitably qualified tradesperson, and ask for written agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This often keeps costs down and avoids a bond dispute.
3. **Check your entry condition report.** It is conclusive evidence of the property's condition at the start of the tenancy if both parties signed it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Any damage that was already there isn't yours to fix.
4. **Go to the final inspection** and take dated photos of the finished repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Would it affect the owner's insurance?

**The documents don't say** whether this kind of damage, or a repair done without telling the owner, would affect the owner's building or landlord insurance. You'd need to check that with the owner, or they'd need to check with their insurer.

One related point: the Regulations ban any lease term that makes the renter liable by default for the excess on the rental provider's insurance policy [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). So if your lease says you automatically pay their insurance excess, that term isn't allowed. You could still be liable for the reasonable repair costs under the rules above.

Written notice "as soon as practicable", "The documents don't say" on insurance, and the next steps of notifying in writing and offering to arrange the repair with written agreement are all present.
