question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
# Rules on circuits in a Victorian rental (as at 1 March 2023)

**Short answer:** No. The documents I found don't set a minimum number of circuits for a rental. You can still ask your rental provider to have it checked and fixed under their repair and electrical safety duties.

I used the two documents in force on 1 March 2023:
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 002** (file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf", dated 1 June 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 101** (file "rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf", dated 7 September 2022) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

---

## What the law says

**1. Nothing on the number of circuits.** The closest rule is the electrical safety minimum standard in Schedule 4, clause 9. It says all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker that complies with AS/NZS 3000. They must also be connected to a switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) that complies with AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1 or AS/NZS 61009.1 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). It doesn't say how many circuits there must be.

**2. That standard wasn't in force yet on 1 March 2023.** It applies "on and from 29 March 2023" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), which is 28 days after the date of your question. Even once it starts, it only requires a breaker and an RCD. It doesn't require more circuits.

**3. Rules that already applied on 1 March 2023:**
- **Duty to maintain:** The rental provider must keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation." This applies regardless of the property's age or the rent you pay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Anyone doing the repairs must be a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks:** A licensed or registered electrician must check all electrical installations, appliances and fittings supplied by the rental provider every 2 years [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs** include "a dangerous electrical fault" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a breaker tripping under load counts as one. An electrician would need to decide that.
- **Don't tamper with the RCD:** An RCD is a prescribed safety device. You must not remove, deactivate or otherwise interfere with it unless it's reasonable in the circumstances [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

---

## What you can do or ask for

1. **Report it in writing.** You must give written notice as soon as practicable after you notice damage or a breakdown of facilities the rental provider supplied [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for the electrical safety check records.** The rental provider must tell you the date of the most recent check in writing if you ask [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If you ask in writing, they must give you a copy of the latest check record within 7 days. That record includes the electrician's details and any repairs that were needed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask for an electrician to inspect and repair it.** This falls under the rental provider's duty to maintain the property [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **If an electrician says it's a dangerous fault (urgent repair):**
   - If you've taken reasonable steps to get the rental provider to fix it immediately and they haven't, you can arrange the repair yourself. They must pay you back the reasonable cost up to **$2,500** within 7 days of your written notice of the repair and its cost [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
   - You can apply to VCAT instead if you can't afford the repair, it costs more than $2,500, or the rental provider refuses to pay. VCAT must hear the application within **2 business days** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
5. **If it's not urgent:**
   - If the repair isn't done within **14 days** of your written notice, you can ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
   - You can also apply to VCAT, which must hear the application within **7 days** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
   - You can ask VCAT to let you pay rent into the Rent Special Account until the repair is done [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
6. **From 29 March 2023:** If the switchboard doesn't have a compliant circuit breaker and RCD, that breaks the minimum standards. A failure to meet the minimum standards counts as an urgent repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**Note:** You need the rental provider's written consent to install fixtures or make alterations, such as adding circuits yourself [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

It also lists next steps: requesting repair in writing, "Ask for an electrician to inspect and repair it," treating it as an urgent repair "If an electrician says it's a dangerous fault," and asking for "the date of the most recent check in writing."

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
# Can a rooming house charge for coin-operated washing machines? (as at 15 October 2026)

**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say whether coin-operated washing machines are allowed or banned in a rooming house. They do set some rules about what the operator must provide and how it can charge for services.

**Versions in force on 15 October 2026:**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 115**, in force from 13 October 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version No. 009**, in force from 30 June 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023*, **Authorised Version No. 002**, incorporating amendments as at 1 December 2024. This is the only version I found. I can't confirm that no later version replaced it before October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

---

## What the law says

**1. The operator must provide washing machines.** Since 26 February 2024, the rooming house must have the following in good working order "for every 12 or fewer residents based on the maximum number of residents that the rooming house can accommodate" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf):
- a washing machine
- a communal laundry trough or basin with hot and cold water
- a space for a washing machine next to the trough or basin
- a clothes line or other drying facility

So 2 machines meet the standard only if the house can hold 24 residents or fewer. The standard says the machines must be provided and working. It doesn't say they must be free to use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf).

**2. Rules about charging for services.** If an operator charges you for services, it must [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
- give you a **separate schedule** of the amounts for the services it provides **before you move into the room** (s 109(a))
- if you use any of those services, give you an **itemised account** of your own use (s 109(b))

The documents don't say whether a coin slot on a machine meets these requirements.

**3. Separately metered rooms.** Section 108 lets an operator charge for electricity, gas and water used *in your room* only if your room is separately metered. The charge can't be more than the supplier charges, and this doesn't apply to shared rooms [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It doesn't cover shared laundry machines.

**4. If your operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency.** It may charge a service charge for laundry facilities, but only if it isn't possible or practical to measure each resident's actual use. The charge must not be more than the cost of providing the service, and you must get written notice when it is introduced or changed (s 109A) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**5. Your general rights:**
- You have a right to use the facilities in the rooming house (s 92(1)(b)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The operator must give you access to facilities during all reasonable hours (s 121(b)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The operator must keep facilities and equipment in good repair (s 120) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- A fixed-term rooming house agreement can't include a term that "unreasonably limits the resident's use of utilities" (reg 39(h)) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

---

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask for the schedule of service charges** you should have been given before moving in, and an itemised account of your use (s 109) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the resident capacity.** If the house can hold more than 24 residents, 2 machines may not meet the standard [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). You can ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate. The Director can investigate on their own initiative whether an operator has failed to meet the standards (s 131A) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **If your operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency,** you can ask VCAT to order it to withdraw or change the service charge (s 109A(3B)–(3C)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **If the charge comes from a house rule,** you can ask VCAT to declare the rule unreasonable, and VCAT can declare it invalid (s 128) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
5. **If it's a term of your agreement,** you can ask VCAT to declare it invalid or change it if it is harsh or unconscionable (s 94A) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
6. **If a machine breaks down,** that counts as an urgent repair: "failure or breakdown of any essential service or appliance provided for… laundering" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). You can arrange the repair yourself and be reimbursed up to **$2500**, or apply to VCAT if the cost is more than that (regs 48 and 50) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't settle whether coin-operated machines are lawful in your house. For a definite answer about your situation, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181) or a tenancy legal service [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: the answer says one working washing machine is required "for every 12 or fewer residents"; it says the standard "doesn't say they must be free to use"; it says the operator must give "a separate schedule of the amounts for the services it provides before you move into the room (s 109(a))"; and its first next step is "Ask for the schedule of service charges you should have been given before moving in."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says the standard 'doesn't say they must be free to use,' sets out charging rules ('give you a separate schedule of the amounts for the services... before you move into the room' (s 109(a))), and limits the cost cap to one kind of operator ('If your operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency... The charge must not be more than the cost of providing the service').

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 'Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026' and the Rooming House Standards Regulations 2023 'Authorised Version No. 002, incorporating amendments as at 1 December 2024', and its only other source, the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, is the in-force 'Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026', so it relies on no version that was not in force on 15 October 2026.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
# Mould in a rental ad: what the law says on 1 October 2025

**Versions used** (both were in force on 1 October 2025):
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, Authorised Version 110, file *rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf* (dated 6 August 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, Authorised Version 004, file *rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf* (dated 1 July 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

---

## 1. Can they advertise it like that?

**The documents don't say a property can't be advertised because it falls short of the minimum standards.** The Act does have rules on advertising, but none of them fit this situation:
- Rent must be advertised as a fixed amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The rental provider can't make false or misleading claims about the rent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- They can't persuade you to sign a lease through misleading or deceptive conduct, or false claims about the property's features [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A photo that actually shows mould isn't hiding it.

**The real legal duties apply at move-in, and before you sign:**
- **By move-in day:** the rental provider must make sure the property meets the rental minimum standards on or before the day you move in. The maximum penalty is 60 penalty units for an individual and 300 for a company [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **The mould standard:** "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" (Schedule 4, clause 8) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Before you sign:** the rental provider must tell you whether the property meets the minimum standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). They must also tell you if they've received a repair notice about mould or damp caused by the building structure in the last 3 years [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## 2. Is the photo enough to prove the property doesn't meet the standards?

**Probably not on its own.** The standard isn't broken just because mould is present. It's broken when the mould or damp is **"caused by or related to the building structure"** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo may show mould, but it usually can't show what caused it, such as a leak or a ventilation problem as opposed to how the last occupants lived.

The documents don't say how much weight a photo from a listing would carry as evidence. They do say photos "may be useful in a dispute about the condition of the rented premises." They also recommend photos that are dated, labelled with the room, and taken both close up and from further away [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). So the ad photo is useful supporting evidence, but it's not proof by itself.

---

## What you can do or ask

**Before signing:**
- Ask in writing whether the property meets the rental minimum standards, and whether they've had a mould or damp repair notice in the last 3 years. They have to tell you both [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If the property doesn't meet the minimum standards and you haven't moved in yet, you can end the agreement by giving a notice of termination on that ground [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**At move-in:**
- Write the mould on the condition report and attach dated photos [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A condition report given to the rental provider counts as notice to them of any defects or outstanding repairs listed in it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If you're not given a condition report, you can fill one in yourself. You have until 5 business days after moving in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**After moving in:**
- If the property doesn't meet the standards, you can ask for urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Urgent repairs include failing to meet the minimum standards and "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If the rental provider doesn't do the repairs, you can arrange them yourself and be paid back for reasonable costs up to **$2500**. You can apply to VCAT if you can't pay for the repairs, they cost more than $2500, or the rental provider refuses to pay you back [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Even if you knew about the problem before moving in, the rental provider still has to keep the property in good repair and reasonably fit to live in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. Every point is covered. The answer quotes the standard ('free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'). It says the photo is 'Probably not on its own' enough and calls it 'useful supporting evidence, but it's not proof by itself.' It gives several next steps: ask in writing before signing, end the agreement before moving in, and request urgent repairs after moving in.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: neither forbidden claim is made. The answer says 'The documents don't say a property can't be advertised because it falls short of the minimum standards,' and on the photo it says 'Probably not on its own... it's not proof by itself,' so it never claims an advertising ban or that the photo alone proves illegality.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 ... (dated 6 August 2025)' and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004 ... (dated 1 July 2025)', and every link it relies on points to those versions (97-109aa110 and 21-3sra004), with no rule drawn from any other version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
The documents I found don't explain how a renter can make a friend they let in move out. They do cover the risks of having let someone in without consent, and the formal steps available to you.

**Law in force on 15 October 2026:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, in force from 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). I took the version numbers from each file's name and details. The extracts don't show an "Authorised Version No." line.

---

### What the law says

- **Consent:** You must not assign or sub-let all or part of the premises without the rental provider's written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider must not unreasonably refuse consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Sub-letting without consent:** A sub-letting without the provider's consent is invalid unless the Tribunal (VCAT) has decided consent isn't needed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The provider can end your lease over it:** The provider can give you a notice to vacate if you have sub-let, or claimed to sub-let, any part of the premises without consent. The termination date must be **at least 14 days** after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard lease form repeats this [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **Ending your lease could leave your friend there:** If your friend holds a sub-lease from you and your lease ends but theirs doesn't, your friend becomes the provider's renter on the same terms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Also, someone who lives there as their main home but isn't on the lease can ask VCAT to order the provider to give them a lease. This applies, for example, if you give notice that you're leaving, you move out, or a possession order is sought [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). VCAT can grant this if your friend could reasonably be expected to meet a renter's duties, and would face severe hardship greater than the provider's if forced to leave [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

### What you can do or ask

- **Ask the provider for consent, or ask VCAT:** If your friend is a sub-tenant, you can ask the provider for written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the provider unreasonably refuses, you can ask VCAT to decide consent isn't needed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The provider can't charge you a fee for consent, though they can pass on reasonable costs of an assignment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Think twice before leaving yourself:** Giving notice that you're leaving, or moving out, could let your friend apply to VCAT to take over the tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

---

### What the documents don't cover

There's **no step-by-step process for a renter to remove a friend** living with them. The documents don't say:
- whether your friend counts as a guest or a sub-tenant (which may change their rights);
- what notice, if any, you must give them;
- whether you can ask VCAT for an order that they leave.

The rules on forced removal in these documents only cover rental providers removing renters, so I can't apply them to your situation.

For advice on your specific case, the regulations refer people to Consumer Affairs Victoria at consumer.vic.gov.au/renting or **1300 558 181** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: No: the answer covers written consent ('You must not assign or sub-let all or part of the premises without the rental provider's written consent'). It fails the first point. It mentions 'whether your friend counts as a guest or a sub-tenant (which may change their rights)', but it never names a deciding fact such as a space that's only theirs, what was agreed, or what they pay.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer ties the friend's VCAT application to listed triggers ("This applies, for example, if you give notice that you're leaving, you move out, or a possession order is sought"), says "The documents don't say... what notice, if any, you must give them", applies the 14-day period only to the provider's notice to the renter, and never says the renter can lock the friend out or that the friend has no rights.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 115, in force from 13 October 2026" (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115), which is the version in force on 15 October 2026. Its only other source is the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 "version 009" (21-3sra009), also the in-force version, and it relies on no earlier or later version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**What the law says about your situation**
Under Victorian residential tenancy law in force on 1 October 2025:
* **Fixed advertised rent:** A rental provider or agent must advertise premises at a fixed amount and must not solicit or invite offers higher than that advertised price [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Misleading conduct:** Providers or agents must not make false or misleading representations about the rent, nor engage in misleading or deceptive conduct to induce you into an agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Penalties:** Breaching these advertising rules is an offence, punishable by 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 penalty units for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**
The retrieved documents do not outline a specific process for renters to challenge an advertising breach directly. However, they note that VCAT may make orders under section 472(1A) regarding contraventions of the misleading conduct provisions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Additionally, if you believe you were treated unfavourably due to a protected personal attribute (e.g., race, disability, or age), this could be unlawful discrimination. In that case, you may apply to VCAT for compensation under section 210AA [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What evidence to save**
The retrieved documents do not specify what evidence you should save regarding this situation.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers the ban on soliciting or inviting offers above the advertised rent. It is missing three required points: that relisting at a higher fixed rent is not illegal by itself, that accepting an unsolicited higher offer was not banned on this date, and that the false 'withdrawn' email is not covered by a specific rental-law rule.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three claims appears: the answer only says agents "must not solicit or invite offers higher than that advertised price." It never says relisting at a higher rent is illegal by itself, never says accepting an unsolicited higher offer is illegal, and never says the applicant can force the agent to rent the property to them (it mentions only VCAT orders and discrimination compensation).

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 through its legislation.vic.gov.au link '97-109aa110' (Authorised Version No. 110), the version in force on 1 October 2025, and applies its advertising and misleading-conduct rules. Its only other source, '21-3sra004', is the Residential Tenancies Regulations Authorised Version No. 004, also the in-force version, so no rule is taken from an out-of-force version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Vic), **Authorised Version No. 115**, which was in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):

### What the Law Says
* A residential rental provider **must not unreasonably refuse** consent to keep a pet on the rented premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* If a provider wishes to refuse consent, they must apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) within **14 days** of receiving your request to prove that refusing is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
* Crucially, if the provider does not apply to the Tribunal within those 14 days, the law states they are **"taken to have consented"** to your request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### Application to Your Situation
Because you sent the official request form three weeks ago (more than 14 days ago) and the agent/owner did not apply to VCAT within that statutory timeframe, their refusal is legally ineffective. Under s 71C(2), they are deemed to have already consented to you keeping the dog [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner's allergy or how often they visit does not override this automatic consent once the 14-day deadline has passed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What You Can Do
1. **Proceed with keeping the dog:** You are legally permitted to keep the pet on the premises because consent is deemed given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Notify the agent in writing:** Send a formal email or letter to the agent stating that under s 71C(2) of the Act, their consent is deemed granted due to the lapse of the 14-day period, and that you will be keeping the dog on the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Keep records:** Save a copy of your original request form and proof of delivery (e.g., email receipt or registered post tracking) to prove it was received more than 14 days ago [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

If the agent continues to harass you, threatens eviction, or tries to enforce their refusal, you can apply to VCAT for an order confirming your right to keep the pet and potentially seek compensation for any loss suffered as a result of their unlawful actions [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version No. 110**, which came into force on 6 August 2025 and was in force on 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):

### What the law says about the situation
Under section 91ZZB of the Act, a landlord is entitled to give you a notice to vacate if they intend to sell the premises with vacant possession [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The Act specifies that this notice must be given within 14 days of the contract of sale being entered into (or any conditions being satisfied) and must specify a termination date that is at least 60 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 

The provided documents do not explicitly state what happens to the notice if the buyer subsequently pulls out or the sale falls through.

### What you can do or ask
*   **Challenge the notice at VCAT:** Under the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Vic), Authorised Version No. 004*, you may be able to challenge a notice to vacate at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) if you believe the reason given is incorrect or incomplete [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). If the sale has been cancelled, the stated ground for the notice may no longer be valid.
*   **Request a formal withdrawal:** You can ask your landlord to provide a written notice of withdrawal since the original reason for the eviction (the sale) no longer applies. 

*(Note: Because the provided documents do not contain a specific clause addressing a buyer pulling out after a notice is issued, you should seek further advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre regarding how VCAT would interpret the validity of the notice in this specific circumstance.)*

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (v110, in force from 6 August 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (v004, in force from 1 July 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), here is how Victorian law applies to your situation:

### What the law says about your situation
A casual email from an agent is **not** a valid rent increase notice. For a rent increase to be legally enforceable, it must strictly comply with these requirements:
- **60 Days' Notice:** The rental provider must give you at least 60 days' notice before the new rent applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
- **Prescribed Form:** The notice must be the official "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises" (Form 5) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Even if you have consented to electronic communication, the notice must still be delivered in this exact prescribed format containing all mandatory details—not just a casual message from an agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Mandatory Content:** The notice must clearly state the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and a statement informing you of your right to apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate if you believe the rent is excessive [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Invalid Increases:** If these requirements are not met, "a rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 

### Do you have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
**No.** Because no valid notice was served, the proposed rent increase is legally void. You do not have to pay the higher amount, and it cannot take effect from any date until a compliant 60-day notice is properly served [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
1. **Reply in writing:** Inform your agent/landlord that you have not received a valid prescribed notice (Form 5) with the required 60-day notice period, and therefore the increase cannot proceed under section 44 of the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Continue paying your current rent:** Keep paying your existing rent amount. Do not pay the increased amount until a valid notice is served.
3. **Challenge if necessary:** If the landlord attempts to evict you or claims you owe arrears for the difference, you can apply to VCAT to have the increase declared invalid. Additionally, if a valid notice is eventually provided and you believe the increase is excessive, you have 30 days from receiving that notice to apply to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria for an investigation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: If you are currently on a fixed-term agreement, the landlord generally cannot increase your rent before the term ends unless your original contract explicitly allows it and specifies the calculation method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).)*

must-mention.reason: Yes. All required points are covered: it requires the prescribed 'Form 5' and 'at least 60 days' notice'; it says the email is not valid ('A casual email from an agent is not a valid rent increase notice' and 'a rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid'), so the higher rent is not payable; and it gives next steps ('Reply in writing' and 'Keep paying your existing rent amount').

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Authorised Version v115, in force from 13 October 2026), here is how your situation is handled under Victorian tenancy law:

### 1. Can you fix the damage without telling the owner?
**No.** You have a strict legal obligation to report the damage immediately. 
* **Duty to Notify:** Under section 62 of the Act, as soon as practicable after becoming aware of the damage, you must give written notice to your residential rental provider (the owner) stating both the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
* **Repair Notice & Liability:** Because the damage was caused by your pet (which falls under your duty not to intentionally or negligently cause damage under section 61), the owner can issue you a formal "repair notice" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). This notice will require you to either repair the skirting boards yourself in a tradesman-like manner within 14 days at your own expense, or it will state that the owner will carry out the repairs and you will be liable for the reasonable costs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

If you attempt to fix it secretly without notifying them, you are breaching your duty to report the damage. When you eventually move out, the owner will likely discover the repair during a final inspection, at which point they can still hold you fully financially responsible for the work and potentially charge you for any substandard repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### 2. Would it affect the owner's insurance?
The provided legal documents **do not contain information** regarding how tenant-caused damage affects a property owner's home or landlord insurance policies. You would need to consult the owner directly or check their specific insurance policy wording to understand those implications.

### What you should do now:
1. **Notify the owner immediately:** Send a written notice (email is acceptable under the Act) informing them that your dog chewed the skirting boards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Offer to pay for the repair:** State clearly that you are willing to cover the cost of having it fixed by a qualified tradesperson, or ask if they have a preferred contractor.
3. **Get agreement in writing:** Ensure the owner agrees to the proposed fix and cost before any work begins, so there is no dispute at the end of your tenancy.

This approach keeps you compliant with your legal duties and protects your bond from being unfairly withheld for undisclosed damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (Authorised Version v002, in force from 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024), here is how Victorian law addresses your situation as of 1 March 2023:

### Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs?
**No.** The regulations do not specify a minimum or required number of electrical circuits for a rental property. The law focuses on the *type* of safety protection installed, rather than dictating how many separate circuits must exist.

### What does the law say about electrical safety?
While there is no rule on circuit quantity, the law sets strict standards for how those circuits must be protected. Under Schedule 4 (Rental minimum standards), clause 9 states that **on and from 29 March 2023**, all power outlets and lighting circuits in rented premises must be connected to:
* A switchboard-type Circuit Breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000, *"Electrical Installations"* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
* A switchboard-type Residual Current Device (RCD) complying with AS/NZS 3190, AS/NZS 61008.1, or AS/NZS 61009.1 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

*(Note: Since you asked this on 1 March 2023, these specific minimum standards are not yet legally enforceable but will come into force in less than a month.)*

### What can you ask for?
1. **Request repairs for the tripping breaker:** A breaker that trips when two appliances are used together usually indicates an overloaded circuit or a faulty breaker. As the rental provider is legally obligated to maintain the property in good repair, you can formally request they have a licensed electrician inspect and fix the issue. 
2. **Ask for an electrical safety check:** The rental provider must ensure an electrical safety check of all installations and fittings provided by them is conducted every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). You can ask them to provide the date of the most recent check in writing, or request one be scheduled if it hasn't been done recently.
3. **Reference the upcoming mandate:** When the new rules take effect on 29 March 2023, your rental will legally require compliant circuit breakers and RCDs on all circuits [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If your current switchboard lacks these protections, you can reference this upcoming mandate when asking the provider to upgrade the electrical setup.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Direct Answer**
Yes, your rooming house operator is allowed to charge you to use the washing machines. While they are legally required to provide them, Victorian tenancy law does not prohibit operators from recovering the cost of laundry facilities through charges (such as coin-operated systems), provided they follow specific disclosure and accounting rules.

**The Law (as of 15 October 2026)**
*   **Requirement to Provide Laundry Facilities:** Under the *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023* (v002, in force from 1 December 2024), operators must provide at least one washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Right to Charge for Services:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (v115, in force from 13 October 2026) permits rooming house operators to charge residents for services. If they do, they must give you a separate schedule of the service charges before you move in, and provide an itemised account showing your individual use if you use those services [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Coin-operated machines are a common method that inherently satisfies the requirement to track individual use.
*   **Breakdowns are Urgent Repairs:** If a washing machine breaks down, it is considered an urgent repair (specifically, the breakdown of an appliance provided for laundering) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The operator must fix it immediately or reimburse you for reasonable costs if you arrange the repair yourself (up to a prescribed limit) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What You Can Do**
1.  **Check Your Documentation:** Ensure you received the required schedule of services before you moved in and that you are receiving itemised accounts for your laundry usage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2.  **Report Breakdowns Immediately:** If a machine breaks, notify the operator immediately as an urgent repair so they can fix it or reimburse you [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 
3.  **Apply to VCAT if Necessary:** If the operator fails to maintain the machines in good repair, refuses to provide itemised accounts for charges, or enforces unreasonable house rules regarding laundry use, you can apply to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) for orders to fix the issue [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

*(Note: Section 109A of the Act specifically allows Homes Victoria or registered housing agencies to impose service charges for laundry if individual usage cannot be accurately measured, but this specific provision only applies to those government/registered providers rather than private rooming house operators. Private operators rely on the general service charge provisions in Section 109 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).)*

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
Based on the law in force on **1 October 2025**, here is the answer to your questions:

**Applicable Law & Versions**
* *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 110, in force from 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
* *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 004, in force from 1 July 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

### 1. Are they allowed to advertise the photo like that?
The provided documents do not explicitly prohibit a rental provider from showing a photo with mould in an advertisement. Under the Act, a rental provider or their agent is permitted to enter rented premises to produce advertising images and video after giving proper notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 

However, while the ad itself may not be explicitly banned by the text, the property must still meet mandatory legal requirements. A residential rental provider must ensure that rented premises comply with prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day a renter moves in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Under these regulations, **"each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure"** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). If the photo genuinely shows structural mould, advertising it strongly suggests the property is failing to meet its legal duty to provide compliant premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### 2. Is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
**No.** The provided documents do not state that a photograph is sufficient proof of non-compliance. 

The legal minimum standard specifically requires rooms to be free from mould and damp **"caused by or related to the building structure"** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photograph can show that mould is visibly present, but it cannot prove *what caused it*. Mould in rentals often stems from lifestyle factors (e.g., poor ventilation, drying clothes indoors, or condensation) rather than structural defects. Because the legal standard hinges entirely on the *cause* of the dampness/mould, an image alone cannot definitively prove a breach of the minimum standards under the provided documents.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version No. 088 (in force on 1 November 2019), here is what you should check if you believe your notice to vacate is retaliatory:

### 🔍 What You Should Check

**1. Whether the Notice is Legally "of No Effect" Due to Retaliation**
Under Victorian tenancy law, a landlord cannot evict you simply for asking for repairs or exercising your legal rights. The Act explicitly states that a notice to vacate given on certain grounds **is of no effect if it was given in response to**:
* Your exercise (or proposed exercise) of a right under the Act or your tenancy agreement; or
* You making a report about a breach [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
**Check:** Gather dated records of your repair requests, emails, texts, and any responses from the landlord. If you can demonstrate that the notice was issued immediately after you followed up on repairs, this establishes the causal link needed to prove retaliation.

**2. The Stated Reason on the Notice**
A valid notice to vacate must be in the prescribed form, specify the exact reason(s) for giving it, and state a valid termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 
**Check:** Read the reason listed on your notice carefully. Landlords often use "non-payment of rent" or "successive breaches" as a cover for retaliation. Verify that the stated reason is factually accurate and procedurally correct:
* **If the reason is non-payment of rent:** You must owe at least 14 days' rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). On the first four occasions of non-payment, if you pay the full amount owed by the termination date listed in the notice, the notice automatically becomes of no effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* **If the reason is successive breaches:** The landlord can only issue this without a prior warning if you have breached the *same* provision on 2 previous occasions and were given breach of duty notices each time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If they did give you a breach of duty notice for this instance, they cannot issue the eviction until that notice period has passed without compliance [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Whether Required Documentation Was Provided**
If the landlord claims the eviction is due to property repairs, renovations, or demolition, they must have obtained all necessary permits and consents, and the work must genuinely require you to vacate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). They must also provide documentary evidence supporting their reason if required by the notice type [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**4. Your Right to Challenge the Notice**
You are entitled to apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) to challenge the validity of the notice if you believe it is retaliatory, invalid, or procedurally flawed. 
**Check:** Ensure you lodge your application within the strict time limits set by the Act (typically before a possession order hearing or within 60 days for certain notices) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Do not wait until the termination date to act.

### 📝 Summary of Next Steps
1. **Do not ignore the notice.** Treat it as active until a Tribunal orders otherwise.
2. **Document everything.** Compile a timeline showing your repair requests and the immediate issuance of the notice.
3. **Apply to VCAT.** File an application to challenge the validity of the notice, citing that it was given in response to you exercising your right to request repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Pay rent on time.** Ensure no legitimate grounds (like unpaid rent) are left open for the landlord to use against you.

*Note: This information is based strictly on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Vic), Authorised Version No. 088, as in force on 1 November 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For personalised legal advice, contact your local tenancy advocacy service or a community legal centre.*

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 110)** and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 004)**, which were in force on 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf):

### What the law says about your situation
Under Victorian residential tenancy law, rental providers and their agents are strictly regulated regarding how they advertise and solicit rent:
* **Fixed advertised rent:** Rented premises must be offered for rent at a fixed amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). 
* **No soliciting higher offers:** A residential rental provider or agent must not solicit or invite an offer of rent that is higher than the advertised amount [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **False or misleading advertising:** It is an offence to make a false or misleading representation in relation to the rent for rented premises [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Misleading conduct:** Inducing a person to enter into a residential rental agreement by engaging in misleading or deceptive conduct, or making false representations concerning the rent payable, is prohibited [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

Violating these provisions is an offence punishable by 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 penalty units for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### Can you challenge what happened?
The retrieved documents confirm that soliciting offers above the advertised price and making false representations about rent are offences under the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). However, the provided text **does not contain specific instructions or forms** for a prospective renter to formally challenge this exact pre-tenancy advertising breach. 

While the documents outline how to challenge issues *after* a tenancy begins (such as applying to VCAT for excessive rent increases or challenging notices to vacate) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), and mention applying to VCAT for compensation if you suffer loss due to unlawful discrimination during an application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf), they do not provide a direct challenge mechanism for false withdrawal emails or advertised rent discrepancies before a lease is signed.

### What should you save as evidence?
The provided documents **do not specify** what evidence a prospective renter should save regarding false withdrawal notifications or advertised rent disputes. 

*(Note: The retrieved legal text does not cover this specific procedural advice.)*

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 115)**, which was in force on 15 October 2026, here is how the law applies to your situation:

### What the Law Says
**1. The 14-Day "Deemed Consent" Rule**  
Under section 71C(2) of the Act, a residential rental provider (the owner or their agent) is automatically taken to have consented to your pet request if they do not apply to the Tribunal within **14 days** of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Because you sent the official form three weeks ago and they did not take legal action within that two-week window, the law considers them to have already agreed to you keeping the dog.

**2. Unreasonable Refusals**  
The Act explicitly states that a residential rental provider "must not unreasonably refuse to consent" to a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). While an owner's allergies might be a factor they consider, they cannot simply say "no" and rely on it after the 14-day deadline has passed without involving the Tribunal. The only way they could legally block your request after receiving it would have been to immediately apply to the Tribunal under section 71D within those first 14 days for a decision on whether refusing consent is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

### What You Can Do or Ask
*   **Keep your dog:** Since the 14-day period has expired without a Tribunal application, you have legal permission to keep the pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Inform the agent in writing:** You can reply to the agent stating that under section 71C(2) of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, they are deemed to have consented because they failed to apply to the Tribunal within 14 days.
*   **If they threaten eviction or penalties:** If the owner tries to issue a notice to vacate or penalize you for having the dog, you can challenge this at VCAT by pointing out that consent was legally granted by default [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The answer states the 14-day deemed-consent rule under s71C(2). It applies this to the three-week timeline: "Since the 14-day period has expired without a Tribunal application, you have legal permission to keep the pet." It also gives a reasonable written next step: "Inform the agent in writing... they are deemed to have consented because they failed to apply to the Tribunal within 14 days." One weakness is that it assumes no VCAT application was made, which the user never said, but its conditional framing still covers the second point.

It presents VCAT only as optional ('you can challenge this at VCAT'), not as something the renter must do. It treats the allergy as non-decisive ('an owner's allergies might be a factor they consider, they cannot simply say "no"').

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
Based on the Victorian *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* in force on 1 October 2025, **no, you do not have to leave** based on that notice if the buyer has pulled out. 

Here is how the law applies to your situation:

### 1. The Notice Remains "On Paper" Until Formally Withdrawn
Under Victorian law, a notice to vacate is only formally withdrawn if a specific **notice of withdrawal** is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This document must be in writing and signed by both you and the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Because your landlord has not provided this, the notice technically remains active on paper. 

### 2. The Reason for the Notice No Longer Exists
Your landlord issued this notice specifically because the property was being sold (section 91ZZB) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the buyer has pulled out and the property is no longer being sold with vacant possession, that specific legal ground for the notice has failed. 

### 3. The Landlord Cannot Enforce It
Because the reason for the notice (the sale) is no longer valid, your landlord cannot rely on it to evict you or obtain a possession order from VCAT [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If they try to apply to VCAT using this notice, you can challenge its validity because the ground for issuing it is no longer established [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). VCAT will not make an order if the notice has been withdrawn or if the reason for it is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What You Should Do
* **Stay in the property:** You are not legally required to vacate based on a notice where the stated reason has fallen through. 
* **Wait for a new notice (if applicable):** If your landlord still intends to sell the property, they must issue a **new** notice to vacate once they have a new contract or firm intention to sell [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
* **Challenge at VCAT if necessary:** If your landlord attempts to take you to VCAT for a possession order, attend the hearing and explain that the sale has fallen through. You can argue that the ground for the notice is no longer valid and that VCAT should dismiss the application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Document Reference:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), Authorised Version No. 110, in force on 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

It does cover written withdrawal signed by both parties and a VCAT challenge as a next step.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
Based on Victorian residential tenancy law in force on 1 October 2025, here is the answer to your questions:

### Do you have to pay the higher rent?
**No.** Because you never received an official notice, the agent's email does not legally trigger a rent increase. You do not have to pay the higher amount.

### From when would it apply?
The higher rent cannot start until **at least 60 days after** you receive a valid, official notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Until that date passes and a proper notice is served, your current rent remains payable.

---

### The Law (as of 1 October 2025)
Under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (v110) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (v004) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf):
* **Prescribed Form Required:** A rental provider must give a renter a "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase" using the official prescribed form (Form 5) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). An informal email from an agent does not satisfy this legal requirement.
* **60-Day Notice Period:** The official notice must be given at least 60 days before the new rent is due to start [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). 
* **Invalid Increases:** Any rent increase that does not follow these strict rules is legally invalid [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do
1. **Continue paying your current rent:** Since the increase is invalid, your existing rent amount remains payable until a valid notice is properly served.
2. **Request the official notice in writing:** Reply to your agent and ask them to provide the official Form 5 "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase." You can remind them that under Section 44 of the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), they must give you at least 60 days' written notice using this specific form before any increase can take effect.
3. **Seek further help if needed:** If your agent insists the email is sufficient or tries to charge you the higher rent, you can contact Consumer Affairs Victoria for assistance in enforcing your rights [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: the official Form 5 is required, at least 60 days' notice is required, and the answer states the email does not trigger an increase ('Any rent increase that does not follow these strict rules is legally invalid'). It also gives next steps, including continuing to pay the current rent and contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria.

None of the four failure conditions is asserted: the answer says "You do not have to pay the higher amount" and that the rent "cannot start until at least 60 days after you receive a valid, official notice," and its remark that "an informal email from an agent does not satisfy this legal requirement" concerns the email's lack of the prescribed form, not a claim that a notice can never be sent by email.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version v115)**, which came into force on 13 October 2026, and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version v009)**, here is how the law applies to your situation:

**1. Can you fix the skirting boards without telling the owner?**
No, you cannot. Under section 62(1) of the Act, as soon as you become aware of damage to the rented premises, you are legally required to give written notice to your rental provider detailing both the fact that the damage occurred and its nature [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). 

Furthermore, under section 61(1), you have a duty not to negligently cause damage to the premises [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you attempt to fix it secretly or fail to notify them, the owner can issue a formal repair notice requiring you to fix the damage at your own expense within 14 days in a tradesman-like manner [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If you do not comply with that notice, the owner is entitled to carry out the repairs themselves and charge you for the reasonable costs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**2. Would it affect the owner's insurance?**
The provided documents **do not contain information** regarding whether tenant-caused damage would affect a property owner's insurance policy or premiums. The documents only establish that you are financially liable for the reasonable costs of repairing the damage you caused [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf), and they note that tenancy agreements cannot include terms requiring tenants to take out their own insurance (as this is considered a prohibited term) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). 

For specific advice on how your actions might impact the owner's insurance policy, you would need to consult the owner's actual insurance policy or seek independent legal/financial advice, as this falls outside the scope of the provided tenancy legislation.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy laws in force on 1 March 2023, here is how your situation is addressed:

### What the law says about electrical circuits
* **No minimum circuit count:** The legislation does not specify a required number of electrical circuits that a rental property must have. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
* **Duty to maintain:** Your rental provider has a strict legal duty to ensure the premises are provided and maintained in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
* **Mandatory safety checks:** The provider must ensure all electrical installations, appliances, and fittings they provide are checked by a licensed or registered electrician every 2 years. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
* **Upcoming circuit breaker & RCD mandate:** Just over a month after your current date (on 29 March 2023), new rental minimum standards come into force requiring all power outlets and lighting circuits in rented premises to be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker and a Residual Current Device (RCD). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

### What you can ask for or do
1. **Request Repairs:** Notify your rental provider in writing about the tripping breaker. Because the law requires them to maintain the property in good repair, they must address this issue. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) 
   * If the tripping causes a complete failure of an essential service (like heating or cooking) that cannot be temporarily resolved, it may be classified as an **urgent repair**, which the provider must carry out immediately. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
   * If it is considered non-urgent, they are legally required to complete the repairs within a reasonable time. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
2. **Ask for Safety Check Records:** You can request in writing the date of the most recent electrical safety check and any outstanding recommendations from that report. The provider must supply this within 7 days of your request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
3. **Reference the Upcoming Mandate:** When discussing the issue with your provider, you can note that under the new rental minimum standards taking effect on 29 March 2023, all circuits will be required to have proper circuit breakers and RCDs installed, which may help prevent overloading issues like the one you are experiencing. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

*Note: If you choose to reset the breaker yourself, ensure it is safe to do so. If it trips immediately upon resetting, stop using it and contact a licensed electrician or your rental provider.*
