question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026**, the rental provider must not unreasonably refuse permission for a pet. To refuse, they had to apply to VCAT **within 14 days after receiving your official request**. If they did not, they are taken to have consented. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

So, **the agent’s “no” is not enough**. Because three weeks have passed, the owner cannot now rely on that refusal if your request was validly given and no VCAT application was made within the 14-day period. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

An owner’s allergy is not listed as an automatic ground for refusal. VCAT could consider it as “any other matter” it considers relevant, alongside the type of pet and the nature of the apartment, but only VCAT can order that refusal is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The Act does not say whether an allergy is sufficient when the owner rarely visits, so the retrieved document does not conclusively decide that point.

**What you can do:** ask the agent to confirm whether the owner lodged a VCAT application within 14 days and request the application details. If they did not, tell them that consent is deemed to have been given under section 71C(2). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Keep your completed form and proof of when it was delivered.

must-mention.reason: Yes. The output covers all three points: it states that if the owner did not apply to VCAT within 14 days 'they are taken to have consented'; it states that after three weeks 'the owner cannot now rely on that refusal if... no VCAT application was made within the 14-day period'; and it gives a next step, 'ask the agent to confirm whether the owner lodged a VCAT application within 14 days and request the application details'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says none of the three failure claims: it rejects the refusal ('the agent's "no" is not enough'), places the VCAT burden on the owner ('they had to apply to VCAT within 14 days'), and denies that the allergy is decisive ('An owner's allergy is not listed as an automatic ground for refusal... only VCAT can order that refusal is reasonable').

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the only required document with its in-force version, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026", links it as 97-109aa115, and takes every rule it applies (the 14-day VCAT application and deemed consent under s 71C(2)) only from that version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## What the law says

**The buyer pulling out does not automatically cancel the notice.** A notice to vacate is withdrawn only through a written notice of withdrawal signed by both the landlord and the renters [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

However, a sale notice is permitted only if the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Therefore:

- If the landlord still intends to sell or offer the property for sale with vacant possession, the notice may remain valid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- If the landlord has abandoned the sale, you can challenge whether the stated ground remains valid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

You cannot be forcibly removed merely because the termination date arrives. The landlord must obtain a VCAT possession order; VCAT must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice, that it has not been withdrawn, and that making a possession order is reasonable and proportionate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Only Victoria Police acting under a warrant for possession can forcibly evict you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Ask the landlord to withdraw the notice in writing.** Both the landlord and renters must sign the withdrawal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask whether the property is still being offered for sale with vacant possession.**
3. **Challenge the notice at VCAT within 30 days after it was given** if you dispute its validity [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If the landlord seeks a possession order, attend the hearing and explain that the buyer withdrew and, if applicable, that the property is no longer being sold [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

The applicable legislation on **1 October 2025** is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110 (6 August 2025)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The prescribed notice information is in the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004 (1 July 2025)** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: No: the answer never states the 60-day minimum notice period. It also does not distinguish the evidence for the ground, such as a planned sale with vacant possession versus a signed contract. It does cover written withdrawal signed by both parties and the VCAT challenge within 30 days.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failure conditions are asserted. The answer rejects automatic cancellation ("The buyer pulling out does not automatically cancel the notice"), says withdrawal needs a notice "signed by both the landlord and the renters", and gives no minimum notice period; its only figure, "within 30 days after it was given", is the deadline for challenging the notice at VCAT.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

**No—an ordinary email saying the rent will increase is not enough.** The rental provider must give you at least **60 days’ notice in the prescribed form**. A rent increase that does not comply with these requirements is invalid. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

The prescribed notice is **Form 5, “Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises.”** It must state the current and new rent, the start date, and the method and calculation used to determine the increase. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Form 5 may be sent by email only if you have consented to electronic service. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Because you say you never received that prescribed notice, you do **not** have to pay the higher rent yet. Continue paying the existing rent. Negotiating about the proposed increase—and the agent refusing to negotiate—does not replace the required notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The higher rent can begin only on the start date stated in a valid Form 5, which must allow at least **60 days’ notice**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) It also generally cannot be increased less than **12 months** after the previous increase; during a fixed term, an increase is permitted only if the agreement provides for it in the way specified by the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent to provide a valid **Form 5** and confirm that you will continue paying the current rent until a valid increase takes effect. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Once you receive it, you have **30 days** to ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate if you consider the proposed rent excessive. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

**Law in force on 1 October 2025:**

- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 110**, dated 6 August 2025. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version No. 004**, dated 1 July 2025. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. (1) The answer names Form 5 as the prescribed notice. (2) It requires 'at least 60 days' notice'. (3) It says 'an ordinary email saying the rent will increase is not enough', that a non-compliant increase is invalid, and 'you do not have to pay the higher rent yet'. (4) It gives next steps: 'Continue paying the existing rent', ask the agent for a valid Form 5, and ask Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate within 30 days of receiving it.

It says the renter does "not have to pay the higher rent yet" and the increase "can begin only on the start date stated in a valid Form 5." It requires "at least 60 days' notice," and says "Form 5 may be sent by email only if you have consented to electronic service," so it never claims email notice is always invalid.

The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025' (link 97-109aa110) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004, dated 1 July 2025' (link 21-3sra004), and relies on no other version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **15 October 2026**, the applicable documents are the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115** (in force from 13 October 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009** (in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

- Damage caused by a dog is not fair wear and tear. A renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the premises and must leave them, as far as practicable, in their original condition apart from fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- You **cannot simply repair it without telling the owner**: once aware of the damage, you must give the rental provider **written notice as soon as practicable**, stating that the damage occurred and describing its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Repairs—urgent or non-urgent—must be done by a **suitably qualified person** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- The rental provider may require you to repair the damage at your expense within **14 days**. If it is not repaired in a proper and tradesman-like manner, the provider may arrange repairs at your expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- At the end of the tenancy, the provider may claim from the bond the **reasonable cost** of repairing damage caused by you, after allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

Notify the rental provider **in writing now**, describe the chewed skirting boards, and ask for written agreement that you may engage a suitably qualified person to repair them before moving out [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Keep photographs, the contractor’s invoice and evidence of the completed work; the prescribed condition report recommends photographs at the beginning and end of the tenancy to help resolve damage disputes [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Insurance

The retrieved documents **do not say whether this damage or a renter-arranged repair would affect the owner’s insurance policy, claim, premium or coverage**. That depends on the particular policy, so the documents do not permit a definite answer.

They do say that a rental agreement cannot make you **liable by default for the excess under the owner’s insurance policy** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). This does not prevent liability for the reasonable cost of repairing damage established under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. Written notice is covered by 'you must give the rental provider written notice as soon as practicable'. Responsibility for pet damage is covered by 'Damage caused by a dog is not fair wear and tear' and the duty to 'leave them... in their original condition apart from fair wear and tear', plus repair at the renter's expense. The insurance point is covered by 'The retrieved documents do not say whether this damage... would affect the owner's insurance policy'. The next step is covered by 'Notify the rental provider in writing now... and ask for written agreement'.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law said on 1 March 2023

The retrieved Victorian tenancy laws **did not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits** for a rental property. Even the electrical minimum standard commencing on **29 March 2023** required power outlets and lighting circuits to be connected to compliant circuit breakers and residual current devices (RCDs); it did not specify how many circuits there must be. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

However, the rental provider had to:

- maintain the premises **in good repair** and in a **reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation**, using a suitably qualified person for repairs;[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- arrange an electrical safety check of all installations, appliances and fittings they provided **every 2 years**, performed by a licensed or registered electrician;[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- provide the date of the latest check in writing on request, and provide a copy of the latest electrical-safety record **within 7 days of a written request**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

A **dangerous electrical fault** counted as an urgent repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not establish that a breaker tripping when a kettle and heater run together is automatically a dangerous fault—that requires assessment.

## What you can ask for

Write to the rental provider or agent describing the repeated tripping and ask for:

1. **A licensed or registered electrician to inspect the circuit and switchboard**, and carry out any work required to make the premises safe, fit for occupation and in good repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
2. **The date and full record of the most recent electrical safety check**; the record must be supplied within 7 days of your written request. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
3. If the electrician finds a dangerous fault, **immediate urgent repairs**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

You can ask for an additional circuit, but the retrieved documents do **not** give you an automatic right to a particular number of circuits. The stronger request is for an electrician’s assessment and whatever repair or upgrade is necessary.

If it is an urgent repair and the provider does not act after reasonable attempts to contact them, you may arrange repairs costing up to **$2,500** and seek reimbursement, giving written notice of the repairs and cost within **7 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) If you cannot pay, the work costs more than **$2,500**, or reimbursement is refused, you may apply to VCAT; it must hear an urgent-repair application within **2 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

**Documents in force on 1 March 2023:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. **002**, 1 June 2022; and *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. **101**, 7 September 2022. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

For next steps, it recommends asking for an electrician to inspect and repair, urgent repairs if a dangerous fault is found, and "the date and full record of the most recent electrical safety check."

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Yes—generally they may charge you to use the washing machines.** The rooming-house standards require at least **one working washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents**, but they do not say its use must be free. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf) The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* also allows an operator to charge separately for services. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If they charge for laundry, you can ask for:

- the **separate schedule of service charges** that should have been provided before you moved in; and  
- an **itemised account showing your individual use** of the service. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If the rooming house is operated by **Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency** and falls within section 109A, a laundry service charge must not exceed the cost of providing it, and written notice must be given when the charge is imposed or changed. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The applicable documents on **15 October 2026** are:

- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, dated 13 October 2026, **Authorised Version 115**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023*, dated 1 December 2024, **Authorised Version 002**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are present. The answer states the standard requires "at least one working washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents" and that the standards "do not say its use must be free." The hardest points, the schedule requirement and the next step, are covered by "you can ask for: the separate schedule of service charges that should have been provided before you moved in."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says "they may charge you to use the washing machines", refers to charge rules such as "the separate schedule of service charges" and "an itemised account", and limits the cost cap to rooming houses "operated by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency and falls within section 109A", so it says none of the prohibited claims.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, dated 13 October 2026, Authorised Version 115' (link 97-109aa115) and 'Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, dated 1 December 2024, Authorised Version 002' (link 23-10sra002), and relies on no version that was out of force on 15 October 2026.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 October 2025**, the relevant law was the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version 110 (6 August 2025)**, and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version 004 (1 July 2025)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

- The retrieved documents do **not** prohibit advertising a property merely because an advertisement accurately shows apparent mould. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- However, every room must be free from mould and damp **“caused by or related to the building structure”**, and the rental provider must ensure compliance with the minimum standards **on or before the day the renter enters into occupation**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Before entering the rental agreement, the provider must disclose whether the premises comply with the minimum standards. They must also disclose any repair notice received within the previous **3 years** concerning mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- They must not induce someone to enter an agreement through misleading or deceptive conduct, including a false or misleading representation about the property’s characteristics. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

**The advertising photo alone is not necessarily enough to prove a breach.** It may show apparent mould, but the minimum standard specifically requires the mould to be caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) The documents say photographs may be useful in a dispute, but do not say that an advertising photograph is conclusive proof; by contrast, a condition report signed by both parties can be conclusive evidence of the property’s condition, subject to stated exceptions. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Before signing, ask the provider or agent in writing:

1. whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards;
2. whether the apparent mould is still present;
3. what caused it and what repairs or treatment have been completed; and
4. whether any mould or damp repair notice was received during the previous **3 years**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

If you move in and the property does not meet the minimum standards, you may request **urgent repairs** to bring it into compliance. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Record the mould in the condition report and attach dated, labelled photographs showing both close-up detail and the wider room; the prescribed condition-report instructions say photographs may be useful in a dispute. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) Mould standard: 'every room must be free from mould and damp "caused by or related to the building structure"'. (2) Photo alone not proof: 'The advertising photo alone is not necessarily enough to prove a breach.' (3) Next steps: asking the agent in writing before signing, and requesting 'urgent repairs' after moving in.

must-not-say.reason: Yes — the answer makes neither failing claim: it says "The advertising photo alone is not necessarily enough to prove a breach" and "The retrieved documents do not prohibit advertising a property merely because an advertisement accurately shows apparent mould."

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 110 (6 August 2025)' and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 004 (1 July 2025)', and relies only on those versions through links 97-109aa110 and 21-3sra004.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2026**, the applicable Act is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

- If your arrangement with your friend amounted to **subletting**, you needed the rental provider’s **written consent**. Without that consent, the subletting is **invalid**, unless VCAT had determined that consent was unnecessary. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider may give **you** a notice to vacate for assigning, subletting, or purportedly subletting without consent. That notice must allow at least **14 days**. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
- If your friend is legally your renter under a residential rental agreement, you cannot simply compel them to leave or take possession yourself. Such an agreement can only end in accordance with the Act, including by agreement, an applicable notice, abandonment, or a VCAT process. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do

1. **Ask your friend to agree in writing to leave on a specified date.** A residential rental agreement may be terminated by agreement between the rental provider and renter. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
2. If they refuse, whether you can give them a notice—and on what ground—depends on whether the arrangement was legally a residential rental agreement rather than merely permission for a guest to stay. The retrieved documents do **not** provide enough information to classify your arrangement.
3. The documents do **not** create a notice-to-vacate ground merely because you have changed your mind. If an applicable statutory ground exists, the notice must use the prescribed form, be addressed and signed, state the reason and termination date, and comply with the required notice period. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The prescribed notice is **Form 6** in the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, incorporating amendments as at 30 June 2026**. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)
4. **Do not assume you can change the locks or physically remove your friend.** The retrieved documents do not establish that right for this situation.

Because the documents do not explain how to remove someone who is only a guest or licensee—and the facts do not establish whether your friend is a sub-renter—the precise removal procedure cannot be answered from these documents without guessing.

must-mention.reason: No — the 'depends on the arrangement' point is missing its deciding fact. The answer does say outcomes depend on 'whether the arrangement was legally a residential rental agreement rather than merely permission for a guest to stay', and it covers written consent for subletting. But it never names a fact that would decide the classification, such as exclusive space, what was agreed, or whether the friend pays rent.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says none of the four things. The only fixed period, "at least 14 days," applies to a notice the rental provider may give the renter, not to ending the friend's occupancy. Whether the renter can give the friend a notice "depends on whether the arrangement was legally a residential rental agreement." It warns "Do not assume you can change the locks or physically remove your friend." It never says the friend lacks rights or can apply to VCAT to be added to the lease.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the required document with its in-force version, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026'; it also relies on 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, incorporating amendments as at 30 June 2026', which is the version in force on that date, and it applies no rule from any other version.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
## What the law says

On **1 November 2019**, the applicable law was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088**, in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

For a month-to-month tenancy, check whether the notice is a **“no specified reason” notice under section 263**. Such a notice had to give a termination date **at least 120 days after it was given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

A section 263 notice has **no effect** if it was given in response to the tenant’s exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Asking for repairs may involve exercising rights connected with the landlord’s duty to maintain the premises in good repair and the statutory repair procedures. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- **Check the notice:** Does it rely on section 263, and is the termination date at least 120 days after the notice date? [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Keep evidence of the connection:** Retain your repair requests, follow-ups, photographs, emails and the notice showing that it was issued the same day. The Act does not specify what evidence proves retaliation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Challenge it at VCAT:** If it is a section 263 notice, you must apply to challenge its validity **within 60 days after the notice was given**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Ask VCAT to find that the notice has no effect** because it was issued in response to your exercise or proposed exercise of repair rights under the Act. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

If the notice relies on a different section, these particular section 263 retaliation and 60-day rules may not apply; check the section and reason stated on the notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The answer says a section 263 'no specified reason' notice 'had to give a termination date at least 120 days after it was given'. It says the notice 'has no effect if it was given in response to the tenant's exercise, or proposed exercise, of a right under the Act', and links this to repair rights. It says the tenant 'must apply to challenge its validity within 60 days after the notice was given' at VCAT.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the landlord had to give a reason; it describes the notice as a "'no specified reason' notice under section 263". The only challenge deadline it gives is "within 60 days after the notice was given".

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088', in force 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 and linked as 97-109aa088, and it applies rules only from that in-force version.

The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?

(2) Inviting higher offers: the agent "must not solicit or invite an offer higher than the advertised rent." (3) The hardest point, unsolicited offers, is covered by "The Act does not expressly prohibit an applicant from voluntarily offering more. The key question is whether the provider or agent solicited or invited that higher offer." (4) The false email: "The retrieved Act does not specifically make a false 'you withdrew' email a separate offence."

The answer says "Relisting at a higher fixed rent is not, by itself, expressly prohibited" and "The Act does not expressly prohibit an applicant from voluntarily offering more", and nowhere claims the applicant can force the agent to rent the property to them.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
## What the law says

Under the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026**, the rental provider had **14 days after receiving your official request** to apply to VCAT for an order allowing refusal. If they did not apply within that period, they are **taken to have consented** to the dog. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Simply telling you “no” because the owner is allergic is **not enough**. If an application was made in time, VCAT—not the agent or owner—decides whether refusal is reasonable. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) VCAT may consider the type of pet, the apartment and its fixtures, any relevant legislation, and any other relevant matter. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The document does not say whether an owner’s allergy—especially where the owner rarely visits—would by itself justify refusal.

## What you can do

Ask the agent, in writing, whether the rental provider **applied to VCAT within 14 days of receiving your request**, and ask for the application details. If no timely application was made, state that consent is taken to have been given under **section 71C(2)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) Since you sent the form three weeks ago, that 14-day period has passed. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes: all three points are covered. The hardest one, that consent is taken as given after three weeks unless VCAT was applied to in time, is covered by 'If no timely application was made, state that consent is taken to have been given under section 71C(2)' together with 'Since you sent the form three weeks ago, that 14-day period has passed.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failure conditions is asserted. The answer says the refusal is "not enough," that the rental provider (not the renter) had to "apply to VCAT," and that "the document does not say whether an owner's allergy... would by itself justify refusal."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, dated 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115), which is the version in force on 15 October 2026, and every rule it applies comes from that version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## What the law says

**The notice does not automatically lapse because the buyer pulled out.** A notice to vacate is withdrawn only through a written withdrawal signed by both the landlord and the renters [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

However, the sale ground applies only where the premises are to be **sold or offered for sale with vacant possession immediately after the termination date**. Therefore, if the landlord is still offering the property for sale with vacant possession, the failed purchase alone does not remove that ground. If the landlord is no longer selling or offering it for sale, you may challenge whether the notice remains valid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

You cannot be forcibly removed merely because the termination date arrives. The landlord must apply to VCAT for a possession order; VCAT must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice, that it has not been withdrawn, and that making the order is reasonable and proportionate. Only Victoria Police may carry out a forcible eviction under a warrant for possession [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the landlord to **formally withdraw the notice in writing**, signed by the landlord and all renters [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Ask whether the property is **still being sold or offered for sale with vacant possession**.
- If it is not, challenge the notice at VCAT. An application specifically challenging a sale notice must generally be made **within 30 days after the notice was given**; you may also dispute the notice if the landlord applies for a possession order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Attend any possession-order hearing and explain that the buyer withdrew and, if applicable, that the property is no longer being sold [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

This answer applies the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025**, which was in force on 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: No. The answer omits the minimum 60-day notice period entirely. It covers the written withdrawal signed by both parties and gives next steps (seek a written withdrawal, or challenge at VCAT within 30 days), and it only partly addresses how the answer depends on the notice's stated ground and evidence.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failure conditions is asserted. The answer states that "The notice does not automatically lapse because the buyer pulled out" and that withdrawal requires "a written withdrawal signed by both the landlord and the renters". It states no minimum notice period at all; the only time limit it gives is the 30-day window to challenge the notice at VCAT, which is not a notice period.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, dated 6 August 2025' (link 97-109aa110), and its only other source is the Regulations link 21-3sra004, which is Version 004, the version in force on 1 October 2025.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

**No—not on the facts you gave.** An email merely saying the rent will increase is not enough unless it gives you the prescribed **Form 5, “Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises.”** A valid notice must state the current and new rent, start date, calculation method, and other required details. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Until a valid Form 5 notice is given, the proposed increase is invalid, so you continue paying your current rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Your attempt to negotiate—and the agent’s refusal—does not replace the required notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

Once a valid notice is given, the higher rent can start **no earlier than 60 days after the notice is given**, on the start date stated in that notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) Rent also cannot normally be increased more than once every 12 months; during a fixed term, it cannot be increased unless the agreement specifies the amount or method of calculating the increase. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do

- Ask the agent to provide a properly completed **Form 5**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- Continue paying the existing rent until the valid notice’s stated commencement date. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- If you think the properly notified increase is excessive, apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria for an investigation **within 30 days after receiving the notice**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

The law in force on **1 October 2025** is in the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110 (6 August 2025)** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), together with the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004 (1 July 2025)**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: All four points are covered. The output says Form 5 is required. It says the increase can start 'no earlier than 60 days after the notice is given.' It says an email alone 'is not enough' and that 'Until a valid Form 5 notice is given, the proposed increase is invalid, so you continue paying your current rent.' It also lists next steps: request Form 5, keep paying current rent, and apply to Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days of receiving a proper notice.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the failure conditions are asserted: the answer says "you continue paying your current rent," states the increase can start "no earlier than 60 days after the notice is given," never ties the start to the email date, and implies an email can work if it "gives you the prescribed Form 5."

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110 (6 August 2025)" and "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004 (1 July 2025)", and its links (97-109aa110, 21-3sra004) rely on no other version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
## What the law says

The **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026**, requires you to give the rental provider **written notice as soon as practicable** after becoming aware of damage, stating that damage occurred and describing it. Therefore, you should not quietly repair the skirting boards without telling the owner or agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

Damage is not fair wear and tear if it was caused intentionally or negligently. When you move out, you must leave the property, as far as practicable, in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner may claim from the bond for the **reasonable cost of repairs or restoration** resulting from damage caused by you or your visitors [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Notify the owner or agent in writing now**, describe the damage and offer to arrange and pay for repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Ask for written agreement about **who will repair it and the required finish**. If the owner gives you a repair notice requiring you to repair it, you have **14 days**, and the work must be completed in a proper and tradesman-like manner [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- Use a **suitably qualified person**: the standard rental agreement in the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026**, states that only a suitably qualified person may perform urgent or non-urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- Keep dated photographs, the quote, invoice and proof of payment. The prescribed condition report says photographs can help resolve end-of-agreement disputes about damage [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Insurance

The retrieved documents **do not say whether this damage or a private repair would affect the owner’s insurance policy**, so that cannot be answered from them. They do say that a rental agreement cannot make you **liable by default for an insurance excess** under the owner’s policy [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). That does not determine whether you might otherwise be liable for the reasonable repair cost.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: written notice 'as soon as practicable'; responsibility for non-fair-wear-and-tear damage, covered by 'you must leave the property, as far as practicable, in the same condition' and 'The owner may claim from the bond for the reasonable cost of repairs... resulting from damage caused by you or your visitors'; the documents 'do not say whether this damage or a private repair would affect the owner's insurance policy'; and next steps such as 'Notify the owner or agent in writing now... offer to arrange and pay for repair'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the prohibited claims are asserted: the answer says "you should not quietly repair the skirting boards without telling the owner or agent," declines to predict an insurance outcome ("The retrieved documents do not say whether this damage or a private repair would affect the owner's insurance policy"), and states that "a rental agreement cannot make you liable by default for an insurance excess."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026" and "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, in force from 30 June 2026" (links 97-109aa115 and 21-3sra009), and relies on no other version.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says on 1 March 2023

The documents **do not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits** for a rental property. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) The electrical minimum standard requiring all power outlets and lighting circuits to be connected to compliant switchboard-type circuit breakers and residual current devices did **not begin until 29 March 2023**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

However, the rental provider must maintain the premises **in good repair and reasonably fit and suitable for occupation**, regardless of the property’s age or rent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) A **dangerous electrical fault** is expressly classified as an urgent repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not establish whether a breaker tripping when a kettle and heater run together is, by itself, a dangerous fault; that requires electrical assessment.

## What you can ask for

- Notify the rental provider or agent **in writing** about the repeated tripping and ask for a licensed or registered electrician to assess whether the circuit or switchboard is faulty, unsafe or needs upgrading. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- Ask for the **date of the most recent electrical safety check**. Checks must occur every **2 years**; if you request the latest record in writing, it must be supplied within **7 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- You can ask for another circuit or other upgrade, but the retrieved documents do not give an automatic right to a particular number of circuits. The provider would need to undertake whatever work is necessary to remedy a fault and meet their repair duties. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- If an electrician identifies a dangerous electrical fault, treat it as an **urgent repair**. If the provider or agent cannot be made to act immediately after reasonable attempts, you may arrange repairs costing up to **$2,500** and seek reimbursement, or apply to VCAT if you cannot afford them or they cost more than $2,500. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- If it is non-urgent and remains unrepaired for **14 days after written notice**, you may apply to VCAT for an order requiring the repairs. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

**Documents in force:** *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, **Authorised Version No. 002**, incorporating amendments as at **1 June 2022** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf); and *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version No. 101**, incorporating amendments as at **7 September 2022** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer states the documents 'do not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits'. For next steps, it advises notifying the provider in writing to request an electrician's assessment and repair, treating a dangerous electrical fault as an urgent repair, and asking for 'the date of the most recent electrical safety check'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither failure condition: it says the documents "do not prescribe a minimum number of electrical circuits" and "do not give an automatic right to a particular number of circuits," and it says the circuit breaker and RCD standard "did not begin until 29 March 2023," so it does not apply on 1 March 2023.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as "Authorised Version No. 101, incorporating amendments as at 7 September 2022" (link 97-109aa101) and the Regulations as "Authorised Version No. 002, incorporating amendments as at 1 June 2022" (link 21-3sra002), both in force on 1 March 2023. It applies no rule from any other version, and its note that the electrical standard began 29 March 2023 only says the law changes later.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## What the law says

**Yes—charging to use the washing machines is not prohibited.** The rooming-house operator may charge for services, but before you move in they must give you a separate schedule showing the charge. If you use the service, they must also provide an itemised account showing your individual use. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The operator must still provide **one working washing machine for every 12 or fewer residents**, calculated using the rooming house’s maximum capacity. The minimum standard does not say that its use must be free. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

This is based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115**, in force from 13 October 2026, [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, Authorised Version No. 002**, in force from 1 December 2024. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf)

## What you can ask

Ask the operator for:

- the required schedule stating the laundry charge; and
- an itemised account showing your individual use. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do not explain exactly how an operator must provide an itemised account for a coin-operated machine, so I cannot say whether the machines’ current setup satisfies that requirement.

must-mention.reason: Yes. The output covers all four points: one working washing machine per 12 or fewer residents; 'The minimum standard does not say that its use must be free'; the operator must give a separate schedule of charges 'before you move in'; and, for the hardest point, the next step 'Ask the operator for: the required schedule stating the laundry charge'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never says the machines must be free, that there are no rules on charges, or that a cost cap applies to all rooming houses. Instead it says "charging to use the washing machines is not prohibited" and that the operator "must give you a separate schedule showing the charge" and "an itemised account showing your individual use."

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names both required documents with the in-force versions, the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115' (link 97-109aa115) and the 'Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023, Authorised Version No. 002' (link 23-10sra002), and relies on no other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **1 October 2025**, the relevant instruments were the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110 (6 August 2025)** [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004 (1 July 2025)** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

- The retrieved documents do **not expressly prohibit advertising a property merely because the advertisement’s photo appears to show mould**. However, a provider or agent must not use misleading or deceptive conduct, or make a false or misleading representation about the property’s characteristics, to induce someone to enter a rental agreement [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- By the day the renter enters occupation, the provider must ensure that the premises meet the rental minimum standards [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The mould standard requires **each room to be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure** [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **The photo alone does not conclusively prove non-compliance.** The documents do not say that an advertising photo is sufficient evidence, and the standard depends not only on whether the substance is mould, but also on whether it is caused by or related to the building structure [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

Before signing, ask the provider or agent:

1. **Whether the property complies with the rental minimum standards**—they must disclose this before entering the agreement [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Whether the provider has received a repair notice during the last 3 years concerning mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure**—that must also be disclosed [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. Whether the pictured area has been inspected or repaired, and for current photos or an inspection. The retrieved documents do not require them to provide an inspection report merely because you ask.

If you sign but have **not yet taken possession**, you may terminate the agreement if the premises do not meet any rental minimum standard [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). If you move in and they do not comply on or immediately after occupation, you may request **urgent repairs** to bring them up to standard [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The output states the mould standard requires 'each room to be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'. It says 'The photo alone does not conclusively prove non-compliance' because the documents do not make a photo sufficient evidence. It gives next steps: ask the agent, terminate before possession, or request urgent repairs after moving in.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says neither forbidden thing: it states "The photo alone does not conclusively prove non-compliance" and that the documents "do not expressly prohibit advertising a property merely because the advertisement's photo appears to show mould."

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110 (6 August 2025)' and the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004 (1 July 2025)', both in force on 1 October 2025, and relies on no other version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

The applicable law is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115**, incorporating amendments as at **13 October 2026**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

If your arrangement with your friend was a **subletting**, you needed the rental provider’s written consent. Without that consent, the subletting is invalid unless VCAT determined that consent was unnecessary. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The rental provider may also give **you** a notice to vacate for unauthorised subletting, with a termination date at least **14 days** after the notice is given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do not provide enough information to decide whether your friend is legally a sub-renter or merely a housemate or licensee. That may depend on the actual arrangement, not simply whether they paid you money.

## What you can do

1. **Tell your friend clearly, preferably in writing, that you withdraw permission for them to live there and specify when they must leave.** Section 344 applies where premises were rented within the previous **12 months** and are occupied by someone who is not a renter and who remains without the applicant’s licence or consent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

2. **If they do not leave, apply to VCAT for a possession order under section 344.** VCAT must make the order if satisfied that you are entitled to possession and there are reasonable grounds to believe the friend is occupying without licence or consent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

3. **If VCAT orders possession and they still remain, obtain a warrant of possession.** A person who obtains a possession order may apply for a warrant; the Act provides for forcible removal by a police officer or authorised person carrying out that warrant. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

Because the classification of your friend’s occupancy determines the correct process, the retrieved documents do not establish conclusively that section 344 applies to your particular arrangement. They do establish that an unapproved subletting is invalid and may put **your own tenancy** at risk. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On the hardest one, the answer says the friend's status "may depend on the actual arrangement, not simply whether they paid you money," which names the arrangement and payment as deciding facts. On consent, it says that for a subletting "you needed the rental provider's written consent."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the four claims is made: the only fixed period is the rental provider's notice to the renter ("at least **14 days**"), not a period for ending the friend's stay. The friend is told only to be given a date ("specify when they must leave"), and the s 344 process is hedged ("do not establish conclusively that section 344 applies"). Removal is only by "a police officer or authorised person carrying out that warrant," not by the renter, and nothing says the friend has no rights or can apply to VCAT to be added to the lease.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026' (link 97-109aa115), which is the version in force on 15 October 2026, and every rule it applies is sourced only from that version.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Source:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf", dated 2 July 2019. Its metadata gives Version 088, in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers 1 November 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The extract I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." line, so the version number comes from the metadata.

The file also contains amending-Act text in its endnotes. That text uses newer terms such as "renter" and "residential rental provider", with section numbers like 91ZZI. I haven't treated it as the law on 1 November 2019. The rules below come from the in-force wording ("landlord" and "tenant"), Part 6 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Notice without a reason.** A landlord may give a notice to vacate without specifying a reason (s 263(1)). For a periodic (month-to-month) agreement, the termination date must be at least 120 days after the notice is given (s 263(2)(c)). One exception is a periodic agreement referred to in s 230(3A), which has its own paragraph. I didn't retrieve s 230(3A), so I can't say whether it applies to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Retaliation protection.** A notice under s 261 or s 263 "is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act" (s 266(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Repair rights.**
  - The landlord must keep the premises in good repair (s 68(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - A tenant can arrange urgent repairs if reasonable steps to get the landlord to act failed (s 72(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - For non-urgent repairs, a tenant can give written notice. If the landlord hasn't acted within 14 days, the tenant can apply to the Director (s 74) and then the Tribunal (s 75) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Time limit.** You can't apply to the Tribunal to challenge a s 263 notice after 60 days from the date it was given (s 266(3)(c)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What to check and do

1. **Which section the notice relies on.** The retaliation rule in s 266(2) names only s 261 (end of fixed term) and s 263 (no specified reason) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). On a month-to-month agreement it is probably a s 263 notice. If it cites another ground, such as sale, owner occupation or repairs, s 266(2) doesn't cover it. Those grounds have their own requirements, including a 60-day minimum notice (e.g. ss 255–260) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **The termination date.** Under s 263(2)(c), a termination date less than 120 days after the notice was given is a defect to raise [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. **The timing and your repair steps.** Gather evidence that the notice came "in response to" your repair request. That means the dates of your repair requests and follow-up, and the notice's date, which you say was the same day. Note whether you gave written notice, since ss 74–75 rely on it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Your deadline.** The 60-day limit runs from the date the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If it was given on 1 November 2019, I count the 60 days as ending about 31 December 2019. Please verify that date, and don't leave it late.
5. **Whether your request was a "right under this Act".** The documents don't say in terms that a repair request or follow-up counts. The repair provisions above are the likely basis [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- The Tribunal's powers when it decides a challenge. The in-force text I retrieved only states the time limit.
- How retaliation is proved.
- The required form and content of a notice to vacate.
- What counts as "urgent" repairs.

I haven't filled these gaps from memory.

The other 60-day figure is a notice period for other grounds, not a challenge deadline.
