question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
**Version applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025). It incorporates amendments as at 6 August 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it was in force until 24 November 2025, so it covers 1 October 2025. The retrieved documents don't say it updates or replaces any other document.

## What the law says

- **Fixed rent only.** A rental provider or their agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount (s 30F(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **No inviting higher offers.** They must not "solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount" (s 30F(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Penalty.** Each of these breaches carries 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **False or misleading rent advertising.** A provider or agent who promotes or advertises rented premises must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent (s 30G(2)). This section applies only to providers and agents not acting in trade or commerce, and it doesn't limit the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading conduct.** A provider or agent must not induce someone to enter a rental agreement through misleading or deceptive conduct. This includes false or misleading representations about the rent payable (s 30E(2)–(3)(b)). It has the same trade-or-commerce limit, and it also doesn't limit the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). A note to s 30E says s 472(1A) allows Tribunal orders on an application about a contravention of that section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't settle

- **The false "withdrawn" email.** The retrieved text has no provision that specifically deals with wrongly recording an application as withdrawn. You could argue it was misleading conduct under s 30E, or part of a scheme to invite higher offers under s 30F(3). That depends on facts I don't have, such as who sent the email and why.
- **The competing offer.** Section 30F(3) bans *soliciting or inviting* higher offers. The retrieved text doesn't say what happens if another applicant offers more without being invited. So whether the provider acted unlawfully depends on whether they invited or encouraged the higher offer.
- **The higher relisting.** The retrieved text doesn't expressly ban relisting at a higher rent. It only requires a fixed advertised amount and bans inviting offers above it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal powers and procedure.** The documents don't set out the text of s 472, the Tribunal's available orders, or any time limits.

## What you can do

1. **Challenge it at the Tribunal.** On the retrieved text, a s 30E misleading-conduct application is the clearest route. Ask the Tribunal what orders are available, because that detail isn't in the retrieved documents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask the provider or agent in writing** why you were recorded as withdrawn. Ask them to confirm whether any higher offer was invited.
3. **If you paid a holding deposit**, s 50 requires it to be refunded. If an agreement is entered into within 14 days, the refund is due when it is entered into. If not, it is due on the next business day after the 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Check whether discrimination could be a factor.** Refusing to let on a protected attribute is separately prohibited (s 30A), and s 210AA allows a compensation application [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What to save as evidence

The documents don't list evidence requirements. These suggestions are based on what the provisions turn on:

- The **original advertisement** showing the advertised rent, with screenshots and dates.
- The **relisting** at the higher rent, also with screenshots and dates.
- Your **application and any confirmation** you received.
- The **"withdrawn" email**, with full headers, sender and timestamp. Also keep anything showing you never withdrew, such as your sent messages or call logs.
- **All messages with the agent or provider**, including anything suggesting offers above the advertised price were welcome.
- **Proof of any payment**, such as a holding deposit or application fee.
- Any **record of who told you about the higher offer**, and when.

If you want a firm view on remedies and time limits, check s 472 of the Act and consider contacting Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal service. The documents I retrieved don't cover those points.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The answer says the retrieved text 'doesn't expressly ban relisting at a higher rent' and that s 30F(3) bans soliciting or inviting higher offers. On the hardest point, it states the text 'doesn't say what happens if another applicant offers more without being invited... whether the provider acted unlawfully depends on whether they invited or encouraged the higher offer.' It also notes there is 'no provision that specifically deals with wrongly recording an application as withdrawn.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three claims is made. On relisting, the answer says "The retrieved text doesn't expressly ban relisting at a higher rent." On the competing offer, it says the text "doesn't say what happens if another applicant offers more without being invited." It never says the applicant can force the agent to rent to them; it only suggests asking the Tribunal "what orders are available."

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'Authorised Version No. 110 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025)' with link 97-109aa110, and every rule it applies (ss 30E, 30F, 30G, 50, 30A, 210AA) comes from that in-force version, with no reliance on any other version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act, a refusal by the agent isn't enough. Whether the owner's allergy is a good reason is for the Tribunal to decide, and the documents don't say.

I relied on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It is the version in force on 15 October 2026. Your request was sent about three weeks ago, which is before 13 October. The documents don't include the earlier version, so I can't confirm its wording for that earlier date.

## What the law says

- **Request:** A renter must ask for consent in the form approved by the Director and give it to the residential rental provider (s 71B) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **No unreasonable refusal:** A provider must not unreasonably refuse consent to a pet (s 71C(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations' standard-form text says the same [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) (*Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Version 009, in force 30 June 2026).
- **14-day rule:** The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal under s 71D (s 71C(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Only the Tribunal can approve a refusal:** The provider can apply for an order that refusing is reasonable (s 71D(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can then either permit the pet, or order that refusal is reasonable and exclude the pet (s 71E(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **What the Tribunal considers (s 71E(2)):** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)
  - the type of pet
  - the character and nature of the premises
  - the appliances, fixtures and fittings
  - whether refusing is permitted under any Act
  - any prescribed matters
  - any other matter it considers relevant

## How this applies to you

- **Timing:** Three weeks is more than 14 days. If the owner or agent did not apply to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your form, the owner is taken to have consented, whatever the agent said [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't tell me whether an application was made, so you should check that.
- **The allergy:** The Act doesn't list an owner's allergy as a valid or invalid ground. It could fall under "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Your point that the owner rarely visits is the kind of fact you could put to the Tribunal. I can't say how it would decide.

## What you can do

1. **Ask in writing:** Ask the agent whether the owner applied to the Tribunal within 14 days of your form. If not, point to the deemed consent in s 71C(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Be careful about bringing the dog in:** A provider who reasonably believes a pet is being kept without consent can apply to the Tribunal for an order excluding it (s 71D(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Know the consequences:** A notice to vacate for keeping a pet is only available if the Tribunal has ordered the pet excluded, at least 14 days have passed since the order took effect, and the renter hasn't complied. The notice must give at least 28 days (s 91ZZG) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say how a renter formally confirms deemed consent, or how to bring a dispute about it. I'd suggest checking with Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT before acting.

must-mention.reason: All three points are covered. (1) The 14-day rule: 'The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal under s 71D.' The answer says 'Tribunal' rather than 'VCAT', but the Tribunal under this Act is VCAT, so the meaning is the same. (2) Applied to three weeks: 'Three weeks is more than 14 days. If the owner or agent did not apply to the Tribunal within 14 days of receiving your form, the owner is taken to have consented, whatever the agent said.' (3) Next step: 'Ask the agent whether the owner applied to the Tribunal within 14 days of your form.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the failing claims appear: the answer rejects the refusal as final ("a refusal by the agent isn't enough"), places the onus to apply on the provider ("unless, within 14 days of being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal"), and treats the allergy as undecided ("Whether the owner's allergy is a good reason is for the Tribunal to decide").

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, incorporating amendments as at 13 October 2026' (file 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf', link 97-109aa115) and the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Version 009' (link 21-3sra009), both in force on 15 October 2026, and it applies no rule from any other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
## What the law says

The law I'm applying is the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf" (dated 6 August 2025). Its metadata labels it version 110 and shows it in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025, so it covers 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The extracts I retrieved don't print the words "Authorised Version No.", so version 110 comes from the metadata.

- **The notice stays in effect until it is formally withdrawn.** A notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a notice of withdrawal is given. That notice must be in writing and signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person who received it [1, s 91ZZQ]. The landlord doing nothing, or the buyer pulling out, doesn't withdraw it. The retrieved text says nothing about a notice lapsing automatically when a sale falls through.
- **You don't have to leave just because the notice exists.**
  - The agreement ends if you move out on or after the termination date in the notice [1, s 91E].
  - A landlord can't require or try to compel you to leave except as the Act allows. Breaching this carries a penalty of 150 penalty units for a natural person [1, s 91P].
  - If you stay, the landlord can apply to VCAT for a possession order [1, s 322(1)]. That application can be made any time after the notice is given, up to 30 days after the termination date [1, s 326(1)].
  - VCAT can't decide the application before the termination date [1, s 329].
- **What VCAT must find before ordering you out.** Among other things, it must be satisfied that the landlord was entitled to give the notice and that the notice has not been withdrawn. It must also be satisfied that making the order is reasonable and proportionate, taking into account your interests and the landlord's [1, s 330(1)(a), (f)].
- **Does the failed sale affect the landlord's entitlement?** A sale notice is allowed where the premises are, immediately after the termination date, "to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession". It is also allowed within 14 days of a contract of sale being entered into or becoming unconditional. It must give at least 60 days' notice [1, s 91ZZB]. The documents don't say whether a buyer withdrawing makes the notice invalid. That is likely to depend on whether the landlord still intends to sell or offer the property for sale with vacant possession. I can't confirm that from the documents.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord to withdraw the notice in writing.** Both you and the landlord must sign it for the withdrawal to count [1, s 91ZZQ].
2. **Challenge the notice at VCAT.** On or before the hearing of a possession application, you can apply to challenge the notice's validity. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given [1, s 91ZZS]. VCAT can decide whether the notice is valid [1, s 91ZZT]. Check the date on your notice, because that window may already be closing or closed.
3. **If a hearing happens, argue it shouldn't result in an order.** You can raise that the order wouldn't be reasonable or proportionate in your circumstances [1, s 330(1)(f)]. The sale falling through is a fact VCAT can weigh under its other relevant matters, though the documents don't list it specifically.
4. **If you want to leave early,** you can give a notice of intention to vacate on 14 days' notice after a sale-related notice, without waiting for the termination date [1, s 91ZB(1)(e), (2), (3)]. The prescribed notice-to-vacate form says the same for "the premises are to be sold" notices [2, Form 6, cl 5]. That form is in the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf" (dated 1 July 2025, version 004, in force until 24 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
5. **Know the 6-month rule.** If the landlord gets possession under a sale notice, they must not re-let the premises as a residence for 6 months after the notice date. The penalty is 150 penalty units for a natural person. Exceptions apply, such as the landlord's own family moving in or VCAT permitting the letting [1, s 91ZZH].

**In short:** the notice remains valid until formally withdrawn in writing, but you can only be made to leave by a VCAT possession order. It would be sensible to get advice from a community legal service or Consumer Affairs Victoria. The prescribed form points to them for this [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The hardest one, that the answer depends on the ground in the notice, is met by the answer separating the two sale grounds ('to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession' versus 'within 14 days of a contract of sale being entered into or becoming unconditional') and saying the effect 'is likely to depend on whether the landlord still intends to sell or offer the property for sale with vacant possession'. The answer also states the 60-day minimum, that withdrawal must be in writing and signed by both parties, and gives next steps: ask for a written withdrawal, or challenge the notice at VCAT within 30 days.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failing claims is asserted: the answer says "The landlord doing nothing, or the buyer pulling out, doesn't withdraw it", that the withdrawal notice "must be in writing and signed by both the person who gave the notice and the person who received it", and that a sale notice "must give at least 60 days' notice" (the 14-day figures cover the timing after a contract of sale and the tenant's own notice of intention to vacate, not the landlord's minimum notice period).

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 with its version ('version 110', file 'rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf', link '97-109aa110'), and the only other document it relies on is the in-force Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 ('version 004', link '21-3sra004'), with no rule drawn from a version not in force on 1 October 2025.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

I've assumed this is an ordinary residential rental agreement. Rooming houses and caravan parks have separate rules.

On 1 October 2025 the relevant documents were:
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997**, file *rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf*, dated 6 August 2025, in force 6 August to 24 November 2025. The file metadata gives its version as **110**. The retrieved text doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." line for the Act, so that number comes from the metadata [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021**, file *rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf*, **Authorised Version No. 004**, incorporating amendments as at 1 July 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Notice is required.**
- Under s 44(1) of the Act, the rental provider must give you **at least 60 days' notice, in the prescribed form**, of a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The notice can only provide for one increase. It must state the amount of the increase, how it was calculated, and your right to ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate within 30 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- The prescribed form is **Form 5**. It says the rental provider "must use this form" and that "a valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- Form 5 allows delivery by email only "if consent has been provided by the renter" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**An increase without valid notice is invalid.** Section 44(5) says "a rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The rent also can't rise at intervals of less than 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). During a fixed term it can only rise if the agreement provides for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## Your situation

- **Do you have to pay the higher rent?** From what you describe, an email saying the rent is going up, with no Form 5 notice, doesn't meet s 44. The increase would therefore be invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). If the email itself wasn't on Form 5, I can't see a basis in these documents for paying the higher amount yet.
- **From when?** Not from the email. The earliest a valid increase could start is **60 days after a proper notice is given** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The documents don't give a more specific start date for your case.
- **Your negotiation attempt.** The documents don't say it affects the notice requirement.
- **Money already paid.** The documents don't say whether you can recover any higher rent you've already paid. I can't answer that from them.

## What you can do

1. **Ask the agent in writing for a valid Form 5 notice** and keep paying your current rent until you get one. The documents don't address whether a particular payment approach has other consequences, so check with Consumer Affairs Victoria first.
2. **If you get a Form 5 notice and think the increase is excessive**, apply in writing to the Director within 30 days after the notice is given. The application is free [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **After the Director's report**, you can apply to VCAT within 30 days of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). If you didn't get a report and 30 days have passed, you can apply directly to VCAT with its leave, if you show reasonable grounds [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **While a VCAT application is pending**, Form 5 says you must pay the increased rent from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
5. **For more information**, Consumer Affairs Victoria's number on the form is 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: Form 5 is required, at least 60 days' notice is required, and the email without Form 5 is invalid (the hardest point, covered by 'an email saying the rent is going up, with no Form 5 notice, doesn't meet s 44. The increase would therefore be invalid'). A next step is given: 'Ask the agent in writing for a valid Form 5 notice and keep paying your current rent.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the failing claims is made: the answer says the increase "would therefore be invalid" and advises to "keep paying your current rent," states "Not from the email," gives "at least 60 days' notice," and says email delivery is allowed "if consent has been provided by the renter."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as version 110 (file 'rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf', link 97-109aa110) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as 'Authorised Version No. 004' (link 21-3sra004), both in force on 1 October 2025, and relies on no other version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents say you must tell the owner about the damage in writing. They don't address insurance at all.

I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf"). That version was in force on 15 October 2026. I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009, dated 30 June 2026 (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf").

## What the law says

- **You must not damage the property.** A renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the rented premises. Fair wear and tear doesn't count as damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Dog-chewed skirting boards are unlikely to be treated as fair wear and tear, but the documents don't say that either way.
- **You must report damage in writing.** A renter who becomes aware of damage must, as soon as practicable, give the rental provider written notice that it has happened and what it is [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard rental agreement form says the same thing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). So fixing it quietly and saying nothing doesn't fit this duty.
- **Not telling can count against you.** If the owner claims compensation, the Tribunal must consider whether you gave the required written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The owner decides how the repair is handled.** The owner can give you a written repair notice. It can require you to repair the damage at your own expense within 14 days. If you don't repair it in a proper, tradesman-like manner in that time, the owner can repair it and charge you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The owner can instead say they are doing the repairs themselves, and you are then liable for the reasonable cost once they give you the cost in writing. You must reimburse them within 14 days after the repairs are completed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who should do the repair.** The standard form says only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). That is a summary in the form, not a section of the Act.
- **Compensation is not the full repair cost.** If the owner applies to the Tribunal for compensation, it must take depreciation of the damaged part into account, using the Uniform Capital Allowance System or another prescribed scale [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal may also consider any action the person claimed against took to repair the damage at their own expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Moving out.** You must leave the premises in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Send written notice now** (email is fine) saying what the damage is and where it is [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Include photos.
2. **Ask the owner or agent how they want it handled.** You could offer to have it repaired by a suitably qualified person at your cost, or ask them to arrange it and tell you the cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). Agreeing this in writing avoids a dispute at the end of the tenancy.
3. **If a repair notice arrives,** the 14-day period applies for you to repair it properly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the owner does the repairs, you can apply to the Tribunal for more time if you can't reimburse them in 14 days. If you are in hardship, you can give written notice asking for an additional 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Insurance

**The retrieved documents don't say whether repairing the damage, or telling the owner, would affect the owner's insurance.** They don't mention insurance. I can't answer that part from them. The owner's insurer or the owner's agent would be the people to ask.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. Written notice 'as soon as practicable' is stated. Responsibility for damage that is not fair wear and tear is covered by the owner's right to require repair 'at your own expense' and 'You must leave the premises in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear'. The output says 'The retrieved documents don't say whether repairing the damage, or telling the owner, would affect the owner's insurance'. Next steps include 'Send written notice now' and agreeing the repair in writing.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: none of the failure conditions are asserted, since the answer rejects a quiet repair ("So fixing it quietly and saying nothing doesn't fit this duty"), states no insurance outcome ("The retrieved documents don't say whether repairing the damage, or telling the owner, would affect the owner's insurance"), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions: the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026" (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", link 97-109aa115) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "version 009, dated 30 June 2026" (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", link 21-3sra009). Every citation points only to these versions, and no rule comes from an earlier or later version.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says

I applied the versions in force on 1 March 2023. These are the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (file rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf), Authorised Version No. 002, incorporating amendments as at 1 June 2022 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The other is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (file rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf), Authorised Version No. 101, as at 7 September 2022 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**There is no rule on the number of circuits.** Neither document sets a minimum number of circuits or says how power points must be spread across them. If you need a rule on that, the documents don't have one.

The rules that do touch on electrics are these:

- **Rental minimum standards.** A rental provider must ensure the premises meet the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Regulations prescribe those standards in Schedule 4 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Circuit breakers and RCDs.** Schedule 4, clause 9 says all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type Circuit Breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000 and a switchboard-type Residual Current Device. It applies only "on and from 29 March 2023" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). On 1 March 2023 that requirement had not yet started. Even once it applies, it covers protective devices, not how many circuits there are.
- **General repair duty.** The rental provider must keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks.** The provider must have a licensed or registered electrician check all electrical installations, appliances and fittings every 2 years. They must give you the date of the latest check in writing if you ask [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can ask for

1. **Ask for the electrical safety check records.** Make a written request. The provider must give you a copy of the most recent electrical safety check within 7 days of receiving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The record must include the electrician's name and licence number, the date, the results (including repairs needed and actions taken), and a report under AS/NZS 3019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). You can also ask for the date of the last check. If no check has been done in the last 2 years when you moved in, the provider must arrange one as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Report the problem in writing and ask for it to be investigated and fixed.** Tell the provider that the breaker trips when two ordinary appliances run together, and ask for a licensed electrician to assess it. Under the standard agreement, you must notify the provider in writing of a breakdown of facilities or fixtures they supplied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **If it is a "dangerous electrical fault", treat it as an urgent repair.** The Act's definition of urgent repairs includes a "dangerous electrical fault" and a failure or breakdown of the electricity supply [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
   - If the provider doesn't act, the standard agreement says you may arrange the urgent repair yourself after taking reasonable steps to get the provider to do it. You can then be reimbursed the reasonable cost up to $2500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
   - You may apply to VCAT if you can't meet the cost, if it costs more than $2500, or if the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
   - The documents don't say whether a breaker tripping from simple overload counts as a "dangerous electrical fault". That is the weak point, so an electrician's assessment would help you.
4. **If it is non-urgent, escalate after 14 days.** The provider must do non-urgent repairs within a reasonable time. You may apply to VCAT for an order if the repairs haven't been done within 14 days of your notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## Limits

- The documents don't say whether your set-up, with most power points on one circuit, breaches any standard. They also don't say that a breaker tripping under combined kettle and heater load is a defect.
- After 29 March 2023, check that your breaker and RCD arrangements meet Schedule 4, clause 9 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer says "There is no rule on the number of circuits" and that neither document sets a minimum number. The hardest point, the next step, is covered by "Report the problem in writing and ask for it to be investigated and fixed", by the advice to treat it as an urgent repair "If it is a 'dangerous electrical fault'", and by "You can also ask for the date of the last check."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer states 'There is no rule on the number of circuits' and that the RCD/circuit breaker requirement 'applies only "on and from 29 March 2023"... On 1 March 2023 that requirement had not yet started', so it asserts neither a minimum circuit count nor that the standard already applies.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions: the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Authorised Version No. 101, as at 7 September 2022" (rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf, link 97-109aa101), and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "Authorised Version No. 002, incorporating amendments as at 1 June 2022" (link 21-3sra002). Every rule it applies is sourced from these versions. The Schedule 4 clause 9 requirement starting 29 March 2023 is also sourced from Version 002, and the answer says it had not yet started on 1 March 2023.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say plainly whether a rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. They do set rules that apply if an operator charges for services.

**Documents used**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf". It is labelled version 115 and is in force from 13 October 2026, so it was current on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The excerpts I retrieved don't show the "Authorised Version No." heading, so I am relying on the version label in the file.
- *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023*, Authorised Version No. 002, in force from 1 December 2024 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). I did not retrieve a later version, so I can't confirm it was the current one on 15 October 2026.
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, dated 30 June 2026 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **No express ban or permission.** None of the retrieved provisions say that coin-operated laundry charges are allowed or forbidden.
- **Schedule and itemised account (s 109).** If a rooming house operator charges an amount for services, the operator must do two things [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf):
  - Give you a separate schedule of the amounts for those services before you take up residency.
  - Give you an itemised account showing your individual use, if you use any of those services.
  
  The Act doesn't say whether a coin-operated machine counts as a "service" here. That is my reading, not something the documents state.
- **Metered charges (s 108).** An operator may charge separately for electricity, gas and water used in your room if the room is separately metered and the operator pays the bills. The charge can't exceed the supplier's charge, and this doesn't apply to shared rooms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It concerns your own room, not shared laundry machines.
- **Laundry service charges (s 109A).** Only Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may impose a service charge for laundry facilities, and only in a rooming house declared under s 19(2) or (3). The charge applies only where it isn't possible or practicable to measure your use. It can't exceed the cost of providing the facility, and you can apply to the Tribunal to have it withdrawn or varied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say who runs your house.
- **Rent definition.** "Rent" is the amount you pay to occupy a room "and use facilities and services". It excludes amounts payable under ss 108 and 109A [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Washing machine standard.** From 26 February 2024, a rooming house must have a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents, plus a wash trough, a hot and cold water outlet space and a clothes line [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). That standard doesn't mention whether use is free.
- **Access and repairs.** The operator must give access during all reasonable hours to the other facilities for residents' use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The operator must also keep equipment it provides in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The model fixed term agreement lists failure of a laundering appliance supplied by the operator as an urgent repair [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Ask in writing for the schedule of services and charges** that s 109 requires before residency starts. If you use a charged service, ask for an itemised account of your use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the house rules.** An operator may make house rules about the use of facilities. They must be reasonable and enforced fairly, and the operator must give 7 days' written notice of any change [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can apply to the Tribunal for an order declaring a house rule unreasonable, and the Tribunal may then declare it invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Find out who the operator is.** If it is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, the s 109A limits apply: the charge can't exceed cost, and you can challenge it at the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Report faults.** If a machine breaks, tell the operator. You can use the repair processes in the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't address whether a coin-operated charge is lawful in your house. For a definite answer, take the schedule of services and your agreement to a tenancy advice service or Consumer Affairs Victoria.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The answer states the one-washing-machine-per-12-residents standard and says 'That standard doesn't mention whether use is free.' It explains that under s 109 the operator must 'give you a separate schedule of the amounts for those services before you take up residency.' Its next step is to 'Ask in writing for the schedule of services and charges.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three claims is made: the answer never says the machines must be free, it says the documents 'do set rules that apply if an operator charges for services' (s 109 schedule and itemised account), and it limits the cost cap to 'Only Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency... in a rooming house declared under s 19(2) or (3)'.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 115" (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", link 97-109aa115) and the Rooming House Standards Regulations 2023 as "Authorised Version No. 002" (link 23-10sra002), and it also cites the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "version 009". All three are the versions in force on 15 October 2026, and no rule is drawn from any other version.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
Both documents below were in force on 1 October 2025. The Authorised Version numbers are taken from the documents' version metadata, because the extracted text doesn't print them.
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025), version 110, in force 6 Aug – 24 Nov 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (file "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf", dated 1 July 2025), version 004, in force 1 Jul – 24 Nov 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

**Mould and the minimum standards**
- The rental minimum standards say each room "must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- The rental provider must ensure the premises meet the standards on or before the day the renter moves in. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- That duty falls on the move-in day. It is not triggered by the advertisement itself.

**Can they advertise it like that?**
- I found no provision in these two documents that bans advertising a property with photos showing mould. The documents do not say an ad like this is unlawful in itself.
- Three rules still matter:
  - Before signing, the provider must disclose prescribed information, with the same penalties (60 and 300 penalty units) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). That includes whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
  - It also includes whether the provider has received a repair notice in the last 3 years about mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
  - A provider or agent not acting in trade or commerce must not induce someone to sign by misleading or deceptive conduct. That includes a false or misleading representation about the characteristics of the premises [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Photos showing mould would be unlikely to mislead on that point. A caption saying the room was "compliant" or "mould-free" could.
- The advertising rule on false or misleading representations (s 30G) covers only representations about rent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**Is the photo enough to prove non-compliance?**
- The documents don't say what evidence is needed or whether a photo is enough, so I can't answer that directly.
- The standard only covers mould and damp "caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo shows mould is present but not what caused it, so on its own it may not establish a breach.
- A condition report signed by both the provider and the renter is conclusive evidence of the state of repair on the day it specifies [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Its form encourages dated, labelled photos of the room [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What the renter can do

1. **Before signing:** Ask the provider or agent for the required disclosures. These are whether the property meets the minimum standards and whether there has been a mould or damp repair notice in the last 3 years [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **If you have not yet moved in:** You can end the agreement by giving notice on the ground that the premises "do not meet any rental minimum standards" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
3. **After moving in:** If the premises don't comply on or immediately after the day you move in, you may issue a request for urgent repairs to bring them up to the standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
4. **Condition report:** Record the mould in writing and with dated photos. A condition report is taken to be notice to the provider of any defects it states [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 4 says that if a renter lists something needing repair, it gives the provider written notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). It also says a renter can apply to VCAT if repairs aren't done within a reasonable time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Under the standard form agreement, VCAT can be asked to order non-urgent repairs if they aren't done within 14 days of notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
5. **Condition report correction:** You can apply to VCAT to amend an inaccurate condition report within 30 days after the agreement starts [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say how VCAT would weigh a photo, or whether it matters that a photo appeared in an ad. For that you would need other sources or advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal service.

must-mention.reason: All three points are covered. (1) The output quotes the standard that rooms 'must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'. (2) On the hardest point it says 'A photo shows mould is present but not what caused it, so on its own it may not establish a breach.' (3) It gives several next steps, including asking for disclosures before signing, ending the agreement before moving in, and requesting urgent repairs after moving in.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer makes neither forbidden claim, saying "I found no provision in these two documents that bans advertising a property with photos showing mould" and that a photo "on its own it may not establish a breach."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'version 110' (file rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf, link 97-109aa110) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as 'version 004' (file rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf, link 21-3sra004), both in force on 1 October 2025, and every rule it applies is sourced only from those versions.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
## What the law says

This is based on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115 (in force as at 13 October 2026, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf"). That version applies on 15 October 2026. I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 009 (30 June 2026, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf").

- **You need written consent to bring someone in as a sub-tenant.** A renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the rental provider's written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Without that consent, the arrangement is invalid.** This holds unless the Tribunal has decided consent isn't required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your rental provider can issue a notice to vacate to you.** This applies if you have assigned or sub-let, or purported to, without consent. The notice must give a termination date at least 14 days after it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations' summary says the same [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The notice must meet formal requirements.** It must be in the prescribed form, addressed to the renter and signed. It must also state the reason and the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **If you don't leave, VCAT decides.** The provider can apply to VCAT for a possession order. Providers can't personally use force to remove a renter, and only Victoria Police can carry out a forced eviction under a VCAT warrant [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

In practice, the main risk is to your own tenancy, because the notice would be addressed to you rather than your friend.

## What you can do or ask

**1. Removing your friend.** The documents I retrieved don't set out a process for a renter to remove a friend from the premises. They also don't say whether a friend staying with you counts as a "sub-let" or is just a guest. I can't say from these documents what steps you must take against your friend. VCAT or a community legal service (the Regulations point to the Consumer Affairs Victoria website and 1300 558 181) could advise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

**2. Dealing with your rental provider.**
- **Ask for consent if you want to keep the arrangement.** A provider must not unreasonably withhold consent, and can't charge a fee for giving it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If consent is refused, you can apply to the Tribunal for a determination that consent isn't required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Watch the consequences if you leave.** If your friend has been living there as their principal place of residence and isn't on the agreement, they can apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the provider to enter into an agreement with them. This is possible if you give a notice of intention to vacate, abandon the premises, or a possession order application has been made. The Tribunal must be satisfied of certain matters, including severe hardship to your friend [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

If you tell me whether the friend pays you rent and whether there is any written arrangement, I can look further. The documents may still not answer how to remove them.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The output says sub-letting requires the rental provider's written consent ('A renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the rental provider's written consent'). For the harder point, it frames the answer as depending on whether the friend 'counts as a "sub-let" or is just a guest' and names deciding facts: 'whether the friend pays you rent and whether there is any written arrangement.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer gives no fixed process for removing the friend ("I can't say from these documents what steps you must take against your friend"), does not suggest a lockout or that the friend has no rights, and limits the friend's VCAT application to listed situations ("if you give a notice of intention to vacate, abandon the premises, or a possession order application has been made"); the 14-day period applies only to the provider's notice to the renter.
