The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Authorised Version No. 115 (in force as at 13 October 2026, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf")" with links to 97-109aa115, and the only other source it relies on, the Regulations, is the in-force "version 009 (30 June 2026)" (21-3sra009), with no earlier or later version cited.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
**Document applied:** *rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 088, dated 2 July 2019. Its metadata shows it in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers 1 November 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The document labels this as version "088". I couldn't see an "Authorised Version No." line in the retrieved text.

The document also has endnotes with amending text that uses "renter" and "residential rental provider" and includes a section numbered 91ZZI. I've ignored those provisions. They are not the operative Part 6 text, and the retrieved text doesn't say when they start. The sections below come from the operative Part 6.

## What the law says

- **Landlord's repair duty.** A landlord must keep the rented premises in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **No-reason notice.** A landlord may give a notice to vacate without giving a reason (s 263(1)). For a tenancy other than a fixed term of more than 5 years, the termination date must be at least 120 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That is the figure for "any other tenancy agreement". The text also refers to a "prescribed period" for some periodic tenancies, and I couldn't see whether that applies to you.
- **Retaliation protection.** Under s 266(2), a notice under s 261 or s 263 "is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This covers the notice for the end of a fixed term (s 261) and the no-reason notice (s 263). I didn't see an equivalent clause in the retrieved text for the other grounds, such as s 255 (repairs) or s 258 (landlord or family to move in).
- **Time limit.** You can't apply to the Tribunal to challenge a s 263 notice "after the end of 60 days after the date on which the notice is given" (s 266(3)(c)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If the notice was given on 1 November 2019, that is about 31 December 2019. Check the exact counting and the date it was actually given, and don't leave it to the last day.

## What to check

1. **Which section the notice relies on.** Look at the reason on the notice. Section 266(2) expressly protects against s 261 and s 263 notices. If the notice cites s 263 (no reason), the retaliation protection applies directly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **The termination date.** A s 263 notice for your type of tenancy needs at least 120 days' notice, as above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Whether your repair request was an exercise of a right under the Act.** The Act gives you several repair rights:
   - the landlord's duty to maintain the premises (s 68) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf);
   - arranging urgent repairs yourself if you can't get the landlord or agent to act (s 72) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf);
   - after giving written notice of non-urgent repairs, applying to the Director if the landlord hasn't acted within 14 days (s 74) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf);
   - applying to the Tribunal over repairs (ss 73, 75–76) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   
   Check that your request, and any written notice, fits one of these. The retrieved text doesn't say whether a follow-up request counts, so treat that as something to confirm.
4. **Timing and evidence.** Your notice came the same day as your follow-up. Keep your dated repair requests, the notice, how and when it was delivered, and any replies. The Act doesn't say timing proves retaliation, but it is the obvious evidence of the link.
5. **Validity of the notice.** The contents list refers to s 319 (form of notice to vacate) and s 321A–321C (challenging a notice to vacate) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved text didn't include those sections, so I can't tell you the form requirements or what the Tribunal can order. Read them directly.

## What you can do or ask

- Apply to the Tribunal to challenge the notice, within the 60-day limit above, arguing it is of no effect under s 266(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Act's contents list also covers possession orders (Part 7) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't set out those provisions. A notice to vacate alone doesn't appear to put you out. A possession order would be a separate step.
- Pursue the repairs themselves. The Act provides for an urgent repairs application to the Tribunal, which must be heard within 2 business days (s 73), and for the Director route for non-urgent repairs (s 74) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you have given repair notice, you may also apply to pay rent into the Rent Special Account (s 77) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

The retrieved documents don't cover what a Tribunal would decide on your facts, or the definition of "urgent repairs" for leaking fixtures. Consider getting advice from a tenant advocacy or legal service before the deadline.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The hardest is the 120-day period, which the answer states as 'A s 263 notice for your type of tenancy needs at least 120 days' notice' despite noting a 'prescribed period' caveat. It also quotes s 266(2) that the notice 'is of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise... by the tenant of a right under this Act', and says the tenant can apply to the Tribunal to challenge it within 60 days.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never says the landlord needed a reason; it states 'A landlord may give a notice to vacate without giving a reason (s 263(1))'. The only challenge deadline it gives is 60 days ('after the end of 60 days after the date on which the notice is given'), and its 'about 31 December 2019' is the date that 60-day period ends, not a different deadline.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 088, dated 2 July 2019", links to 97-109aa088, and applies ss 263 and 266(2)–(3) from that in-force version, expressly setting aside the later 'renter' amending text.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
## What the law says

I've used the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110** (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it was in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025, so it applied on 1 October 2025.

- **Fixed advertised rent.** A rental provider or their agent must not advertise or offer premises unless the rent is advertised or offered as a fixed amount (s 30F(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Soliciting higher offers.** They must not "solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount" (s 30F(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Penalty.** Both rules carry 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading rent advertising.** Under s 30G, a provider or agent who promotes or advertises premises must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent. The same penalties apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Section 30G applies to providers and agents who are not acting in trade or commerce, and it does not limit the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Discrimination.** A provider must not refuse to let premises on the basis of a protected attribute (s 30A) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 3 gives examples, such as processing your application differently or not passing it to the provider because of an attribute [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**Limits of what I found:**
- Section 30F targets *soliciting or inviting* higher offers. The text I retrieved does not say that a higher offer someone made unprompted is unlawful, or that the property can't be relisted at a higher rent.
- Nothing I retrieved addresses an email wrongly saying an applicant "withdrew".
- So whether a rule was broken depends on facts you don't yet have. These include whether the agent invited offers above the advertised rent, and whether the withdrawal was a pretext.

## What you can do

1. **Raise a challenge based on s 30F and s 30G.** If the agent invited or encouraged higher offers, or the advertised rent was misleading, those sections are the relevant ones [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You can also ask the agent in writing to explain the "withdrawal" and to reinstate your application.
2. **Seek compensation if discrimination was involved.** If the withdrawal was because of a protected attribute, you can apply to the Tribunal (VCAT) for compensation for loss or damage under s 210AA, which covers contraventions of s 30A [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 3 gives VCAT's contact details (vcat.vic.gov.au, 1300 018 228) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). You can't use this route if you have already brought a dispute under Part 8 of the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 on the same facts [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You can also complain to VEOHRC (1300 292 153) or call Victoria Legal Aid (1300 792 387) for advice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **The general compensation route probably doesn't fit.** Section 210 is open to "a party to a residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). You never signed one, so it likely doesn't apply.

**Gaps in the documents:**
- They don't say who enforces the s 30F and s 30G offences, or how to make a complaint about them.
- They don't give a remedy that lets you take over the tenancy.
- They contain no list of what evidence to keep.

## What to save

The documents don't specify evidence. As a practical suggestion tied to the provisions above, keep:
- the original advertisement or listing, with screenshots showing the advertised rent and the new, higher rent, and the dates;
- your application and any confirmation of it;
- the "withdrawal" email, with full headers, and any related messages, calls or texts;
- anything showing the agent inviting offers above the advertised rent (for example "best offer", or messages asking applicants to offer more);
- anything suggesting the reason for the withdrawal, if you think discrimination was involved;
- a timeline of events.

Consider getting advice from Victoria Legal Aid before you take any step.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The answer says s 30F(3) bans soliciting or inviting offers above the advertised rent. It also says 'The text I retrieved does not say that a higher offer someone made unprompted is unlawful, or that the property can't be relisted at a higher rent', which covers both the relisting point and the unsolicited-offer point under the rubric's 'documents do not say' rule. Finally, it says 'Nothing I retrieved addresses an email wrongly saying an applicant "withdrew"'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three claims is made: the answer says 'The text I retrieved does not say that a higher offer someone made unprompted is unlawful, or that the property can't be relisted at a higher rent', and it notes the documents 'don't give a remedy that lets you take over the tenancy', offering only a written request to 'reinstate your application'.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Authorised Version No. 110" (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", link 97-109aa110) and relies on it for ss 30F and 30G. The only other document it cites is Form 3 via the link 21-3sra004, which is the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 Version 004, the version in force on 1 October 2025. No rule comes from a version that was not in force on that date.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** The agent's "no" doesn't settle it. Under the law in force on 15 October 2026, the owner can only block the dog by applying to VCAT within 14 days of getting your request. Three weeks have passed, so if no application was made, the owner is taken to have consented.

I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf"). That was the current version on 15 October 2026.

## What the law says

- **Consent or a Tribunal order is needed.** A renter may keep a pet if the provider consented in writing or the Tribunal has ordered that the pet is permitted [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The request must be in the approved form.** It must be in the form approved by the Director and be given to the residential rental provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **A provider must not unreasonably refuse.** Section 71C says so directly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Regulations repeat this in the standard agreement terms (Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, in force 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The 14-day rule.** The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days after being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal under section 71D [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That application asks for an order that refusing consent is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal factors.** The Tribunal can make an order only if it is satisfied that refusing is reasonable. It may consider the type of pet, the character and nature of the premises, the appliances, fixtures and fittings, whether an Act permits refusal, any prescribed matters, and any other matter it considers relevant [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Applying it to you

- **The refusal was probably not enough.** A refusal by the agent is not an application to VCAT. If the form was given to the provider and no application was lodged within 14 days, the deemed consent in section 71C(2) applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You are at 21 days.
- **The allergy and the owner's visits.** The documents don't say whether an owner's allergy is a reasonable ground for refusal. They don't say whether rare visits matter either. The only closest hook is the Tribunal's power to weigh "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I can't say how VCAT would decide this, and I found no prescribed matters in the retrieved text.
- **Giving the form to the agent.** The retrieved text says the request must be "given to the residential rental provider" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It doesn't say whether giving it to the agent counts, so I can't confirm that point.

## What you can do

1. **Check whether VCAT received an application.** Ask the agent in writing whether the owner applied under section 71D within 14 days of your request. If none was made, state in writing that you rely on the deemed consent under section 71C(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Keep your records.** Keep proof of the date you gave the approved form and the agent's refusal.
3. **Be aware the owner can still go to VCAT.** A provider who reasonably believes you are keeping a pet without consent can apply to have the pet excluded [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If the Tribunal orders the pet out, it must set a date the order takes effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Know the eviction pathway.** A notice to vacate for a pet can be given only if the Tribunal has ordered the pet excluded, at least 14 days have passed since the order took effect, and you haven't complied. The notice must give at least 28 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

This is general information from the retrieved documents, not legal advice. If a dispute starts, community legal services or VCAT can advise you.

must-mention.reason: Yes: all three points are covered. For the hardest point, the answer says "Three weeks have passed, so if no application was made, the owner is taken to have consented." It also states the 14-day deemed-consent rule and gives the next step "Ask the agent in writing whether the owner applied under section 71D within 14 days of your request."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the fail conditions is asserted: the answer says "The agent's 'no' doesn't settle it," puts the VCAT burden on the owner ("the owner can only block the dog by applying to VCAT within 14 days"), and leaves the allergy undecided ("The documents don't say whether an owner's allergy is a reasonable ground for refusal... I can't say how VCAT would decide this").

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026' (file 'rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf', links '97-109aa115') and applies rules only from that version and from the in-force 'Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 009, in force 30 June 2026' (link '21-3sra009'), with no other version relied on.

question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not immediately, but the notice stays in force until it is properly withdrawn. You also shouldn't ignore it.

I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", version 110, dated 6 August 2025). Its metadata shows it was in force from 6 August to 24 November 2025, so it covers 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf", version 004, dated 1 July 2025), in force 1 July to 24 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **The buyer pulling out doesn't cancel the notice.** A notice to vacate is withdrawn only if a written notice of withdrawal is given. It must be signed by the landlord and by you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZQ).
- **The landlord can't make you leave themselves.** Except as the Act allows, a landlord or their agent must not require or try to compel you to vacate. The penalty is 150 penalty units for a person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91P). Only Victoria Police can carry out a forced eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **If you stay past the termination date, the landlord must go to VCAT.** They can apply for a possession order once the notice is given, and up to 30 days after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (ss 322(1), 326(1)). VCAT can't decide the application before the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 329).
- **VCAT must be satisfied of several things before ordering you out.** These include that the landlord was entitled to give the notice, that the notice has not been withdrawn, and that an order is reasonable and proportionate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 330(1)(a), (f)). It must consider matters such as whether another course of action is reasonably available instead [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 330A).
- **The retrieved documents don't say whether a failed sale cancels the notice.** I found no provision saying a sale notice lapses automatically when the buyer withdraws. A sale notice must say the premises are to be "sold or offered for sale with vacant possession" immediately after the termination date, and must give at least 60 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZB). Whether that ground still holds after the buyer pulled out is for VCAT to decide.
- **If you do vacate on or after the termination date, your agreement ends** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91E).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord for a signed written withdrawal.** Both of you must sign it for it to count [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZQ). Get it in writing.
2. **Challenge the notice at VCAT.** You can apply to challenge its validity on or before the possession hearing. The application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (ss 91ZZS, 91ZZR). The notice form also says you can challenge validity if the landlord applies for a possession order [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **If a hearing happens, explain the changed circumstances.** You can ask VCAT for more time if you'd be in hardship [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **Consider leaving early if you want to.** For a sale notice, you can give a notice of intention to vacate with at least 14 days' notice, even during a fixed term [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZB(1)(a), (2), (3)); [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
5. **Know the 6-month rule.** If the landlord gets possession after a sale notice, they generally can't re-let the premises as a residence within 6 months of the notice date. The penalty is 150 penalty units for a person. There are exceptions, including where VCAT allows the letting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZH).

If the termination date is close, get advice from a community legal centre or Consumer Affairs Victoria. The notice form suggests this too [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers the 60-day minimum notice period, withdrawal only by a written notice signed by both landlord and renter (s 91ZZQ), and next steps (ask for a signed withdrawal, or challenge at VCAT within 30 days). It misses the first point: it never says the outcome depends on the ground stated in the notice and its supporting evidence, such as a planned sale with vacant possession versus a signed contract of sale. It only quotes 'sold or offered for sale with vacant possession' and then defers with 'Whether that ground still holds after the buyer pulled out is for VCAT to decide.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says "The buyer pulling out doesn't cancel the notice," that a withdrawal "must be signed by the landlord and by you," and that a sale notice "must give at least 60 days' notice" (the 14-day period it mentions is for the tenant's own notice of intention to vacate, not the landlord's notice), so it asserts none of the failing claims.
