question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

I applied the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Version 110 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", in force 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025), which was current on 1 October 2025. I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 004 (file "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf", incorporating amendments as at 1 July 2025). The Act excerpts I retrieved don't print the "Authorised Version No." line. The 110 comes from the document's version metadata and file name.

- **Notice is required.** A rental provider must give the renter at least 60 days notice, in the prescribed form, of a proposed rent increase (s 44(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **The form is Form 5.** The regulations prescribe the "Notice of Proposed Rent Increase to Renter of Rented Premises" (Form 5, Regulation 21) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). Form 5 says "A valid notice of a proposed rent increase is required for all rent increases" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **An increase without valid notice is invalid.** "A rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" (s 44(5)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Other limits:**
  - The rent can't be increased at intervals of less than 12 months (s 44(4A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
  - Under a fixed term agreement, the rent can't be increased before the term ends unless the agreement provides for it (s 44(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
  - One notice can cover only one increase (s 44(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Email delivery.** Form 5 lists email as a delivery method only "if consent has been provided by the renter" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## Do you have to pay the higher rent, and from when?

On your facts, an email from the agent with no Form 5 notice doesn't meet s 44. The documents say a non-compliant increase is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf), so you don't have to pay the higher rent. Keep paying your current rent.

There is no date from which the higher rent applies yet. The earliest it could start is at least 60 days after a valid notice is actually given to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The date also has to respect the 12-month gap and any fixed-term limits above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say whether the agent's email could itself count as a valid notice. That would only be so if it was in the Form 5 format and was properly delivered. They also don't say what happens to rent you've already paid at the higher amount.

## What you can do

- **Ask the agent for a proper notice.** The notice must be in Form 5. It must state the amount of the increase and how it was calculated, and it must tell you about your right to ask the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria to investigate (s 44(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Form 5 also has a field for the start date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenge a valid notice if you think it's excessive.** The agent refusing to negotiate doesn't stop you doing this.
  1. Apply in writing to the Director within 30 days after the notice is given (s 45) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). This is free [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
  2. You can then apply to VCAT within 30 days after receiving the Director's report (s 46) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
  3. If you skipped the Director and 30 days have passed, you can apply to VCAT directly, but only with VCAT's leave, and only if you have reasonable grounds for not going to the Director first (s 46(3)–(5)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **If you do challenge a valid notice, keep paying.** Form 5 says you must pay the increased rent from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes: all four points are covered. Form 5 is required, at least 60 days notice is stated (s 44(1)), and the next step is given as 'Keep paying your current rent.' The hardest point is covered by 'an email from the agent with no Form 5 notice doesn't meet s 44... a non-compliant increase is invalid, so you don't have to pay the higher rent.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the four failing claims is asserted: the answer says "you don't have to pay the higher rent. Keep paying your current rent" and "There is no date from which the higher rent applies yet", gives the notice period as "at least 60 days", and allows email delivery "if consent has been provided by the renter" (the only 'must pay the increased rent' statement is limited to challenging a valid notice).

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Version 110 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf")" with link 97-109aa110, and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "Authorised Version No. 004 (file "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf")" with link 21-3sra004; both were in force on 1 October 2025, and no rule is drawn from any other version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Sources:** I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", which is Version 115 and in force from 13 October 2026. That version was current on 15 October 2026. I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", Version 009, dated 30 June 2026.

## What the law says

- **Pet damage is the renter's responsibility.** A renter and any visitor must not intentionally or negligently damage the rented premises. Fair wear and tear doesn't count as damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether chewed skirting boards count as negligence rather than wear and tear is a judgment call. The documents don't answer it.
- **You must tell the owner in writing.** A renter who becomes aware of damage must give the rental provider written notice, as soon as practicable, of the damage and its nature [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Email is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard agreement says the same: where damage occurs, the renter must notify the rental provider in writing [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The standard form says repairs must be done by a suitably qualified person.** It says "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The owner can require you to repair or can do the repair and bill you.** The owner can give a written repair notice. It can require the renter to repair the damage at their own expense within 14 days. If it isn't repaired in a tradesman-like manner, the owner may repair it at the renter's expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The owner can claim the cost from your bond.** The owner can claim the reasonable cost of repairing damage caused by the renter or a visitor, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). At least 3 days before claiming the bond, the owner must give you bond claim evidence. That evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**So, can you fix it without telling the owner?** The documents don't say a renter is banned from repairing their own damage. But the Act requires written notice of damage, so staying silent is not an option [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A quiet fix also has risks. The work should be done by a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). If the owner or agent later sees a problem, they can still serve a repair notice or claim against the bond [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. Give the owner or agent written notice of the damage now.
2. Offer to arrange a suitably qualified person to repair it at your cost, and ask for their agreement. If they give you a repair notice, you have 14 days to repair it in a tradesman-like manner [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. Keep photos and receipts. The end-of-tenancy condition report is completed within 10 days after the agreement ends [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Insurance

**The documents I retrieved don't say whether this would affect the owner's insurance.** They contain nothing about landlord insurance. Please check the owner's policy or ask the owner or agent. For general guidance, you could ask Consumer Affairs Victoria.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers written notice 'as soon as practicable', says the documents 'don't say whether this would affect the owner's insurance', and gives next steps such as written notice and offering to repair. But the responsibility point is only partly covered: it says 'Pet damage is the renter's responsibility' and that fair wear and tear doesn't count, yet it never states that the renter must leave the home in the same condition as at the start (it only mentions the end-of-tenancy condition report and bond claims).

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the prohibited claims appear: the answer rejects a quiet repair ('staying silent is not an option'), states no insurance outcome ('The documents I retrieved don't say whether this would affect the owner's insurance'), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions: the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Version 115" (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", link 97-109aa115) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "Version 009" (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", link 21-3sra009). It relies on no rule from any other version.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
## What the law says

**There is no rule on the number of circuits.** Neither document sets a minimum number of circuits or says how many power points may share one. I searched both documents for this.

I applied the versions in force on 1 March 2023:
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 002** (incorporating amendments as at 1 June 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 101** (file `rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07`, in force 7 Sept 2022 to 23 May 2023). I took the "101" from the file's metadata, because the text I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

**Electrical rules that do exist:**
- **Electrical minimum standard, not yet in force.** Schedule 4, clause 9 of the Regulations requires all power outlets and lighting circuits to be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker and a residual current device. It applies only "on and from 29 March 2023", which is after your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). It is about protection devices, not how many circuits there are.
- **Duty to maintain.** The rental provider must keep the premises "in good repair" and "in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation" (s 68(1)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Anyone doing the repairs must be a suitably qualified person (s 68(4)) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Electrical safety checks.** The standard-form agreement requires a licensed or registered electrician to check the electrical installations, appliances and fittings the rental provider supplied every 2 years [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If no check was done in the 2 years before you moved in, the provider must arrange one as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say whether a breaker tripping when you run a kettle and heater together is a "defect". It may just be the breaker working as designed. I can't say from these documents whether your wiring breaches s 68.

## What you can ask for

1. **Give written notice.** You must tell the provider in writing as soon as practicable about damage or the breakdown of facilities or fixtures they supplied (s 72AA) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Ask for a repair.** Say that the circuit overloads under normal use and ask for it to be assessed and fixed under the s 68 duty [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask for the electrical safety check date.** The provider must give you the date of the most recent check in writing on request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). They must give you a copy of the most recent check within 7 days of your written request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Check it for any recommendations about the wiring.
4. **If nothing happens:**
   - **Director.** After 14 days from your written notice, you can apply to the Director to investigate non-urgent repairs (s 74) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
   - **VCAT.** You can also apply to VCAT for an order to carry out the repairs (s 75) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). VCAT must hear the application within 7 days of it being made [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Its orders can include specified repairs by a suitably qualified person and compensation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Urgent repairs.** If the repair is urgent, you can arrange it yourself after reasonable steps to get the provider to act. You must then give 7 days' written notice of the cost, and the provider must reimburse you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The reimbursement cap is $2,500 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The Act's definition of "urgent repairs" (s 3) wasn't in the retrieved text, so I can't say whether your problem qualifies.

You can't alter the wiring or fixtures yourself without the provider's written consent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered: the answer says 'There is no rule on the number of circuits', and as next steps it says to 'Ask for a repair' under s 68, covers urgent repairs, and says to ask for 'the date of the most recent check in writing on request'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer says 'There is no rule on the number of circuits' and describes the RCD/circuit breaker standard as 'not yet in force', applying only 'on and from 29 March 2023, which is after your date', so it asserts neither a minimum number of circuits nor that the standard applies on 1 March 2023.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 002 (incorporating amendments as at 1 June 2022)' and 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 101 (file rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07)', with links 21-3sra002 and 97-109aa101, and every rule it applies comes from those versions.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't say whether a rooming house operator can charge for coin-operated washing machines. They have no provision that expressly allows or bans it. They do set rules that apply if you are charged for services.

I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf". It is dated 13 October 2026 and its metadata says version 115. That is the version in force on 15 October 2026. I also used the *Residential Tenancies (Rooming House Standards) Regulations 2023*, file "rt-rooming-house-standards-regs-2023-v002-2024-12-01.pdf", dated 1 December 2024 (version 002). This is the only version I retrieved. I can't confirm from the documents that nothing later has replaced it.

## What the law says

- **Charges for services (s 109 of the Act).** If an operator charges for services, it must give you a separate schedule of the amounts before you take up residency. If you use those services, it must also give you an itemised account showing your individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Public and community housing (s 109A).** Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may charge for "laundry… services or facilities" in certain declared rooming houses. This applies only if it isn't possible or practicable to accurately measure your use. The charge can't exceed the cost of providing the facility [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal challenge under s 109A.** If the operator is one of those bodies, you can apply to the Tribunal to have the charge withdrawn or varied. You must be given written notice of the charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Separately metered rooms (s 108).** This section covers electricity, gas and water in separately metered rooms, not shared laundry machines. It doesn't apply to shared rooms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Minimum standard for laundries (reg 14).** Since 26 February 2024, a rooming house must have a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents. It must also have a wash trough or basin and a clothes line or other drying facility [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). Two machines would cover up to 24 residents. The regulation says nothing about whether use must be free.

## What you can do

1. **Ask for the schedule of service charges** and an itemised account of your use. The operator must give these if it charges for services [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Check your house rules and agreement.** Operators may make house rules about using facilities. They must be reasonable and enforced fairly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You can apply to the Tribunal for an order declaring a house rule unreasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
3. **Check who your operator is.** If it is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency, you can challenge a laundry charge at the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If it is a private operator, s 109A doesn't apply, and the documents don't say what else limits the charge.
4. **Report broken machines in writing.** The operator must keep facilities and equipment in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A breakdown of a laundering appliance the operator supplies counts as an urgent repair [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
5. **Watch for excessive charges.** If the operator ceases to provide a service, it must reduce your rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). An operator also can't withdraw facilities or stop you using them to push you out [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

For a firm answer on coin-operated charging, I'd contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal centre.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: reg 14 requires 'a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents'; the answer says 'The regulation says nothing about whether use must be free'; s 109 requires 'a separate schedule of the amounts before you take up residency'; and the next step is 'Ask for the schedule of service charges'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer avoids all three failure points, since it says the regulation 'says nothing about whether use must be free', states the documents 'do set rules that apply if you are charged for services', and limits the cost cap to Homes Victoria or registered housing agencies ('If it is a private operator, s 109A doesn't apply').

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'version 115' (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf) and the Rooming House Standards Regulations 2023 as 'version 002' (file rt-rooming-house-standards-regs-2023-v002-2024-12-01.pdf), and its other citation is to the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 via link 21-3sra009, which is version 009, the version in force on 15 October 2026.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
**Documents applied (both in force on 1 October 2025):**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf") [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 004, incorporating amendments as at 1 July 2025 (file "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)

## What the law says

**Advertising the photos.** I found no provision in these documents that bans advertising a property with photos that appear to show mould. The related rules I found are these:
- The provider must ensure the premises meet the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter moves in. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- Before the agreement is entered, the provider must disclose prescribed information. That includes whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. It also includes whether the provider received a repair notice in the last 3 years about mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- A provider or agent must not induce someone to enter an agreement through misleading or deceptive conduct. They must also not make a false or misleading representation about the characteristics of the premises. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) That rule is about misleading representations. It does not say that showing a defect in a photo is unlawful.
- The Act's false-advertising section covers representations about rent only. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

**Is the photo enough to prove a breach?** The documents don't say. The mould standard reads: "Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure." [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)
- The standard is tied to mould caused by or related to the building structure.
- My reading is that a photo may show mould is present but not its cause. This is my inference. The documents state no rule on whether a photo is sufficient proof.
- A condition report signed by both the provider and the renter is conclusive evidence of the premises' state of repair on the day stated. It does not apply to anything the renter disagreed with in writing. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter (or applicant) can do

- **Ask for the disclosures** above before signing. These cover compliance with the minimum standards and any mould or damp repair notice in the last 3 years. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **If you haven't moved in yet:** the agreement ends if you give the provider a notice of termination on the ground that the premises "do not meet any rental minimum standards". [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **If you have moved in and the premises don't comply:** you may issue a request for urgent repairs so the premises meet the standards. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Non-urgent repairs:** give written notice. If the provider hasn't done the repairs within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate. You can also apply to the Tribunal, which must hear the application within 7 days. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)
- **Evidence:** in a non-urgent repairs application, the Tribunal must consider whether the renter has provided documentary evidence of the repair. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) Keep your photos and notices.
- **Rent Special Account:** if you gave notice requiring repairs and the provider hasn't done them, you can ask the Tribunal to let you pay rent into this account. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

I can't tell you from these documents whether a specific ad breaks the law. That depends on the facts, such as the cause of the mould and whether the ad misrepresents the property.

must-mention.reason: Yes. The answer quotes the mould and damp standard ('Each room in the rented premises must be free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure'). On the hardest point it says 'a photo may show mould is present but not its cause' and 'The documents state no rule on whether a photo is sufficient proof.' It also gives next steps: ask for disclosures, end the agreement before moving in, and request urgent repairs after moving in.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer does not say the photo alone proves illegality (it says "a photo may show mould is present but not its cause" and "The documents state no rule on whether a photo is sufficient proof"), and it does not claim a ban on advertising non-compliant premises ("I found no provision in these documents that bans advertising a property with photos that appear to show mould").

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 110, incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025' (link 97-109aa110) and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 004, incorporating amendments as at 1 July 2025' (link 21-3sra004), and every rule it applies comes from those versions.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
I've assumed you are the renter and the agent acts for your rental provider.

**Document and version:** I relied on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" (version 115, in force from 13 October 2026). That is the version in force on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf" (version 009, in force from 30 June 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Consent:** You must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the rental provider's written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Validity:** An assignment or sub-letting without consent is invalid, unless the Tribunal has determined that consent isn't required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Risk to you:** If you have assigned or sub-let, or purported to, without consent, the rental provider can give you a notice to vacate. It must give a termination date at least 14 days after the notice is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice form:** The notice is only valid if it is in the prescribed form, addressed to you and signed. It must also state the reason and the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **If you don't leave:** The rental provider must give a notice to vacate before applying to VCAT for a possession order. Only Victoria Police can carry out a forced eviction, and only under a VCAT warrant [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask for consent:** The agent must not unreasonably withhold consent to sub-letting [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The agent can't charge a fee for giving consent, apart from reasonable expenses linked to an assignment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to the Tribunal:** If the agent refuses and you think that's unreasonable, you can apply to the Tribunal for a determination that consent isn't required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Challenge a notice:** If you receive a notice to vacate, you can raise its validity at the possession hearing. The Form 6 information sheet says you may also challenge a notice at VCAT if it wasn't given properly or the reason is wrong or incomplete [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- **Removing your friend:** I found nothing on how a renter makes a friend leave, such as notice periods or steps to take against an occupant. If you want them out, the documents don't tell you how.
- **Whether this is "sub-letting":** The documents don't say whether a friend who simply moves in, perhaps without paying rent, counts as sub-letting. A person on the premises with the renter's permission is defined as a "visitor" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether that applies here depends on facts I don't have.
- **Your friend's rights:** A person living in the premises as their main home who isn't on the agreement can apply to the Tribunal for their own agreement in some circumstances. These include when a possession order application has been made or the renter has given notice of intention to vacate. The Tribunal must be satisfied of several things, including severe hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

You may want to seek advice from a community legal organisation or Consumer Affairs Victoria, as the Form 6 information sheet suggests [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The output says the outcome depends on the arrangement and names payment as a deciding fact: "The documents don't say whether a friend who simply moves in, perhaps without paying rent, counts as sub-letting... Whether that applies here depends on facts I don't have." It also states that you must not sub-let "without the rental provider's written consent."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the four failure conditions is asserted: the answer says 'I found nothing on how a renter makes a friend leave, such as notice periods'; the only 14-day period applies to the rental provider's notice to the renter; it does not suggest a lockout or deny the friend rights; and it limits the friend's Tribunal application to 'some circumstances. These include when a possession order application has been made or the renter has given notice of intention to vacate.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'version 115, in force from 13 October 2026' (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115) and the Regulations as 'version 009' (link 21-3sra009); both are the versions in force on 15 October 2026, and every rule it applies is sourced only from them.

question: It is 1 November 2019. I followed up repairs to leaking fixtures and got a notice to vacate the same day. I am renting month to month. What should I check if I think the notice is retaliation for asking for repairs?
answer:
# Retaliatory notice to vacate (as at 1 November 2019)

I've relied on the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* in the file **rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf**. It is dated 2 July 2019 and is version **088**, with an in-force period of 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That covers 1 November 2019.

## What the law says

- **Repairs are a right under the Act.** The landlord must keep the premises in good repair (s 68) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can arrange urgent repairs yourself if the landlord or agent won't act (s 72) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For non-urgent repairs you give written notice, and if the landlord hasn't acted within 14 days you can apply to the Director to investigate (s 74) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can then order repairs (ss 75–76) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Retaliation protection.** A notice under s 261 or s 263 is "of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act" (s 266(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Which section applies to you.** Section 261 is for the end of a *fixed term* tenancy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You are month to month, so the relevant one is likely s 263, "Notice to vacate for no specified reason" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Time limit to challenge.** You cannot apply to the Tribunal to challenge a s 263 notice after 60 days from the date it was given (s 266(3)(c)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For a notice given on 1 November 2019, count the 60 days from that date.

## What to check

1. **Which ground the notice states.** The retaliation rule in s 266(2) names only ss 261 and 263 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A notice on another ground would need to be checked against that ground's own requirements. Some grounds allow a same-day termination date, including damage (s 243), danger (s 244) and condition of premises (s 245) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Condition of premises covers premises that are unfit for human habitation or destroyed or unsafe [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Other grounds need longer notice:
   - 14 days for non-payment of rent (s 246) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
   - 60 days for landlord repairs, demolition, sale and similar (ss 255–259) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **The notice period.** The retrieved text shows a period of "not less than 120 days" for "any other tenancy agreement" in the s 263 area [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The opening of s 263 was not in the extract, so I can't confirm the full wording. A notice that gives you far less than that is worth querying.
3. **Timing and evidence.** Gather proof that you asked for repairs: written notices, emails, texts and dates. Showing the notice came the same day you followed up supports the argument that it was "in response to" your exercise of a right [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Form of the notice.** The contents list shows s 319 (form of notice to vacate) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The text of that section was not retrieved, so I can't say what it requires.

## What you can do

- **Challenge the notice at the Tribunal within the 60 days** above, arguing it is of no effect under s 266(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Keep pursuing the repairs.** You can use the urgent-repairs route or the written-notice, Director and Tribunal route described above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You can also apply to pay rent into the Rent Special Account if you have given notice requiring repairs and the landlord has failed to carry them out (s 77) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Possession.** The contents list shows that possession orders are dealt with in Part 7 (ss 322 onwards) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The detailed text was not retrieved, so I can't say how a possession application would work for your notice.

## Limits of this answer

- The retrieved file also contains amending-Act wording in its endnotes that uses different terms ("renter", "residential rental provider") and has its own rules on retaliatory notices. I haven't applied it. It is not part of the operative sections I've cited, and the extracts don't show it was in force on 1 November 2019.
- The retrieved text of s 263, s 319 and ss 321A–321C (challenging a notice) is incomplete or missing, so check those sections before relying on this.
- This is a summary of the documents, not legal advice.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. The answer identifies s 263 'Notice to vacate for no specified reason' as applying to a month-to-month tenancy, with a period of 'not less than 120 days'. The caveat about the incomplete extract does not obscure the requirement. It quotes s 266(2), that the notice is 'of no effect if it was given in response to the exercise, or proposed exercise, by the tenant of a right under this Act'. It also states the tenant can 'Challenge the notice at the Tribunal within the 60 days'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the landlord needed to give a reason; it identifies the likely ground as s 263, "Notice to vacate for no specified reason". The only challenge deadline it gives is 60 days ("You cannot apply to the Tribunal to challenge a s 263 notice after 60 days from the date it was given"). The 14-day and 120-day figures refer to repair requests and notice periods, not to challenging the notice.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'version 088' in the file 'rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf' (link 97-109aa088), which was in force on 1 November 2019, rests on ss 263 and 266(2)–(3) of that version, and does not apply the later amending-Act 'renter' rules it mentions.

question: It is 1 October 2025. I applied for a rental at the advertised price, then got an email saying I had withdrawn even though I had not. The property is now listed at a higher rent, and I heard someone else offered more than the advertised price. Can I challenge what happened, and what should I save as evidence?
answer:
# Withdrawn rental application and a higher rent

The Act applies to your situation in some ways but not others. I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 110 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it was in force from 6 Aug 2025 to 24 Nov 2025, so it covers 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Fixed advertised rent.** A rental provider or their agent must advertise or offer premises at a fixed amount of rent. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 30F(1)).
- **No inviting higher offers.** They must not "solicit or otherwise invite an offer of an amount of rent that is higher than the advertised amount". The same penalties apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 30F(3)). This is the rule against rental auctions.
- **Misleading advertising.** A provider or agent promoting or advertising premises must not make a false or misleading representation about the rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 30G(2)). The section does not limit the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Misleading conduct.** A provider or agent must not induce someone to enter a rental agreement by misleading or deceptive conduct. This includes a false or misleading representation about "the rent payable under the agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 30E).
- **Holding deposits.** If you paid anything "as a sign of good faith", it must be refunded. If the agreement is not entered into within 14 days, the refund is due the next business day after that period [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 50).

**Limits of these provisions:**
- Section 30F(3) bans *soliciting or inviting* higher offers. The retrieved text does not say that an unsolicited higher offer, or relisting at a higher rent, is itself unlawful. Whether it breached the Act depends on whether the agent invited it.
- I found no provision in the retrieved text about an agent wrongly recording that an applicant "withdrew". That email may be evidence of the breaches above, but the documents don't make it a standalone breach.
- If you think you were treated differently because of a protected attribute, such as age, disability, race or having children, discrimination rules apply. The Act bars refusing to let premises on that basis [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 30A). The prescribed statement for applicants says VCAT compensation is available under s 210AA if you suffered loss [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Go to VCAT.** The Tribunal can hear matters about "a proposed residential rental agreement" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 446(a)). Since you have no agreement, you would need leave to apply, which requires an "interest and personal involvement" sufficient to justify it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 452(5), (7)). The Tribunal must also consider the Director's guidelines [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 452(9)).
2. **Dispute any holding deposit.** A person can apply to the Tribunal about any amount paid to a proposed rental provider under s 50 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 452(4)).
3. **Ask about remedies.** For a breach of s 30E, the Act notes that s 472(1A) sets out the Tribunal's orders. The text of s 472 was not in my results, so I can't say what orders are available. Offences under the Act can also lead to a listing on the Rental Non-compliance Register [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 439P). Whether a prosecution is brought isn't something the documents let me assess.
4. **Get advice.** The prescribed statement for rental applicants lists VCAT (1300 018 228) and Victoria Legal Aid (1300 792 387) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). It is in the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Version 004, in force from 1 July 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

## What to save as evidence

The documents don't list evidence to keep, so this is my practical suggestion based on what the provisions turn on:
- The original advertisement showing the advertised rent and date, and the new listing at the higher rent. Screenshots with dates are best.
- Your application and its submission confirmation, plus the "withdrawn" email with full headers and time stamp.
- All messages with the agent, including any reply to your query about the withdrawal and any mention of other offers or of "best offers".
- Proof of anything you paid, such as a holding deposit.
- Anything showing who told you about the higher offer. Evidence that the agent *invited* higher offers is what s 30F(3) turns on.

Please check these points with VCAT or Victoria Legal Aid, because the documents don't fully answer whether you can get a remedy as an unsuccessful applicant.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. The answer says s 30F(3) bans soliciting or inviting higher offers. On the hardest point it says "The retrieved text does not say that an unsolicited higher offer, or relisting at a higher rent, is itself unlawful. Whether it breached the Act depends on whether the agent invited it." This covers both the relisting point and the unsolicited-offer point. It also says it "found no provision in the retrieved text about an agent wrongly recording that an applicant 'withdrew'" and that the documents "don't make it a standalone breach."

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three failing claims is asserted. The answer says "The retrieved text does not say that an unsolicited higher offer, or relisting at a higher rent, is itself unlawful," and adds that a breach "depends on whether the agent invited it." It never claims the applicant can force the agent to rent the property to them.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Authorised Version No. 110 (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", incorporating amendments as at 6 August 2025)" and relies on ss 30F and 30G from it; its only other source, the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 "Version 004, in force from 1 July 2025", is also the version in force on 1 October 2025.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I sent the official request form to keep a dog in my apartment three weeks ago. The agent said no because the owner is allergic, but the owner hardly ever visits. Can they refuse?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the Act, the owner's allergy does not by itself let the agent refuse. A refusal only counts if the provider took the matter to VCAT within 14 days. Your request is now three weeks old.

*Source: Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 115, in force from 13 October 2026 (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf"). This is the version in force on 15 October 2026.*

## What the law says

- **Request:** You must ask in the form approved by the Director and give it to the residential rental provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **No unreasonable refusal:** The provider "must not unreasonably refuse" consent to a pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **14-day deadline:** The provider is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal under s 71D [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Refusing, or having the agent say no, is not an application to the Tribunal.
- **Provider's remedy:** The provider can ask the Tribunal for an order that refusal is reasonable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The Tribunal may then order that you can keep the pet. If it is satisfied refusal is reasonable, it may instead order that refusal is reasonable and exclude the pet [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Allergy:** The Tribunal's listed factors are the type of pet, the character of the premises, the appliances, fixtures and fittings, whether refusal is permitted under any Act, and prescribed matters. It may also consider "any other matter the Tribunal considers relevant" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text does not mention allergies or how often an owner visits, so I can't say whether this refusal would be found reasonable. That is the Tribunal's decision.

## What you can do

1. **Check whether VCAT proceedings were started.** If the provider made no s 71D application within 14 days of receiving your request, they are taken to have consented [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The agent's "no" does not change that. Ask the agent in writing whether any Tribunal application was lodged, and when.
2. **Be aware of the "in writing" wording.** Section 71A says a renter may keep a pet if the provider consented in writing or the Tribunal has ordered it. Its note says the provider is taken to have consented if no application is made within 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It would be sensible to ask for written confirmation.
3. **If the provider applies later,** they can ask the Tribunal to exclude a pet they reasonably believe is being kept without consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). You would then be heard on the reasonableness of the refusal.
4. **Know the risk.** A notice to vacate for a pet is only available if the Tribunal has made an exclusion order, at least 14 days have passed since it took effect, and you haven't complied. The notice must give at least 28 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## Gaps in the documents

- **Timing:** Your request was sent about 24 September 2026, so the 14-day window ended around 8 October, before Version 115 started on 13 October. The documents I retrieved only include Version 115. I have no earlier version to check whether the rules were the same during that window.
- **Delivery to the agent:** Section 71B says the request must be given "to the residential rental provider" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether giving it to the agent counts, because the rules on giving documents were not retrieved.
- **Regulations:** The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", dated 30 June 2026, metadata version 009) contain a standard-form summary. It says the provider "must not unreasonably refuse a request to keep a pet" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). It adds no further test for allergies.

This is general information from the retrieved documents, not legal advice. Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service could help you check whether VCAT proceedings were started.

The answer says the provider "is taken to have consented unless, within 14 days of being given the request, they apply to the Tribunal under s 71D." It applies this to the three-week-old request ("A refusal only counts if the provider took the matter to VCAT within 14 days. Your request is now three weeks old"). It gives a next step: "Ask the agent in writing whether any Tribunal application was lodged, and when."
