question: It is 1 October 2025. Our landlord gave us a notice to vacate because they were selling. The buyer pulled out, but the landlord hasn't withdrawn the notice. Do we still have to leave?
answer:
# Do you still have to leave after the buyer pulled out?

**Short answer:** Probably yes, unless the notice is withdrawn in writing or successfully challenged. The documents don't say that a failed sale cancels the notice automatically.

I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* ("rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", version 110, dated 6 August 2025). Its metadata shows it in force from 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025, so it covers 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* ("rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf", version 004, dated 1 July 2025), also in force on that date [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The excerpts don't show an "Authorised Version No." label, so I've given the version numbers from the file names and metadata.

## What the law says

- **Why the notice was allowed.** A landlord can give a notice to vacate if the premises are, immediately after the termination date, to be sold or offered for sale with vacant possession. The notice must give at least 60 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZB(1), (4)).
- **A notice stays in effect until it is withdrawn.** It is withdrawn only if a written notice of withdrawal is given. That notice must be signed by the landlord and by you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZQ). The buyer pulling out does not do this, and the landlord's silence is not a withdrawal.
- **The landlord can't make you leave.** A landlord must not require or try to compel you to vacate except in accordance with the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91P). They must apply to VCAT for a possession order. The application can be made any time after the notice is given, up to 30 days after the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 322(1), s 326(1)). VCAT can't decide it before the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 329).
- **VCAT's test.** It must make a possession order if it is satisfied of several things [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 330(1)):
  - the landlord was entitled to give the notice;
  - the notice has not been withdrawn; and
  - it is reasonable and proportionate to make the order, taking into account the interests of both sides.
- **If you move out.** The agreement ends if you vacate on or after the termination date in the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91E(1)).

**A gap in the documents:** They don't say whether a collapsed sale makes a s 91ZZB notice invalid. The wording of s 91ZZB(1) only requires that the premises be "sold or offered for sale" after the termination date. A landlord who re-lists the property may therefore still be entitled to the notice. That is my reading of the text, not something the documents state.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask the landlord to withdraw the notice.** It only counts if it is in writing and signed by both of you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZQ).
2. **Challenge the notice at VCAT.** You can apply to challenge a sale notice's validity on or before the possession hearing, but the application must be made within 30 days after the notice was given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZS). If that deadline has passed, the documents don't say whether you can still challenge. VCAT can also reconsider a valid-notice finding only in exceptional circumstances [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZT(2)).
   - Possible grounds are that the notice wasn't in the prescribed form, wasn't signed, or didn't give a reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZO).
   - Another is that it lacked the required documentary evidence [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZO(e)).
   - A sale notice is also of no effect if giving it would be direct discrimination [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZI(2)).
3. **Attend the possession hearing and make your case.** VCAT will only order you out if that is reasonable and proportionate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 330(1)(f)). The prescribed notice form says you can ask for more time if you would be in hardship. It also says only Victoria Police, acting on a VCAT warrant, can forcibly evict you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
4. **Leave early if you choose.** For a sale notice, you can give a notice of intention to vacate with at least 14 days' notice, instead of waiting for the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZB(1)(a), (2), (3)); [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
5. **Resale protection.** If the landlord gets possession under a sale notice, they can't re-let the premises as a residence within 6 months of the notice date. There are exceptions, including a Tribunal determination that the premises may be let. The penalty is 150 penalty units for an individual [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf) (s 91ZZH). This is relevant if the sale was a pretext.

The prescribed notice form also recommends seeking advice if you think you have grounds to challenge. It lists Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 558 181 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers the 60-day minimum ('must give at least 60 days'), written withdrawal signed by both landlord and renter (s 91ZZQ), and next steps (ask for a signed written withdrawal, or challenge at VCAT within 30 days). It misses the first point: it never says the outcome depends on which ground and evidence the notice relied on (a planned sale with vacant possession versus a signed contract of sale), and instead treats the notice as resting on a single 'sold or offered for sale' ground.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says none of the three, stating that "The buyer pulling out does not do this", that a withdrawal "must be signed by the landlord and by you", and that the notice "must give at least 60 days" (the 14 days refers only to the tenant's own notice of intention to vacate).

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'version 110, dated 6 August 2025' ('rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf', link 97-109aa110) and the Regulations as 'version 004, dated 1 July 2025' (21-3sra004), both in force on 1 October 2025, and it relies on no other version for any rule it applies.

question: It is 1 October 2025. My agent emailed to say the rent is going up. I tried to negotiate and they said no, but I never got an official rent increase notice. Do I have to pay the higher rent, and from when?
answer:
## What the law says

I've used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 004, incorporating amendments as at 1 July 2025). Both were in force on 1 October 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). The Act's text that I retrieved doesn't print an "Authorised Version No." heading. The file metadata labels it version 110, in force 6 August 2025 to 24 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

- **Notice is required.** A rental provider must give you at least 60 days' notice, in the prescribed form, of a proposed rent increase (s 44(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **The notice has set contents.** It must state the amount of the increase, the method used to calculate it, and your right to ask the Director of Consumer Affairs to investigate within 30 days (s 44(3)). It can cover only one increase (s 44(2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **The prescribed form is Form 5** (Regulation 21). It says a valid notice is required for all rent increases [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). It lists email as a delivery method only "if consent has been provided by the renter" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- **An increase without a valid notice is invalid.** Under s 44(5), "a rent increase in contravention of this section is invalid" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Other limits apply.** Rent can't be increased at intervals of less than 12 months (s 44(4A)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). In a fixed-term agreement, it can't be increased before the term ends unless the agreement provides for it by a specified amount or calculation method (s 44(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## Applied to your situation

- **Do you have to pay the higher rent?** Based on what you've told me, no. If you have only an email and no notice in the prescribed form, the increase doesn't meet s 44 and is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). I haven't seen the email, so I can't say whether it was in fact a Form 5 notice. The agent's refusal to negotiate doesn't change the notice requirement.
- **From when?** No date applies yet, because no valid notice has been given. If a valid notice is given later, the increase can't start until at least 60 days after it is given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). It must also respect the 12-month gap and any fixed-term restrictions above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Ask the agent in writing** for a Form 5 notice, or confirm that the email was one. Check that it includes the amount, the calculation method, a start date at least 60 days away, and the 30-day investigation right [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
2. **If a valid notice arrives and you think the rent is excessive:**
   - You can apply in writing to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria within 30 days after the notice is given (s 45). This is free [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
   - After receiving the Director's report, you can apply to VCAT within 30 days for an order declaring the rent excessive (s 46) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
   - If you haven't asked for a report and 30 days have passed, you can apply to VCAT directly, but you need its leave and must show reasonable grounds (s 46(3)–(5)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
   - Form 5 says you must pay the increased rent from the date on the notice unless VCAT decides otherwise [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
3. **VCAT's test.** It must declare the rent excessive if it is more than a renter should reasonably pay. It considers comparable premises, the condition of the property, and the number and timing of increases in the past 24 months, among other factors (s 47(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## Not covered

The retrieved documents don't say whether paying the higher rent in the meantime affects your rights. They also don't say what happens if you withhold the increase. I can't answer those from these sources.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered: Form 5 as the prescribed form, at least 60 days' notice, the next steps of asking the agent in writing and applying to the Director of Consumer Affairs within 30 days, and the hardest point, invalidity, stated clearly despite a minor caveat: 'Based on what you've told me, no. If you have only an email and no notice in the prescribed form, the increase doesn't meet s 44 and is invalid.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes, none of the fail conditions are asserted: the answer says the renter does not have to pay ("Based on what you've told me, no"), says "No date applies yet, because no valid notice has been given", gives a 60-day minimum ("at least 60 days' notice"), and allows email delivery "if consent has been provided by the renter".

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Act by its file name and version, "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025, with the link 97-109aa110, and names the Regulations as "Authorised Version No. 004, incorporating amendments as at 1 July 2025" (link 21-3sra004); both were in force on 1 October 2025, and no rule is drawn from any other version.

question: It is 15 October 2026. Our dog chewed the skirting boards. We're moving out soon. Can we just get someone to fix it quickly without telling the owner? Would it affect the owner's insurance on the property?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't support fixing it quietly without telling the owner. They don't address insurance at all.

*Sources: Residential Tenancies Act 1997, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf" (version 115, in force from 13 October 2026), and Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf" (version 009, in force from 30 June 2026). Both were in force on 15 October 2026. The files show a version number but not the words "Authorised Version No.", so I've given the version numbers as they appear.*

## What the law says

- **Damage:** A renter must not intentionally or negligently damage the rented premises. Fair wear and tear is not "damage" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Whether chewing by a dog counts as negligent damage or fair wear and tear isn't decided in the documents.
- **Telling the owner:** A renter who becomes aware of damage must give the rental provider written notice as soon as practicable. The notice must say that the damage happened and what it is [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Section 72AA says the same. Email is allowed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Who does repairs:** The standard-form agreement summary says "Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs—both urgent and non-urgent" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). A "suitably qualified person" includes a registered or licensed tradesperson where the work requires it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Leaving the property:** At the end of the tenancy, the renter must leave the premises in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your possible liability:**
  - **Bond:** The owner can claim from the bond the reasonable cost of repairing or restoring damage caused by the renter, taking fair wear and tear into account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Before claiming the bond, the owner must give you their supporting evidence at least 3 days ahead. That evidence must not conflict with the condition report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - **Repair notice:** The owner can also give a written repair notice. It can require you to repair the damage at your expense within 14 days, in a tradesman-like manner. If you don't, the owner can repair it at your expense [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Alternatively, the owner can say they will do the repairs and you are liable for the reasonable cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do

1. **Give written notice now.** Email is fine. Describe the skirting board damage [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
2. **Offer to arrange the repair, but ask the owner or agent first.** If you hire someone, the documents point to a suitably qualified person [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). They don't say you may skip telling the owner. Asking first also avoids a dispute over whether the work was done properly.
3. **If you get a repair notice and can't pay on time:**
   - You must reimburse the owner within 14 days after the repairs are finished [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - You can apply to the Tribunal for an extension if you can't pay and the owner won't agree to longer [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
   - If you're experiencing hardship, you can give written notice that you need an additional 14 days. You must provide proof of hardship if the owner asks [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
4. **Protect yourself at checkout.** The owner or agent must complete the final inspection within 10 days after the agreement ends. They must give you a chance to attend if possible [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The form also advises taking photos at the start and end of the tenancy [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

## Insurance

The retrieved documents don't say anything about how repairs or undisclosed damage affect the owner's insurance. I won't guess. Check the owner's policy with the owner or their insurer, or get independent advice.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are covered. (1) The answer says the renter 'must give the rental provider written notice as soon as practicable.' (2) It states renter liability for damage, excluding fair wear and tear: 'claim from the bond the reasonable cost of repairing or restoring damage caused by the renter, taking fair wear and tear into account' and 'repair the damage at your expense.' It also says the renter 'must leave the premises in the same condition as when they moved in, allowing for fair wear and tear.' Point 2 is the hardest: the answer hedges on whether dog chewing counts as negligent damage, but its liability section and next steps make clear the renter should expect to cover it. (3) It says 'The retrieved documents don't say anything about how repairs or undisclosed damage affect the owner's insurance.' (4) It gives next steps: 'Give written notice now' and 'Offer to arrange the repair, but ask the owner or agent first.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the three fail conditions appear: the answer rejects a quiet repair ("The documents don't support fixing it quietly without telling the owner"), declines to state any insurance outcome ("The retrieved documents don't say anything about how repairs or undisclosed damage affect the owner's insurance. I won't guess"), and never says the renter must pay the owner's insurance excess.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 115" (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", links "97-109aa115") and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "version 009" (file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", links "21-3sra009"), both in force on 15 October 2026, and relies on no other version.

question: It is 1 March 2023. Most of the power points in my rental are on one circuit, and the breaker trips when we run the kettle and the heater together. Is there a rule about how many circuits a rental needs, and what can I ask for?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I retrieved don't set a minimum number of circuits for a rental. They also don't say how many power points can share a circuit.

## What the law says

- **Electrical rule (not yet in force).** The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 002, incorporating amendments as at 1 June 2022) have a rental minimum standard on electrical safety. It applies "on and from 29 March 2023". From then, all power outlets and lighting circuits must be connected to a switchboard-type circuit breaker complying with AS/NZS 3000 and to a switchboard-type residual current device (RCD) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Today is 1 March 2023, so this standard isn't operative yet. Even once it is, it covers protective devices, not how many circuits there are [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **General repair duty.** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 101, as at 7 September 2022) requires the rental provider to keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs.** The Act's definition includes a "dangerous electrical fault", a failure or breakdown of the electricity supply, and a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a breaker tripping from overload counts as a "dangerous electrical fault".

## What you can ask for

1. **Electrical safety check records.** The rental provider must have an electrical safety check done every 2 years by a licensed or registered electrician. They must give you the date of the most recent check in writing if you ask [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If no check was done in the last 2 years when you moved in, they must arrange one as soon as practicable [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). You can also ask in writing for a copy of the most recent check. It must be provided within 7 days of the provider receiving your request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **A repair request in writing.** The standard-form agreement says to notify the rental provider in writing of urgent repairs. For non-urgent repairs, it says the provider must act in a reasonable time. You can apply to VCAT if the repairs aren't done within 14 days of your notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Urgent repairs, if it is one.** If the problem is an urgent repair, the standard-form agreement summarises your options. You can arrange the repair yourself if the provider doesn't act, and be reimbursed up to $2500. You can apply to VCAT if you can't meet the cost, the cost is over $2500, or the provider refuses to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Only a suitably qualified person may do repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

## Gaps in the documents

- The documents don't say that adding circuits can be required.
- The retrieved text doesn't include the full urgent-repairs sections of the Act, so I've relied on the summary in the standard form.
- Because the electrical minimum standard starts on 29 March 2023, you can't yet rely on it for this issue.

The output says "The documents I retrieved don't set a minimum number of circuits for a rental", which covers the no-rule point under the rubric's 'documents do not say' allowance. For next steps, it recommends asking for "the date of the most recent check in writing" and making "A repair request in writing", with urgent repairs if the fault qualifies.

The answer does not set a minimum number of circuits or say that sharing one is illegal; it states "The documents I retrieved don't set a minimum number of circuits for a rental." It also says the breaker and RCD standard applies "on and from 29 March 2023" and that "this standard isn't operative yet."

Its links (97-109aa101 and 21-3sra002) match these versions, and it relies on no other version for any rule it applies.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I live in a rooming house and the two washing machines are coin-operated. Are they allowed to charge us to use them?
answer:
## What the law says

**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether a rooming house operator may charge for coin-operated washing machines. Nothing I found expressly allows or bans it. The rules below are the closest ones.

I used the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115. It is in force from 13 October 2026, so it was current on 15 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The file's metadata gives "version 115". I can't see a separate "Authorised Version No." label in the extracts.

- **Schedule and itemised account (s 109).** If an operator charges for services, it must give the resident a separate schedule of the amounts for those services before the resident takes up the room. If the resident uses any of those services, the operator must also provide an itemised account of the resident's individual use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
  - The Act doesn't say whether a coin-operated machine counts as a "service". It does list "laundry facilities" within "facilities" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Charges on metered rooms (s 108).** An operator may charge separately for electricity, gas and water used in a room, but only if the operator pays the bills and the room is separately metered. The charge can't exceed the supplier's charge. This doesn't apply to shared rooms [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). It covers utilities in your room, not shared laundry machines.
- **Public and community housing (s 109A).** Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency may impose a service charge for "laundry… services or facilities". This applies only to rooming houses declared under s 19(2) or (3), and only where it isn't possible or practicable to accurately measure the resident's use. The charge can't exceed the cost of providing the facility [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Access and repair (ss 121 and 120).** Operators must give access to other facilities during all reasonable hours [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). They must also keep any facilities and equipment they provide in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Laundry standard.** The *Rooming House Standards Regulations 2023* (version 002, dated 1 December 2024) require, from 26 February 2024, a washing machine in good working order for every 12 or fewer residents. They also require a wash trough or basin and a clothes line or other drying facility [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-11/23-10sra002-authorised.pdf). This text says nothing about charging. I can't confirm from the retrieved material that this was the latest version on 15 October 2026.

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask for the schedule of charges.** If the operator charges for services, ask for the separate schedule of amounts, and for an itemised account of your use [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the house rules.** Operators may make house rules about using facilities. They must be reasonable and enforced consistently and fairly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). A resident may apply to the Tribunal for an order declaring a house rule unreasonable, and the Tribunal may declare it invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **If the operator is Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency,** you may apply to the Tribunal to have a laundry service charge withdrawn or varied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Report faults.** Tell the operator about any breakdown of the machines [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The operator must keep them in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't settle whether a coin charge is lawful in your house. It may depend on who the operator is and on your agreement and house rules, so I'd get those documents first.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All four points are present. The hardest one, that charges must be set out in a schedule given before moving in, is covered by: 'it must give the resident a separate schedule of the amounts for those services before the resident takes up the room.' The answer also states the one-machine-per-12-residents standard, says nothing found expressly allows or bans charging, and advises 'Ask for the schedule of charges.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never says the machines must be free or that there are no rules on charges (it cites s 109's schedule and itemised-account requirements), and it limits the cost cap, saying it "applies only to rooming houses declared under s 19(2) or (3)" run by Homes Victoria or a registered housing agency and "can't exceed the cost of providing the facility."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 115" (file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", link 97-109aa115), and the Rooming House Standards Regulations 2023 as "version 002, dated 1 December 2024" (link 23-10sra002). Both are the versions in force on 15 October 2026, and every rule it applies comes from those versions.

question: It is 1 October 2025. The photos in a rental ad look like they show mould in one of the bedrooms. Are they allowed to advertise it like that, and is the photo enough to prove the place doesn't meet the minimum standards?
answer:
# Mould in a rental ad: advertising and minimum standards (as at 1 October 2025)

**Documents used.** Both were in force on 1 October 2025.
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version No. 004, as at 1 July 2025 (file "rt-regs-2021-v004-2025-07-01.pdf") [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf", dated 6 August 2025. Its metadata gives the version as 110. The excerpts I retrieved don't show the "Authorised Version No." wording itself [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

**1. Is the advert allowed?** The documents I retrieved don't contain a rule that bans advertising a property because the photos show mould, so I can't say it is either allowed or prohibited on that ground alone. These provisions are relevant:
- A rental provider must ensure the premises meet the prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day the renter enters occupation. The penalty is 60 penalty units for a natural person and 300 for a body corporate [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The duty is tied to move-in day, not to the advert.
- A provider or agent must not induce someone to enter an agreement through misleading or deceptive conduct. They must also not make a false or misleading representation about the "characteristics of the premises". The same 60 and 300 penalty units apply. This section applies to providers (and their agents) who are not acting in trade or commerce, and it doesn't limit the Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- Before the agreement is signed, the provider must disclose prescribed information. That includes whether the premises comply with the rental minimum standards. It also includes whether a repair notice about mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure was received in the last 3 years [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

**2. Is the photo enough to prove non-compliance?** The documents don't say what evidence is needed, so they can't confirm that a photo is enough. What they do say is this:
- The mould standard is that "each room" must be "free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf). A photo of apparent mould shows the mould, but not on its face that it was caused by or related to the building structure. The documents don't say how that is proved.
- The standards are checked against the premises at move-in. A photo in an ad may not reflect the current condition.
- A condition report signed by both the provider and the renter is conclusive evidence of the state of repair on the day it specifies. A condition report given to the provider counts as notice of any defects it lists [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). These are the formal ways to record the problem.

## What the renter can do or ask

- **Ask before signing.** Ask whether the premises meet the rental minimum standards, and whether there has been a repair notice about mould or damp in the last 3 years. The provider must disclose both [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Walk away before moving in.** A renter who hasn't yet taken possession can end the agreement by notice if the premises "do not meet any rental minimum standards" or "are not in good repair" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Request urgent repairs after moving in.** If the premises don't meet the standards on or immediately after the day the renter moves in, the renter may request urgent repairs to bring them up to standard [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Record it on the condition report.** Note the mould in the condition report. A report given to the provider counts as notice of the defect [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).
- **Rely on the general repair duty.** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

The documents I retrieved don't cover how to challenge the advert itself, such as a complaint process. They also don't cover what evidence would prove non-compliance in a dispute.

must-mention.reason: Yes. The answer gives the standard that each room must be 'free from mould and damp caused by or related to the building structure' and lists several next steps (ask before signing, end the agreement before moving in, request urgent repairs). For the hardest point it says the documents 'can't confirm that a photo is enough' because 'A photo of apparent mould shows the mould, but not on its face that it was caused by or related to the building structure.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the photo alone proves illegality or that a ban on advertising non-compliant properties applies; instead it states "The documents I retrieved don't contain a rule that bans advertising a property because the photos show mould, so I can't say it is either allowed or prohibited on that ground alone" and "they can't confirm that a photo is enough."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as version 110 ('rta-1997-v110-2025-08-06.pdf', link 97-109aa110, dated 6 August 2025) and the Regulations as 'Authorised Version No. 004, as at 1 July 2025' (link 21-3sra004), and relies on no other versions.

question: It is 15 October 2026. I let a friend move into my rental without telling the agent. Now I want them out. What do I have to do?
answer:
**Documents used:** the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf", version 115, in force from 13 October 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v009-2026-06-30.pdf", version 009, dated 30 June 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf). The Act version was the one in force on 15 October 2026. The retrieved text doesn't print the words "Authorised Version No.", so I'm taking the version numbers from the file names and metadata.

## What the law says

- **You need written consent.** A renter must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the rental provider's written consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **The arrangement is invalid without consent.** An assignment or sub-letting without consent is invalid, unless the Tribunal has determined that consent isn't required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **You could get a notice to vacate.** If you have assigned, sub-let, or "purported to" do so without consent, the rental provider may give you a notice to vacate. It must give at least 14 days' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). The standard-form agreement says the same [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).
- **The notice must be valid.** It must be in the prescribed form, addressed to you, signed, and give the reason and the termination date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- **Your friend may have a route to stay.** A person who lives in the premises as their principal place of residence and isn't a party to the agreement can apply to the Tribunal for their own agreement with the rental provider. They can do this if a possession order has been applied for, or if you have abandoned the premises, handed back vacant possession, or given a notice of intention to vacate. The Tribunal can order this only if the friend could be expected to comply with a renter's duties, would suffer severe hardship if forced out, and that hardship would be greater than the rental provider's [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask your friend to leave.** The documents give no step-by-step process for a renter removing someone they let in, so I can't tell you more than this.
2. **Think about telling the agent.** If you ask for consent, the rental provider can't unreasonably withhold it or charge a fee for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). If they refuse and you think that's unreasonable, you can apply to the Tribunal for a determination that consent isn't required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). That only helps if you wanted the friend to stay, so it doesn't fit your goal.
3. **Be careful about timing.** Giving your own notice of intention to vacate or handing back possession could trigger your friend's right to apply to the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't answer

- They don't say whether a friend moving in, especially one who pays no rent, counts as "sub-letting" under these provisions. That decides whether the notice-to-vacate risk applies to you.
- They don't set out any procedure or power for a renter to evict a non-party occupant.

For those points, check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a community legal service. The form in the Regulations lists these as sources of advice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Both points are covered. On written consent, the answer says a renter 'must not assign or sub-let the whole or any part of the premises without the rental provider's written consent'. On the hardest point, it makes the outcome depend on the arrangement and names payment as a deciding fact: whether a friend 'especially one who pays no rent, counts as "sub-letting"... That decides whether the notice-to-vacate risk applies to you.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. None of the failing claims are made: the answer says "The documents give no step-by-step process for a renter removing someone they let in", applies the 14-day notice only to the rental provider's notice to the renter, never suggests a lockout or removing belongings, and says the friend "may have a route to stay" only in listed situations ("if a possession order has been applied for, or if you have abandoned the premises, handed back vacant possession, or given a notice of intention to vacate").

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 115, in force from 13 October 2026" (file rta-1997-v115-2026-10-13.pdf, link 97-109aa115), which is the version in force on 15 October 2026; it also relies on the Regulations "version 009, dated 30 June 2026", which is the in-force version, and it relies on no other version.
